# Conservation of Endangered Plants in Urban Fire-Prone Habitats

## Tony D. Auld and Judith Scott

*New South Wales National Parks and Wildlife Service, PO Box 1967, Hurstville N.S.W. 2220, Australia*
*Tel. +61 02 9585 6497; Fax +61 02 9585 6495; E-mail tauld@pws.nsw.gov.au*

**Abstract.** A number of endangered plant species occur in National Parks and associated bushland that are adjacent to urban areas in the Sydney Region of south-eastern Australia. Within these areas fire is a repeated and frequent disturbance event that potentially threatens not only the endangered flora but life and property as well. These threats were well illustrated by the impact of the fires that occurred in January 1994 in Sydney.
For the management of such fire-prone areas there is a need to identify those fire regimes likely to drive the endangered flora to extinction. Management of fire-sensitive, threatened *Darwinia* (Myrtaceae) and *Grevillea* (Proteaceae) species illustrates how conservation goals can be applied along with protection of life and property. A regime of frequent fire will lead to local population declines and extinction in both *Darwinia* and *Grevillea* species. Consequently, frequent burning on a regular basis for hazard reduction to protect property assets is inappropriate for the conservation of these species. *Darwinia* species also require fires that cause significant soil heating (high consumption of fine fuel) to break seed dormancy in soil stored seed, while *Grevillea* species require fires of a large spatial extent to minimise the impact of mammalian seed predators on seed outputs from the first few seed-crops produced by plants after a fire.

**Keywords:** Fire regime; Threatened species; *Darwinia*; *Grevillea*

## Introduction

In the Sydney Region of southeastern Australia, much of the vegetation is highly flammable and fires are a common and frequent event. For example, during January of 1994, some 90% and 65% respectively of the two major, large urban reserves (Royal and Ku-ring-gai Chase National Parks) were burnt. In this rich and diverse floristic area, around 2000 plant species regularly experience fire. As a consequence, the management of fire is one of the principal challenges facing managers of natural ecosystems in the Sydney Region. Managers must attempt to protect life and property from the dangers posed by fire in urban bushland as well as conserving this biodiversity.

Given the high potential for extreme fire events, where effective control of wildfire is not always possible (as happened in January 1994), there is increasing pressure for widespread fuel reduction burning in urban bushland adjacent to human assets such as houses. Such areas contain a number of endangered, vulnerable or rare plant species that are of high conservation significance, as well as more common species, all of which will have particular fire requirements which may or may not be compatible with burning for fuel reduction purposes. Hence, there is a potential for a conflict over protection versus conservation priorities (Bradstock, Keith & Auld 1995, Bradstock & Scott 1995). To attempt to resolve such conflicts we must have a sound knowledge of the effects of different fire regimes on plant and animal species and as land managers apply an informed choice of appropriate fire regimes to ensure the maintenance of populations of plants and animals.

This paper presents data on the effect of different components of the fire regime on several threatened plant species in order to provide land managers with potential conservation prescriptions for threatened plant species. In particular, we identify those fire regimes that may cause populations to decline. Such prescriptions can then be incorporated into planning and the implementation of a fuel reduction program, so that conservation issues are not ignored and fire regimes which threaten plant conservation are avoided.

## Study Area

The Sydney area in south-eastern Australia is a large urban area fringed with large bushland reserves and containing many smaller reserves (Figure 1). Within this area, the vegetation is dominated by sclerophyll heathlands, woodlands and forests, situated on infertile sandy soils derived from Hawkesbury sandstone (Beadle 1981), in a landscape of dissected sandstone plateaux. Rainfall is around 1200mm per annum with a peak in late summer. Average monthly maximum/minimum temperatures for

######## PDF PAGE 2 ########
164 Auld, T. D. and Scott, J.

[Map legend: Cleared areas; Vegetated areas; National Parks; scale 0-25 km; symbols for *Grevillea caleyi*, *Grevillea longifolia*, *Grevillea shiressii*, *Darwinia biflora*, *Darwinia diminuta*, *Darwinia glaucophylla*, *Darwinia procera*; label Sydney]

**Figure 1.** The Sydney urban area and adjacent bushland reserves showing the distribution of *Darwinia* and *Grevillea* study species.

Sydney are 26/18°C in summer and 16/8°C in winter. A broad range of fire regimes are possible in the Sydney Region. High intensity wildfires occur in the order of once every 5-10 years, while deliberate prescriptions of low intensity fires are commonly used for fuel reduction. Arson is a major source of wildfire ignitions.

## The Fire Regime

For the long term survival of plants and animals we need to know how they are affected by the fire regime, ie. (frequency, intensity, season, spatial extent). Here we concentrate on fire-sensitive plants.

### *Fire frequency*

All fires burn areas of vegetation that have been burnt some time before. Consequently, the vegetation is really a mosaic of fire histories, with some parts having had more fires than others over a given time period. We need to try and understand how important this unequal patchiness of fires through time is for the survival of plants.

Plants that are killed by fire rely on seed germination after fires to survive at a particular location. For these fire-sensitive plants, there must be sufficient time between successive fires for seedlings to mature and produce more seeds and hence, add seeds to the seedbank. In the Sydney area, this time will vary between species and loca-

######## PDF PAGE 3 ########
- Conservation of Endangered Plants in Urban Fire-Prone Habitats - 165

tions (Benson 1985), from species that flower within 1-2 years after fire (*Actinotus helianthi*, *Acacia suaveolens*) to those that may take 4-8 years to reach maturity (*Banksia ericifolia*). If another fire should occur before these plants have matured, dramatic changes in the vegetation may occur. Fire-sensitive plants with seed stored in woody capsules usually release all their seeds after a fire and no residual seeds remain in cones. These plants are the group of species most susceptible to two fires in short succession. Plants that have seeds stored in the soil usually have some residual seedbank remaining in the soil following post-fire germination. For these species, a second fire before seedlings mature may severely reduce population numbers but it may not eliminate species locally. However, in some places, after some fires, the entire soil seedbank may be exhausted, eg. Restionaceae and Epacridaceae (Meney et al. 1994), *Grevillea* (Auld unpubl.) and local extinction will occur if two fires occur close enough together to kill seedlings from the first fire before they are mature. Ideally, as land managers with concerns for the conservation of biodiversity, we should allow the interval between fires to be long enough not only simply for plant species to mature, but at a minimum, several fruiting seasons beyond this so that a sufficiently large seedbank can be established before the next fire occurs.

### *Fire Intensity*

How hot a fire is will depend on how much combustible fuel is available, how dry this fuel is, the topography of the area and the weather conditions, such as humidity and windspeed. When an area is burnt, the important thing for plants and animals is how much heat is produced, and in many areas around Sydney, this usually varies markedly even on a very small scale (i.e., over tens of meters). How much heat a fire produces can affect the survival of plants. In intense fires there is likely to be higher levels of resprouting plants killed, and longer periods needed before the next fire for recovery, than in mild fires. For plants, the more heat produced by a fire, the greater are the opportunities for seedling recruitment and the greater the magnitude of seedlings that are recruited (Auld & O'Connell 1991). Many plant species have seeds which lie dormant in the soil and for a number of these the amount of soil heating that occurs during the passage of a fire will govern the degree of germination after the fire. This heat response is widespread in many plant families, particularly legumes, in fire-prone communities throughout the world (Martin et al. 1975, Jeffery et al. 1988, Auld & O'Connell 1991, Keeley 1991). Bradstock and Auld (1995) have shown that in Hawkesbury sandstone soil around Sydney, it is the amount of fine fuel that is consumed during a fire that governs the degree of soil heating.

### *Fire season*

Given the prevalence of arson and widespread hazard reduction burning for the protection of life and property, fires can now be expected to occur at just about any time of the year in the Sydney Region. The question is, for the long-term survival of plants does it matter when the vegetation is burnt? In Sydney, Bradstock and Bedward (1992) have suggested that seedling survival after fire is largely independent of season of burn because rainfall is very variable. Although there is a trend for wetter periods in late summer/autumn and drier periods in spring this pattern is not strong enough to allow accurate predictions about the impact of season of burn on seedling survival post-fire. Perhaps the most critical role season of burning may play is in influencing fire intensity. Fires in the hot dry summer months when fuel moisture is low will generally be of higher intensities than burns in winter when the vegetation is moister, an ambient temperatures are lower.

### *Fire Spatial Extent*

What is the impact of the spatial extent of fires on plants? In Sydney, fires come in all shapes and sizes. Some burn very extensive areas, while others may only burn a hectare or so. Within the boundaries of a burnt area, fires may be widespread and burn most of the vegetation or leave large parts of the vegetation unburnt or simply lightly scorched. All fires will be different, depending on the terrain, rate of fire spread, amount of fuel available and its moisture content and weather conditions and natural or man-made fire breaks. This results in a patchiness of fires in area and intensity.

For plants, the spatial extent of fires may be important where burns occur on a very small scale (a few hectares). In such cases, native animals from surrounding unburnt vegetation may graze heavily on the new green shoots that appear after fire and hence, cause a decline in some plant species. These native animals may also consume many of the seeds that are produced in the first few years after fire for those fire-sensitive plants that are trying to replenish their soil seedbanks. This will slow the rate of recovery of such plants.

## Study Species

The threatened species examined, *Darwinia* spp. (Myrtaceae) and *Grevillea* spp. (Proteaceae), are all killed by fire (fire-sensitive, see Gill 1981) and rely on germination from a soil seedbank for persistence at a site after a fire. They are all restricted to the vicinity of Sydney (Figure 1). Threat codes are from Briggs and Leigh (1996).

######## PDF PAGE 4 ########
166 Auld, T. D. and Scott, J.

*Darwinia biflora* (Cheel) B.Briggs. Vulnerable. A small shrub to 1 m in height in woodland communities mainly in the Hornsby Plateau area in the northern suburbs of Sydney and associated with the Hammondville soil group (Burkitt, Wilson & Benson 1984). The largest populations occur in Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park, with small outliers in Lane Cove National Park, Marramarra National Park and Pennant Hills Park. This species is threatened by habitat loss, disturbance leading to weed invasion and an inappropriate fire regime.

*Darwinia diminuta* B Briggs. Rare. A small shrub to 60 cm in height in woodland and heath communities. Found on sandstone in a few localities in Royal National Park, Heathcote National Park, Garawarra State Recreation Area and Kelly's Falls to the south of Sydney and Garigal National Park in the northern Sydney suburbs. *D. diminuta* is threatened by habitat loss, site disturbance and an inappropriate fire regime.

*Darwinia glaucophylla* B. Briggs. Rare. A spreading prostrate shrub in heath. Confined to a few localities on sandstone in the Gosford area north of Sydney. *D. glaucophylla* is threatened by urban development and an inappropriate fire regime.

*Darwinia procera* B. Briggs. Rare. An erect shrub to 2 m in height in heath to open forest communities. Mostly confined to sheltered gullies and creek banks on sandstone. Restricted to a few localities between Garigal NP and Brisbane Water NP, in the northern suburbs of Sydney. *D. procera* is threatened by habitat loss, urban runoff and an inappropriate fire regime.

*Grevillea caleyi* R.Br. Endangered. A shrub to 4m by 4m occurring on laterite soils in open forests or low open forests and restricted to roughly a 6 x 6 km area centred on the northern Sydney suburb of Terrey Hills. Habitat destruction has divided the original distribution of the species into a series of discrete population fragments (Scott et al. 1995) separated by urban development (houses, roads, business parks etc). Some 85% of the former habitat of *G. caleyi* has been lost to urban development. Only two of the remaining sites are relatively undisturbed and only one of these two has any long-term protection as it occurs in Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park. The remaining large patches are highly disturbed. The major threats to the survival of *G. caleyi* arise from human interference in the environment. These threats range from loss of habitat through clearing, urbanisation and associated infrastructure, changes in landuse and an inappropriate fire regime, to localised disturbance at sites including invasion of weed species and the dumping of rubbish (Scott et al. 1995).

*Grevillea longifolia* R.Br. Rare. A bushy shrub 2-4 m in height by the same wide. It is found in the southern half of the Sydney Region and Woronora plateau and the Jamieson Valley of the Blue Mountains. Usually found in moist areas adjacent to creeks in open forest, but occasionally on escarpments and ridgetops in woodlands on Hawkesbury sandstone. *G. longifolia* is threatened by urban development, runoff, weed encroachment and an inappropriate fire regime.

*Grevillea shiressii* Blakley. Vulnerable. A bushy shrub 2-5 m in height. Found only on the banks of two creeks in closed forest in Brisbane Water National Park in the north of Sydney on soils derived from Narrabeen group geology. *G. shiressii* is threatened by disturbance (a fire trail passes through one population) and an inappropriate fire regime.

## The Effects of the Fire Regime on Threatened Plant Species

For all study species, demographic data were collated on threatened *Darwinia* and *Grevillea* species (Scott 1986, Auld et al. 1991, Auld et al. 1993, Auld and Tozer 1995, Scott et al. 1995) and the impacts of components of the fire regime were assessed. A summary of the significant demographic characteristics of our threatened study species is presented in Table 1.

### *Darwinia* spp. (Myrtaceae)

As the *Darwinia* spp. studied are all killed by fire, a fire-free period is needed after any one fire to allow seedlings to mature and replenish the soil seedbank. Plants can produce a few fruits two years after fire. As plants grow, fecundity increases and for all *Darwinia* species, soil seedbanks should increase rapidly 5-10 years after a fire. Most of the annually produced seed-crop is released in a viable, dormant state and would be incorporated into this seedbank, although there is some yearly variation in the proportion of non dormant seeds produced (eg. *D. glaucophylla*, Table 1).

For *D. biflora*, some 75% of the dormant seed released in any one annual seed-crop becomes non dormant and has germinated by 24 months after release, i.e., most seeds from any one seed-crop are short-lived in the soil. The seedbank should buildup in the soil rapidly after a site is burnt, but the seedbank will also decline rapidly should adult plants senesce. The low level of seed longevity in the soil in *D. biflora* (Table 1) suggests that both adult survival and the level of adult fecundity are the critical factors that govern persistence of the soil seedbank. As seeds decay rapidly in the soil, adult plants must regularly produce seeds to maintain a soil seedbank. The longevity of annual seed inputs to the soil seedbank is currently unknown for the other *Darwinia* spp. However, for *D. diminuta*, *D. glaucophylla* and *D. procera* the seedbank size is likely to be much larger than in *D. biflora*, given the higher fecundity levels in these species (Figure 2).

The fate of those seeds in the soil which lose their dormancy and germinate is unknown. It seems likely that

seedlings which emerge during the inter-fire period do not establish because of competitive pressure from an established cover of shrubs, herbs and grasses (c.f. *Acacia* spp. Weiss 1984, Auld 1986). Alternatively, some limited on-going establishment could be possible if seedlings were able to tolerate the existing cover of shrubs, herbs and grasses.

All *Darwinia* spp. showed some breaking of seed dormancy in response to heating. This suggests that the degree of soil heating during the passage of a fire, itself controlled by available fuel loads (Bradstock & Auld 1995), will influence the number of seeds within the seedbank that germinate after a fire. Near the soil surface lethal soil temperatures (>120°C) are likely to cause some seed death. The seedbank of these *Darwinia* spp. will be unaffected in a fire where soil heating is below the critical level needed to break seed dormancy, i.e., fires consuming small quantities of fuel.

### *Grevillea* spp. (Proteaceae)

All *Grevillea* species studied were killed by fire and relied on seed germination after a fire to maintain populations. For all species, the magnitude of the soil seedbank will be largely controlled by the levels of adult fecundity, mammal seed predation and adult mortality.

In *G. caleyi* and *G. longifolia*, seedlings do not flower and produce seeds before 2.5-5 years of age. Fecundity is low in *G. caleyi* with only about 3% of flowers resulting in mature seed (Scott 1986). The level of fecundity in both *G. caleyi* and *G. longifolia* increases until around 10 years of age in response to plant growth (Figure 3). No fecundity estimates have been made for *G. shiressii*. Seeds had a high level of viability and were largely released in a dormant state in *G. caleyi* and *G. shiressii*. In *G. longifolia*, a large fraction of seeds were released in a non dormant state (Table 1), although this is variable across populations and years. Predispersal seed predation is known to be high in *G. caleyi* and *G. shiressii* with significant losses to the weevil *Cydmaea dorsalis* Lea (Coleoptera: Curculionidae) in *G. caleyi* and to the wasp *Eurytoma* sp. (Hymenoptera: Eurytomidae) in *G. shiressii*. In *G. caleyi* and *G. longifolia*, seed dispersal is minimal. At maturity the fruits dehisce, dropping the seed to the ground beneath the parent plant. The seeds lack any lipid body attachment that would make them attractive to ants (Auld 1995). In contrast, *G. shiressii* seeds have a lipid body attachment and some 28% of seed are dispersed by ants. In all three threatened *Grevillea* spp. and other more common *Grevillea* spp., post-dispersal seed predation is very high (Auld 1995, Auld & Denham in prep.). Most of the seeds lying on the soil surface are consumed by

two native mammals, swamp wallabies (*Wallabia bicolor*) and bush rats (*Rattus fuscipes* and possibly other *Rattus* species). As a result, very few of the developing fruits from any one season contribute seeds to the seedbank. The relationship between mammal densities and the size of area burnt needs to be examined. In the past, some *G. caleyi* sites have been subjected to small patch burns. In these burnt areas, the level of seed losses to mammals was similar to adjacent unburnt areas and the establishment of a soil seedbank was expected to be retarded.

The major difference between *G. caleyi* and *G. longifolia* was the level of adult mortality within a population. Adult mortality was high in *G. caleyi*, while there was little adult mortality in *G. longifolia*. This means that as populations age beyond about 15 years post-fire, annual seed output (and the amount of seed successfully reaching the soil seedbank) will decline in *G. caleyi* at a much greater rate than in *G. longifolia*. The soil seedbank in *G. caleyi* is small and declines to low levels some 20 years after fire. In *G. longifolia*, the soil seedbank, although limited in magnitude by mammal seed predation, is more persistent through time. This suggests that *G. longifolia* will better tolerate long unburnt periods that *G. caleyi*. Comparable data is not available for *G. shiressii*.

In Sydney, heat from a fire does not break seed dormancy in *Grevillea* species, although a post-fire flush of seedlings is evident (Auld and Tozer 1995, Table 1). Hence, the amount of fuel consumed in a fire may have no effect on post-fire germination levels. Such germination should be governed by the response of seeds to another fire-related germination cue as well as the rate of decay of dormant seeds to a non dormant state in the soil seedbank. Leachates from charred wood (Keeley 1991), smoke (Brown 1993, Dixon et al. 1995) and nitrate and ammonium ions (Thanos and Rundel 1995) have all been shown to be fire-related cues that break seed dormancy

in fire-prone habitats. Which cues are critical in *Grevillea* species in Sydney remains to be investigated.

The key management indicators for healthy populations of *G. caleyi* in long unburnt (>15-20 year old) areas would appear to be the levels of adult survival and mammal seed predation. Such areas now occur as very small isolated pockets within urban areas. At sites where survival is low and mammals are destroying most of the seeds produced in any one year, seeds in the soil will continue to persist, but the magnitude of the soil seedbank will decline and the population is likely to be reduced after the next fire. This suggests that consideration should be given to burning such sites before the seedbank declines too much. Any such burning should be of a large spatial extent to reduce the densities of mammalian seed predators after fire.

## Implications for Fire Management

What are the implications for the management of these obligate seeding species? The most critical aspect of fire management for obligate seeders is the impact of frequent fires on these populations. Population declines or local extinctions are predicted after 2-3 fires occurring in close succession and hence, minimum fire-free intervals are needed to maintain the species. The fire free-intervals will vary depending on the rate of replenishment of the soil seedbank after any one fire and the proportion of seeds that emerge from the seedbank after a fire (ie, the degree to which the seedbank is depleted after a fire). Estimates of the minimum fire free intervals needed to maintain populations of threatened *Darwinia* and *Grevillea* species vary from 5-10 to 8-12 years (Table 2). It is not only important to maintain these threatened species, but also the species with which they co-habit. These suggested minimum fire-free intervals do not contradict with suggested minimum fire-free intervals for other plants species that co-habit with threatened *Darwinia* and *Grevillea* species (Bradstock and Auld 1987). Consequently, for the long-term survival of threatened species of *Darwinia* and *Grevillea* and their associated vegetation communities, under a regime of repeated fires, care should be taken to accurately record the fire histories of all remaining populations. This will allow sites potentially threatened by high fire frequency to be identified.

In *Darwinia* species, where heat is the fire-related cue that breaks seed dormancy, some residual seedbank should be present after any single fire. The amount and location of this seed will depend on the level of soil heating during the passage of a fire (Bradstock and Auld 1995). In *Grevillea*, the fire-related dormancy breaking cue is unknown, although it is not simply heat (Auld and Tozer 1995). In *Grevillea*, a high proportion of seeds within the soil seedbank may emerge after any one fire and in some

cases no residual seed may remain after a fire (Auld unpubl.). Hence, *Darwinia* species are likely to be more resilient than *Grevillea* species to two fires close enough together to prevent seedlings from the first fire from maturing. For *Grevillea* species, there is a significant risk of local extinctions under such a scenario, in the same manner as for many fire-sensitive species with a canopy seedbank where the entire seedbank is exhausted after a single fire (Lamont et al. 1991).

Where protection of life or property dictates a fire frequency less than that prescribed in Table 2, consideration should be given to alternative fuel reduction methods in sites containing threatened *Darwinia* or *Grevillea* species, eg. manual fuel removal. These areas will usually be those sites adjacent to urban areas and large expanses of natural vegetation. At other sites, where small patches of remnant vegetation are now isolated within the urban area, there is evidence that when populations of *G. caleyi* are left unburnt for 15-20 years or longer, the number of adult plants declines such that inputs to the soil seedbank are minimal. Consideration should also be given to burning such areas if all adults within the population have died and no seedling recruitment has occurred.

For *Darwinia* species, fires allowing high levels of ground fuel consumption should produce soil temperatures that cause seed dormancy to be broken. Fires where little ground fuel consumption occurs will not produce high enough soil temperatures to break seed dormancy and hence, are likely to lead to population declines, although some post-fire germination should also occur in response to seeds in the soil seedbank decaying from a dormant to a non dormant state through time. For *Grevillea* species, the role fire intensity (or its components) plays in controlling germination is currently unknown.

Finally, as post-dispersal seed predators can consume most of the annual seed-crops in threatened *Grevillea* species, consideration should be given to the size and patchiness of fires in areas containing these plants. Fires that burn large spatial areas are recommended to reduce the impact of mammalian seed predators in the first 10 years post-fire. If small scale burns are used to protect or manipulate sites containing threatened *Grevillea* species, then the mammalian seed predators may have a large impact on the amount of seed that reaches the soil seedbank. If large areas are burnt, there will be declines in the densities of the mammalian species (cf. Fox and McKay 1981) and less impact on the number of seeds reaching the soil seedbank from annual seed-crops, at least in the first few fruiting years after fire. The complex nature of this relationship requires further investigation. Where large area burns are not possible consideration should be given to fencing sites to exclude these seed predators while the seedbank is being replenished.

#### **Abstract**

**Question:** What is the role of dispersal, persistent soil seed banks and seedling recruitment in population persistence of fleshy-fruited obligate seeding plant species in fire-prone habitats?

**Location:** Southeastern Australia.

**Methods:** We used a long-term study of a shrubby, fleshy-fruited *Persoonia* species (*Proteaceae*) to examine (1) seed removal from beneath the canopy of adult plants; (2) seedling recruitment after fire; (3) the magnitude and location of the residual soil seed bank; and (4) the implications for fire management of obligate seeding species. We used demographic sampling techniques combined with Generalised Linear Modelling and regression to quantify population changes over time.

**Results:** Most of the mature fruits (90%) on the ground below the canopy of plants were removed by *Wallabia bicolor* (Swamp wallaby) with 88% of seeds extracted from *W. bicolor* scats viable and dormant. Wallabies play an important role in moving seeds away from parent plants. Their role in occasional long distance dispersal events remains unknown. We detected almost no seed predation *in situ* under canopies (< 1%). Seedling recruitment was cued to fire, with post-fire seedling densities 6-7 times pre-fire adult densities. After fire, a residual soil seed bank was present, as many seeds (77-100%) remained dormant and viable at a soil depth where successful future seedling emergence is possible (0-5 cm). Seedling survival was high (> 80%) with most mortality within 2 years of emergence. Plant growth averaged 17 cm per year. The primary juvenile period of plants was 7-8 years, within the period of likely return fire intervals in the study area. We predicted that the study population increased some five-fold after the wildfire at the site.

**Conclusions**: Residual soil seed banks are important, especially in species with long primary juvenile periods, to buffer the populations against the impact of a second fire occurring before the seed bank is replenished.

**Keywords:** Fire frequency; Macropod; Mammal; Obligate seeder; Soil seed bank.

**Nomenclature:** Harden, G.J. (1990-1992).

# **Dispersal and recruitment dynamics in the fleshy-fruited** *Persoonia lanceolata* **(Proteaceae)**

**Auld, Tony D.**1\***; Denham, Andrew J.**1,2 **& Turner, Ken**<sup>3</sup>

1*Biodiversity Science, Department of Environment and Climate Change (NSW), PO Box 1967, Hurstville NSW 2220 Australia;* 2*E-Mail andrew.denham@environment.nsw.gov.au;* 3*Native Vegetation Science, Department of Environment and Climate Change (NSW), PO Box 867 Wollongong, NSW 2520 Australia; E-mail ken.turner@dnr.nsw.gov.au \*Corresponding author; E-mail tony.auld@environment.nsw.gov.au*

## **Introduction**

Persistence of plant populations is influenced by a range of factors (Harper 1977). Ultimately, all plant populations rely on recruitment from seed to compensate for the death of individuals. For plants that occur in fireprone habitats and are killed by fire (obligate seeders), recruitment is often linked to the passage of fire (Keeley 1991; Tyler 1995; Whelan 1995). The abundance and distribution of new recruits in such plant populations is controlled by a combination of factors. These include: (1) amount of seed produced (e.g. Enright & Lamont 1989); (2) seed dispersal to safe sites (Hughes & Westoby 1992; Lamont et al. 1993); (3) factors that govern the breaking of seed dormancy and promote seed germination (Auld & O'Connell 1991; Baskin & Baskin 1998; Keeley & Fotheringham 2000; Ooi et al. 2006); and (4) early seedling survival (Tyler 1995, 1996). As adults of obligate seeding species are killed by fire, sufficient time between fires is needed to replenish seed banks. Fire regimes that allow fires to repeatedly occur before seed banks are replenished may cause population declines or local extinction. Avoiding such fire regimes is necessary in order to manage fire-prone habitats for the conservation of biodiversity (Bradstock et al. 1998; Keeley & Fotheringham 2000; Gill 2001; Keith et al. 2002; Whelan 2002). An understanding of the dynamics of seed dispersal and factors influencing recruitment is necessary to determine how obligate seeding species respond to changes in fire regimes that result from direct human activities and climate change (Whelan 1986).

Seed dispersal of woody species in many fire-prone habitats can be limited, as indicated by the predominance of myrmecochory in SE and SW Australia (Berg 1975; Rice & Westoby 1981) and elsewhere (Gomez & Espadaler 1998). For such species, the capacity to reoccupy sites should a species be adversely affected by fire regimes is limited (Whelan 1986, 1995), especially where habitats are highly fragmented by urban and rural development. For some species, there is a greater 

{1}

######## PDF PAGE 3 ########
capacity for dispersal, through either wind dispersal of small seeds or dispersal by animal vectors. Fleshyfruited species that may be moved by vertebrates are a small component of the heath and woodland flora of southeastern Australia (French & Westoby 1996) and other fire-prone floras (Bullock 1978; Milewski & Bond 1981; Keeley 1991). This may be the result of the low soil fertility that characterises the vegetation in these areas (Westoby et al. 1990). We estimate, based on seed morphology characteristics, that in the Sydney region, only some 9 % of species (in 57 genera) that occur in fire-prone heaths, woodlands and dry forest habitats have fleshy fruits that are likely to be dispersed by vertebrates. The most abundant groups are from two diverse families, *Persoonia* in the Proteaceae (29 taxa) and *Acrotriche*, *Astroloma, Brachyloma*, *Leucopogon, Lissanthe, Melichrus*, *Monotoca* and *Styphelia* in the *Ericaceae* (formerly included in the Epacridaceae, 43 taxa). The role of seed dispersal in maintaining populations or in moving seeds between populations in such taxa is poorly known.

*Persoonia* is an endemic Australian genus of ca. 100 species (Weston 2002), with two main centres of radiation, southeastern and southwestern Australia. Obligate seeding *Persoonia* spp. may have long primary juvenile periods, relative to the average inter-fire interval (Benson 1985; Auld unpubl.) and a number are threatened in the Sydney Basin of southeastern Australia (Rymer 2006). Such species are at risk of decline if fire frequencies are increased via arson, climate change or burning for protection of life and property.

In this paper we report on a long-term study of one obligate seeding shrub species, *Persoonia lanceolata*  Andrews, that is common in eastern Australia and is a significant structural component of vegetation in heaths and woodlands. We ask:

- 1. Is seed removed or eaten from beneath the canopy of adult plants?
- 2. What agents are involved in seed removal or seed predation?
- 3. What is the magnitude of seedling recruitment after fire? Does this suggest population stability under the current fire regime?
- 4. What is the magnitude and location of the residual soil seed bank? How is this related to the pre-fire seed density? and
- 5. What are the implications for fire management of obligate seeding *Persoonia* spp.?

## **Methods**

#### *Study species and site*

*Persoonia lanceolata* is a bushy shrub that grows to 3 m high. It is a fire sensitive obligate seeder, common in the understorey in heath and woodlands along the east coast and ranges of New South Wales, Australia (Weston 2002). Flowering occurs in summer (December to February) with mature fruits ripening in the following spring (September to October, Benson & McDougall 2000). The fruit of *Persoonia* species is a drupe (Weston 2002) of approximately 1300 mg (Westoby *et al.* 1990), with a pulpy flesh surrounding a hard woody pyrene. There is mostly one seed per pyrene in *P. lanceolata* (Westoby et al. 1990; pers. obs.). Seed dispersal is thought to be mostly by mammals and birds (Benson & McDougall 2000).

We examined a population of *P. lanceolata* at one site within Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park 20 km north of Sydney (33°53' E, 151°13' S) southeastern Australia. Annual precipitation for Sydney is around 1300 mm, while the average monthly maximum/minimum temperatures are 26/18 °C in summer and 16/8 °C in winter. The area of the site was ca. 2 ha and contained a dense mature population of *P. lanceolata* occurring in a periodically wet heathland. *Persoonia lanceolata* was one of the dominant shrubs along with *Angophora crassifolia*, *Eucalyptus stricta* and *Hakea teretifolia.*  There was a range of smaller shrub species (0.5 - 2 m), particularly members of the *Proteaceae* and *Fabaceae*  (common species include: *Banksia oblongifolia, Boronia pinnata, Dillwynia floribunda, Epacris pulchella, Grevillea speciosa, Hakea dactyloides, Leptospermum squarrosum, Mirbelia rubiifolia, Persoonia pinifolia, Pultenaea elliptica* and *Xanthorrhoea* spp.) and a ground cover of sedges, grasses, and herbs (common species include: *Actinotus minor, Anisopogon avenaceus, Bauera rubioides, Cyathochaeta diandra, Lindsaea linearis, Lomandra cylindrica, L. glauca, Mitrasacme polymorpha, Patersonia* sp.*, Restio* spec.). The site was burnt by an extensive summer (January) wildfire in 1994 that burnt all the surrounding habitat. It had previously been burnt in a summer wildfire 15 years prior.

#### *Seed dispersal and predation*

Prior to the wildfire, we established plots under randomly selected mature *P. lanceolata* plants over two consecutive fruiting seasons. In the first season, we established five plots in a pilot experiment that ran for 12 days. In the second season, we established ten plots and followed the fates of seeds for 40 days. At each plot we established two treatments;

{2}

######## PDF PAGE 4 ########
(1) a cache of 10 mature fruits; and (2) a cache of 10 mature fruits covered by a wire mesh cage (mesh 1 cm × 1 cm), cage 15 cm by 15 cm by 6 cm high. Each cage was placed over a petri dish and secured with wire stakes. These cages excluded vertebrates.

All caches were placed in 9 cm diameter petri dishes to avoid fruits being washed away in storms. The fate of seeds in caches was checked twice daily for 4 days then daily for 10 days and then 2-3 times per week. Searches were made around the caches for fruits or fruit/seed remains if seeds were removed from the caches. Where mammals were suspected of taking seeds (where pieces of seed testa were found or whole seeds were removed overnight) additional trials were established to identify the likely animals responsible. Adhesive tape was placed on the edges of petri dishes containing seeds and hair samples of the mammal species removing seeds were collected. These animal hairs were identified by B. Triggs. Field trapping using Elliott type A aluminium folding box traps was conducted to determine which small mammal species were present at the site.

A 2-factor GLIM was used to compare the proportion of caches where fruit were removed in the first 12 days in the caged and uncaged treatments, across two years (12 days being the length of time the experiment was run in the first season). A separate 1-factor GLIM examined the proportion of caches where fruit removal occurred across treatments at the end of the second season. In both cases a binomial error structure was used.

We also searched the surrounding habitat for any scats that contained pyrenes or fruits. We collected numerous scats and removed the pyrenes from them. For 10 replicate samples of 10 pyrenes from these scats we estimated the non-dormant seed fraction by placing replicate batches of seeds into 9-cm diameter petri dishes on Whatmans Grade 1 filter paper at room temperatures. Distilled water was added to ensure the filter paper remained moist and germination was followed for 2 months after which seeds were extracted from pyrenes and tested for viability using tetrazolium (Lakon 1949).

#### *Seedling recruitment, survival and growth after fire*

After the 1994 wildfire, we established 23 permanent 1-m2 quadrats within the population using a randomised grid. Within each quadrat we scored the number of dead adults that were rooted in the quadrat and tagged new emerging seedlings of *P. lanceolata* for a period of 12 years. New seedlings (71) were identified by their distinctive cotyledons. At each sampling, we scored plant survivorship, assessed whether the plants had reached maturity (as indicated by the production of flowers and then fruits), and measured the height of all tagged *P. lan-* *ceolata* plants as an indicator of their growth to maturity. The time to first flowering was recorded for all seedlings and the magnitude of fruit production estimated in several flowering seasons by counting large (near mature) fruits on all tagged plants. The rate of growth of plants was examined using non-linear regression (power function) of plant height (lognormal transformed) against plant age. As plants were repeatedly sampled, we also carried out an Analysis of Covariance with previous sample plant height as a covariate. We also compared the pre-fire density of plants with the post-fire seedling density as an estimate of population turnover after the fire.

#### *Residual soil seed bank*

Within a randomly chosen subset (8) of the 23 available 1-m2 quadrats described above to follow seedling emergence, survival and growth, we examined the residual soil seed bank. In 2003, 9 years after the 1994 fire (after seedlings had had their first flowering, but before the first post-fire seed fall) we excavated the soil in each of the 8 (1-m2) plots. All the soil in each plot was excavated in two parts, i.e. 0 to 5 cm and 5-10 cm depths. Pyrenes were extracted by sieving. Samples were wet sieved by washing through firstly a 6.3 mm followed by a 4.2 mm sieve. The retained parts were allowed to dry and hand sorted. Pyrenes passed through the first sieve and were retained by the second. Intact pyrenes were opened to determine if the fruit contained a viable seed (filled, firm and white).

## **Results**

#### *Seed dispersal and predation*

Seed removal outside cages after 12 days occurred in both sampled seasons (GLIM Δ dev = 14.1, 1 df, *P* < 0.005), with no interaction between years and treatment (GLIM Δ dev = 0.0, 1 df, *P* > 0.05) and no year effect (GLIM Δ dev = 0.1, 1 df, *P* > 0.05). Averaged across the two years some 17% of seed was removed (removal occurring in 53 % of seed caches) in 12 days (Fig. 1). At the end of the second sample season, where we followed the fate of seeds for 40 days, the treatment effect was again significant (GLIM Δ dev = 16.9, 1 df, *P <* 0.005), with an average of 90% of fruits removed in the open (removal occurring in 100 % of seed caches). The rate of seed removal outside the cages was slow but continued over the 40 day trial (Fig. 1). Inside cages, there was occasional consumption of the flesh around pyrenes, and occasionally whole fruits were removed. Outside of cages most losses were fruit removals, although in a very few cases the pyrene was removed and the flesh remained.

We estimate, based on seed morphology characteristics, that in the Sydney region, only some 9 % of species (in 57 genera) that occur in fire-prone heaths, woodlands and dry forest habitats have fleshy fruits that are likely to be dispersed by vertebrates. The most abundant groups are from two diverse families, *Persoonia* in the Proteaceae (29 taxa) and *Acrotriche*, *Astroloma, Brachyloma*, *Leucopogon, Lissanthe, Melichrus*, *Monotoca* and *Styphelia* in the *Ericaceae* (formerly included in the Epacridaceae, 43 taxa). The role of seed dispersal in maintaining populations or in moving seeds between populations in such taxa is poorly known.

*Persoonia* is an endemic Australian genus of ca. 100 species (Weston 2002), with two main centres of radiation, southeastern and southwestern Australia. Obligate seeding *Persoonia* spp. may have long primary juvenile periods, relative to the average inter-fire interval (Benson 1985; Auld unpubl.) and a number are threatened in the Sydney Basin of southeastern Australia (Rymer 2006). Such species are at risk of decline if fire frequencies are increased via arson, climate change or burning for protection of life and property.

In this paper we report on a long-term study of one obligate seeding shrub species, *Persoonia lanceolata*  Andrews, that is common in eastern Australia and is a significant structural component of vegetation in heaths and woodlands. We ask:

- 1. Is seed removed or eaten from beneath the canopy of adult plants?
- 2. What agents are involved in seed removal or seed predation?
- 3. What is the magnitude of seedling recruitment after fire? Does this suggest population stability under the current fire regime?
- 4. What is the magnitude and location of the residual soil seed bank? How is this related to the pre-fire seed density? and
- 5. What are the implications for fire management of obligate seeding *Persoonia* spp.?

## **Methods**

#### *Study species and site*

*Persoonia lanceolata* is a bushy shrub that grows to 3 m high. It is a fire sensitive obligate seeder, common in the understorey in heath and woodlands along the east coast and ranges of New South Wales, Australia (Weston 2002). Flowering occurs in summer (December to February) with mature fruits ripening in the following spring (September to October, Benson & McDougall 2000). The fruit of *Persoonia* species is a drupe (Weston 2002) of approximately 1300 mg (Westoby *et al.* 1990), with a pulpy flesh surrounding a hard woody pyrene. There is mostly one seed per pyrene in *P. lanceolata* (Westoby et al. 1990; pers. obs.). Seed dispersal is thought to be mostly by mammals and birds (Benson & McDougall 2000).

We examined a population of *P. lanceolata* at one site within Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park 20 km north of Sydney (33°53' E, 151°13' S) southeastern Australia. Annual precipitation for Sydney is around 1300 mm, while the average monthly maximum/minimum temperatures are 26/18 °C in summer and 16/8 °C in winter. The area of the site was ca. 2 ha and contained a dense mature population of *P. lanceolata* occurring in a periodically wet heathland. *Persoonia lanceolata* was one of the dominant shrubs along with *Angophora crassifolia*, *Eucalyptus stricta* and *Hakea teretifolia.*  There was a range of smaller shrub species (0.5 - 2 m), particularly members of the *Proteaceae* and *Fabaceae*  (common species include: *Banksia oblongifolia, Boronia pinnata, Dillwynia floribunda, Epacris pulchella, Grevillea speciosa, Hakea dactyloides, Leptospermum squarrosum, Mirbelia rubiifolia, Persoonia pinifolia, Pultenaea elliptica* and *Xanthorrhoea* spp.) and a ground cover of sedges, grasses, and herbs (common species include: *Actinotus minor, Anisopogon avenaceus, Bauera rubioides, Cyathochaeta diandra, Lindsaea linearis, Lomandra cylindrica, L. glauca, Mitrasacme polymorpha, Patersonia* sp.*, Restio* spec.). The site was burnt by an extensive summer (January) wildfire in 1994 that burnt all the surrounding habitat. It had previously been burnt in a summer wildfire 15 years prior.

#### *Seed dispersal and predation*

Prior to the wildfire, we established plots under randomly selected mature *P. lanceolata* plants over two consecutive fruiting seasons. In the first season, we established five plots in a pilot experiment that ran for 12 days. In the second season, we established ten plots and followed the fates of seeds for 40 days. At each plot we established two treatments;

{2}

######## PDF PAGE 4 ########
(1) a cache of 10 mature fruits; and (2) a cache of 10 mature fruits covered by a wire mesh cage (mesh 1 cm × 1 cm), cage 15 cm by 15 cm by 6 cm high. Each cage was placed over a petri dish and secured with wire stakes. These cages excluded vertebrates.

All caches were placed in 9 cm diameter petri dishes to avoid fruits being washed away in storms. The fate of seeds in caches was checked twice daily for 4 days then daily for 10 days and then 2-3 times per week. Searches were made around the caches for fruits or fruit/seed remains if seeds were removed from the caches. Where mammals were suspected of taking seeds (where pieces of seed testa were found or whole seeds were removed overnight) additional trials were established to identify the likely animals responsible. Adhesive tape was placed on the edges of petri dishes containing seeds and hair samples of the mammal species removing seeds were collected. These animal hairs were identified by B. Triggs. Field trapping using Elliott type A aluminium folding box traps was conducted to determine which small mammal species were present at the site.

A 2-factor GLIM was used to compare the proportion of caches where fruit were removed in the first 12 days in the caged and uncaged treatments, across two years (12 days being the length of time the experiment was run in the first season). A separate 1-factor GLIM examined the proportion of caches where fruit removal occurred across treatments at the end of the second season. In both cases a binomial error structure was used.

We also searched the surrounding habitat for any scats that contained pyrenes or fruits. We collected numerous scats and removed the pyrenes from them. For 10 replicate samples of 10 pyrenes from these scats we estimated the non-dormant seed fraction by placing replicate batches of seeds into 9-cm diameter petri dishes on Whatmans Grade 1 filter paper at room temperatures. Distilled water was added to ensure the filter paper remained moist and germination was followed for 2 months after which seeds were extracted from pyrenes and tested for viability using tetrazolium (Lakon 1949).

#### *Seedling recruitment, survival and growth after fire*

After the 1994 wildfire, we established 23 permanent 1-m2 quadrats within the population using a randomised grid. Within each quadrat we scored the number of dead adults that were rooted in the quadrat and tagged new emerging seedlings of *P. lanceolata* for a period of 12 years. New seedlings (71) were identified by their distinctive cotyledons. At each sampling, we scored plant survivorship, assessed whether the plants had reached maturity (as indicated by the production of flowers and then fruits), and measured the height of all tagged *P. lan-* *ceolata* plants as an indicator of their growth to maturity. The time to first flowering was recorded for all seedlings and the magnitude of fruit production estimated in several flowering seasons by counting large (near mature) fruits on all tagged plants. The rate of growth of plants was examined using non-linear regression (power function) of plant height (lognormal transformed) against plant age. As plants were repeatedly sampled, we also carried out an Analysis of Covariance with previous sample plant height as a covariate. We also compared the pre-fire density of plants with the post-fire seedling density as an estimate of population turnover after the fire.

#### *Residual soil seed bank*

Within a randomly chosen subset (8) of the 23 available 1-m2 quadrats described above to follow seedling emergence, survival and growth, we examined the residual soil seed bank. In 2003, 9 years after the 1994 fire (after seedlings had had their first flowering, but before the first post-fire seed fall) we excavated the soil in each of the 8 (1-m2) plots. All the soil in each plot was excavated in two parts, i.e. 0 to 5 cm and 5-10 cm depths. Pyrenes were extracted by sieving. Samples were wet sieved by washing through firstly a 6.3 mm followed by a 4.2 mm sieve. The retained parts were allowed to dry and hand sorted. Pyrenes passed through the first sieve and were retained by the second. Intact pyrenes were opened to determine if the fruit contained a viable seed (filled, firm and white).

## **Results**

#### *Seed dispersal and predation*

Seed removal outside cages after 12 days occurred in both sampled seasons (GLIM Δ dev = 14.1, 1 df, *P* < 0.005), with no interaction between years and treatment (GLIM Δ dev = 0.0, 1 df, *P* > 0.05) and no year effect (GLIM Δ dev = 0.1, 1 df, *P* > 0.05). Averaged across the two years some 17% of seed was removed (removal occurring in 53 % of seed caches) in 12 days (Fig. 1). At the end of the second sample season, where we followed the fate of seeds for 40 days, the treatment effect was again significant (GLIM Δ dev = 16.9, 1 df, *P <* 0.005), with an average of 90% of fruits removed in the open (removal occurring in 100 % of seed caches). The rate of seed removal outside the cages was slow but continued over the 40 day trial (Fig. 1). Inside cages, there was occasional consumption of the flesh around pyrenes, and occasionally whole fruits were removed. Outside of cages most losses were fruit removals, although in a very few cases the pyrene was removed and the flesh remained.

## n_pages=9 ######## PDF PAGE 5 ######## #### *Seedling recruitment, survival and growth after fire* Most seedlings emerged in the first 10 months after the 1994 fire (the time of our first sample). There was only limited emergence after this (Table 1), but occasional seedlings appeared until 6 years post-fire. This subsequent emergence was not confined to any particular season (summer 11, autumn 6, winter 3 seedlings, respectively), and declined in magnitude over time. Seedling survival was high with most observed mortality in the first 1-2 years after seedlings were tagged (Fig. 2). Our sampling did not allow us to detect mortality in the first 10 months post-fire. The post-fire seedling density was 6-7 times greater than the pre-fire adult density (0.5 vs. 3.3/m2). Seedlings reached a height of ca. 1 m (range 0.10 - 1.7m) at 6-7 years old, growing at an average rate of 0.17m per year (Fig. 3). Age was a good predictor of plant **Fig. 1.** Seed removal rates over two annual fruit-crops in *Persoonia lanceolata*, (**a**) year 1; (**b**) year 2. Treatments are: caged for vertebrate exclusion (filled circles); uncaged (open triangles). Error bars are 1 SE. **Fig. 2.** Survival of seedlings of *Persoonia lanceolata* over time. **Table 1.** Fecundity data for maturing juveniles of *Persoonia lanceolata.*

Only two fruits in the experiment in the first year were observed to have been eaten *in situ*. Where whole seed removals occurred, two lines of evidence suggested that the fruits were eaten by the macropod *Wallabia bicolor* (swamp wallaby). Hair samples from around batches of seeds were identified as this species and scats of the species frequently contained *Persoonia* pyrenes. Field trapping of small mammals using Elliott Traps showed that only *Rattus fuscipes* and *Antechinus* sp. (a marsupial mouse) were commonly trapped at the site. Neither species is known to remove large fleshy fruits. For the pyrenes extracted from *Wallabia bicolor* (Swamp Wallaby) scats we found high seed viability (88 ± 3%), but all viable seeds were still dormant. {4} ######## PDF PAGE 6 ######## height with a power function of log height accounting for some 87% of the variation in mean plant height. The Analysis of Covariance showed a significant effect of both plant age (*P* < 0.001) and previous plant height (*P* < 0.001), suggesting that although a number of smaller plants persist for a while (see Fig. 3), the height of a plant at a particular age was not simply dependent on its previous height. No plants flowered until 6 years after the fire. At this time only 13% of plants were mature and resultant fruit production was very low (Table 1). The proportion of plants that reproduced increased over time up to 92% 12 years after the fire. The magnitude of fruit production also increased markedly from the first to the second fruiting season and in subsequent seasons (Table 1). #### *Residual soil seed bank* Residual seeds in the soil were found in all sampled quadrats, independent of whether or not above ground seedlings were present at the time of sampling (Fig. 4). The density of seeds in the soil (21.2 ± 5.1 seeds/m2) was some 6-7 times greater than the density of seedlings that emerged after fire. On a 1-m2 plot basis, we estimate that between 72-100% of the available soil seed bank did not germinate after the wildfire. This may be an overestimate, as some seeds that germinated may not have been observed as seedlings at our first census 10 months after the fire. Most of the residual soil seed bank was in the top 5 cm of soil (90%). ## **Discussion** Fire plays an important part in the life cycle of many plant species, including woody *Persoonia* species. Like many other obligate seeders, for the common *P. lanceolata*, fire caused population-scale adult mortality and promoted the recruitment of new plants. Population persistence in this obligate seeding species will be influenced by fire frequency, fire patchiness and the dispersal capability of seeds. After a single fire, most seedling recruitment was confined to the first 1-2 years, suggesting that seeds of this species respond to fire cues and/or that the post-fire environment provides favourable conditions for seedling establishment. For obligate seeding shrubs in general, recruitment is often linked to the first 12 months after fire, e.g. southeastern Australia (Purdie 1977; Auld & Tozer 1995; Benwell 1998); Spanish matorral (Fernández-Santos & Gómez-Guitérrez 1994); Florida sand pine scrub (Carrington 1999); Californian chaparral and sage brush (Keeley et al. 2006). However, there was no seasonal component observed in seedling emergence after the initial flush (in comparison to Auld et al. 2000; Ooi et al. 2004). Some continued seedling recruitment occurred for up to 6 years post-fire. The number of seedlings recruited post-fire exceeded pre-fire adult numbers by 6-7 times. The likely change in population abundance after the wildfire can be compared using an estimate of pre-fire adults to post-fire seedlings, and incorporating estimated subsequent seedling mortality levels. This included mortality prior to plants reaching maturity (Fig. 2, ca. 14 (± 4)% after 7.5 years) and an estimate of the likely subsequent adult mortality in the following 7.5 years (to allow equivalent populations estimates for a 15-year old stand). We assumed mortality from 7.5-15 years post-fire matched that of the 2-12 year old plants in the study (Fig. 2). Based on these estimates, we predict that the population density 15 years after the **Fig. 3.** Plant height against age for seedlings of *Persoonia lanceolata*. The line refers to the power function: Ln(plant height) = 2.215\*(plant age)0.367; *R*2 = 0.87). **Fig. 4.** Magnitude of the residual soil seed bank in *Persoonia lanceolata* in 1-m2 quadrats. {5} ######## PDF PAGE 7 ######## 1994 wildfire would be some 5 × that of the pre-fire density. Few comparable examples of quantitative estimates of population change in response to fire are available. Keeley et al. (2006) observed an increase in abundance in obligate seeding shrubs in the first five years postfire in southern California, whilst Auld & Scott (2004) showed that the ratio of pre vs. post-fire plant abundance in obligate seeders was dependent upon the time since the previous fire (i.e. pre-fire plant ages). This general lack of data in fire-prone habitats limits quantitative comparison of the impact of varying fire regimes on persistence of obligate seeding plants. Survival of new seedlings of *P. lanceolata* is of a Deevey Type III (*sensu* Harper 1977), with highest mortality when plants are young and small, and reduced mortality once the seedlings are established and grow. This matches the pattern for seedlings in other fireprone habitats (Fernández-Santos & Gómez-Guitérrez 1994; Whelan 1995). Plant growth is relatively slow compared to co-habiting obligate seeding shrubs and in this study, flowering did not occur until 6 years after the fire. As it takes over 6 months for fruits to mature and as the first flowering effectively produced almost no seed, we consider the first effective fruit set was some 7-8 years after the fire. This relatively long primary juvenile period has been noted at other sites for this species (Benson & McDougall 2000; Auld unpubl.), although it has also been observed to be slightly shorter (Benson & McDougall 2000). It is also typical of other co-habiting, obligate seeding *Persoonia* spp. such as *P. pinifolia* and *P. isophylla* (Benson & McDougall 2000; Auld unpubl.). Fires may readily re-occur in the habitat of *P. lanceolata* every 5-10 years, with most (75%) areas in nearby comparable vegetation having a current fire return interval of 7-17 years (Bradstock & Kenny 2003). Consequently, the species may be at risk of population declines unless either a significant proportion of the soil seed bank remains available after a fire (as a residual seed bank), or seeds can readily disperse back into the population from unburnt populations. We found considerable residual seed at our study site and much of this lay in the top 5 cm of the soil, the area most likely to be influenced by fire-related germination cues such as heat (Bradstock & Auld 1995), and possibly smoke. These buried seeds are unlikely to be killed by the lethal heating effects of a fire. Seeds in the top 5 cm will also be least affected by limitations to successful emergence due to depth constraints (Bond et al. 1999). Residual seed values varied, but all greatly exceeded those of some other obligate seeders that co-occur with *P. lanceolata* (Auld & Denham 2006). However, even the residual soil seed bank detected in this study does not ensure there will be population level replacement should a fire occur before there has been replenishment of the soil seed bank. The magnitude of any germination event will be governed by factors relating to the fire itself (heat and smoke output) and post-fire rainfall levels. Removal of fruits from below parent shrubs by Swamp Wallabies was common. In contrast, removal by invertebrates was uncommon, as observed for this species at other sites by French & Westoby (1996). Very few seeds were consumed below canopies. In contrast to some other members of the *Proteaceae* such as *Grevillea* (Auld & Denham 1999), seed removal does not seem to be a mechanism for seed escape from seed predators. Rather, seed removal by Swamp Wallabies would likely reduce future seedling densities adjacent to pre-fire parent plants. Seeds that were removed passed though the gut of animals in a viable and dormant state. Hence, Swamp Wallabies are likely to be an effective dispersal agent for *Persoonia* spp., in agreement with Rymer (2006). Most seeds are likely to be deposited within a population, as evidenced by numerous scats containing seeds in the population. The question remains as to whether these dispersal agents have the ability to move seeds between populations, especially in order to prevent local population extinctions under a regime of too frequent fire. It has been suggested that vertebrate dispersal of *Persoonia* seeds may be a mechanism for gene flow between populations (Rymer & Ayre 2006) or for re-establishment of populations after local extinction (French & Westoby 1996). The long-term nature of this study allowed us to quantify population processes and changes over time. Such studies are a trade off between parameter estimation and predictability across the landscape (Silvertown & Lovett Doust 1983; Whelan 1995). The utility of these data for making predictions about other populations of *Persoonia lanceolata* remains to be investigated. ## **Conclusions** The observed maintenance of a large post-fire residual soil seed bank was potentially an effective means of buffering the population from local extinction if fires occasionally re-occur at short intervals. A long-term high frequency fire regime that prevents the replenishment of the soil seed bank is likely to lead to population declines and possible local extinction. We suggest that a sound understanding of how fire impacts on obligate seeding species, such as *Persoonia,* will be best developed by a combination of long-term studies at particular sites combined with detailed multi-site or multi-species comparisons of key demographic attributes, e.g. seed germination, seed dispersal patterns, residual soil seed banks. {6}

1	## n_pages=11
2	
3	######## PDF PAGE 1 ########
4	Cunninghamia 1(3), 339-349 (1985)
5	
6	# MATURATION PERIODS FOR FIRE-SENSITIVE SHRUB SPECIES IN HAWKESBURY SANDSTONE VEGETATION
7	
8	D. H. BENSON
9	
10	(Accepted for publication 11.5.1984)
11	
12	## ABSTRACT
13	
14	*Benson, D. H. (National Herbarium of New South Wales, Royal Botanic Gardens, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia 2000) 1985. Maturation periods for fire-sensitive shrub species in Hawkesbury Sandstone vegetation. Cunninghamia 1(3), 339-349.* The maturation times (period from germination to flowering) for a number of fire-sensitive shrub species in Hawkesbury Sandstone vegetation at sites in Brisbane Water National Park and at Glenorie near Sydney were recorded from marked seedlings established after hot fires. They range from two to seven years for different species. The implications for fire management, particularly for controlled burning, are discussed. A fire-free period of at least nine to ten years is recommended for similar vegetation if successful flowering and seed set, and continued species survival is to occur.
15	
16	## INTRODUCTION
17	
18	Plant species fall into two main groups with regard to their response to fire: some are characterized by vegetative regrowth, where individuals either resprout from epicormic shoots on the trunk and major surviving limbs or, following the death of all above-ground stems, resprout from underground rootstocks, lignotubers or rhizomes (sprouters); others regenerate from seed either stored in the soil before the fire, carried on the plants in woody fruits and released after the fire, or carried in from adjacent unburnt areas (non-sprouters). Adults in the second group are fire-sensitive and generally killed outright (Gill, 1975, 1981; Bradstock, 1981).
19	
20	The relative proportions of these groups of species appear to be related to the fire frequency in the habitat (Christensen, Recher & Hoare, 1981). In wet sclerophyll forest the proportion of fire-sensitive species is roughly 50 to 60 per cent (Ashton, 1981). In the more frequently burnt dry sclerophyll forests near Canberra, Purdie & Slatyer (1976) found 65 per cent regenerated vegetatively but only 27 per cent of species were fire-sensitive and only regenerated from seed.
21	
22	The time necessary for reproduction after fire is an important characteristic, especially in fire-sensitive species. Specht, Rayson & Jackman (1958) noted that fires at intervals of five years in heath vegetation are likely to eliminate or reduce numbers of some species that take several years to reach reproductive maturity. Similarly, for bushland north of Sydney, Siddiqi, Carolin & Myerscough (1976) recorded the localized elimination of the woody fire-sensitive species *Banksia ericifolia*, *Allocasuarina distyla* and *Hakea teretifolia* by repeated burning. However, to predict the impact of a series of fires, data on the maturation periods for fire-sensitive species are needed. With some exceptions, e.g. *Banksia ericifolia* (Carpenter & Recher, 1979) and *Leptospermum laevigatum* (Burrell, 1968), such data are not available. The potential effect of frequent burning on fire-sensitive species has become particularly relevant with the increased adoption of "controlled" or "prescribed" burning in bushland areas. Such burning generally involves the application of regular fires of low intensity, commonly at intervals of between two and five years.
23	
24	This paper documents the time required for a group of fire-sensitive species to reach maturity and discusses the implications for regular, frequent burning programs.
25	
26	######## PDF PAGE 2 ########
27	340 Cunninghamia Vol. 1(3): 1985
28	
29	## METHODS
30	
31	The main study locality was in Brisbane Water National Park (33° 30'S, 151° 15'E), 40 km north of Sydney. Bushland here is eucalypt-dominated scleromorphic vegetation on low-nutrient Hawkesbury Sandstone. Rainfall is about 1250 mm per annum (Bureau of Meteorology, 1979). The general vegetation is described by Benson & Fallding (1981). A second locality was studied at Glenorie (33° 35'S, 151° 00'E), 15 km north-west of Hornsby, on similar Hawkesbury Sandstone, but with average rainfall of 930 mm per annum, to see whether similar results were obtained in a lower rainfall.
32	
33	A hot summer (1974-75) fire occurred at the Brisbane Water locality six months before the first observations were made and the size of dead bushes at the time indicated that the area had been unburnt for about 15 years before this. As a result of topographic and drainage features, there was considerable variation in microhabitat; therefore, four sites in generally similar, but slightly different, vegetation were chosen as follows:
34	
35	- Site A — low-woodland with *Eucalyptus haemastoma* and *E. gummifera* on a gently sloping hillside
36	- Site B — open-heath on a broad rocky ledge
37	- Site C — low open-forest of *Banksia serrata* and *Eucalyptus gummifera*
38	- Site D — woodland of *Eucalyptus piperita* subsp. *piperita* and *E. gummifera* on a sandy ledge below a small cliff-line.
39	
40	A shrubby understorey characterized all the sites, although site C also had a considerable amount of grassy growth. Sites A and B were poorly drained. All sites were within about 0.5 km of each other.
41	
42	The Glenorie site was in woodland of *Eucalyptus eximia* and *E. gummifera* on a dry ridgetop and had been burnt in January 1975.
43	
44	At each site a transect of 10 contiguous 1 m × 1 m plots was established. Each of these plots was subdivided into four 0.5 m × 0.5 m sub-plots and two seedlings within each sub-plot were selected and marked with coloured wires. Seedlings were distinguished from plants regenerating from rootstocks or rhizomes by the presence of cotyledons or by comparison with similar plants that had been dug up and their roots examined. Although restricted to dicotyledonous species, as wide a range of species as possible was chosen, and the most healthy seedlings marked. Table 1 lists the 37 species included in this study, their susceptibility to fire and the total number of seedlings marked ("?" indicates species that are probably fire-sensitive). Initially, 320 seedlings were marked. Many of these died during the first years of recording. Additional plants were marked to replace dead plants during the first two years, after which no additional plants were marked. The occurrence of flowering was recorded four times a year (at Brisbane Water in early March, June, September and December; at Glenorie in early February, May, August and November) for the following eight years.
45	
46	At the same time all species flowering within about 30 m of the transect were recorded. Because of the range of microhabitats, such as minor cliff-lines, rock platforms and moist soaks, some of which remained unburnt during the fire, flowering recordings may represent as few as one or two individuals of a species.
47	
48	In July-August 1980 a low-intensity fire burnt part of the Brisbane Water area, including half of the site A transect. There was no canopy scorch and the fire was of
49	
50	######## PDF PAGE 3 ########
51	Benson, Fire-sensitive shrub species 341
52	
53	such low intensity that in places it was stopped by the trampled single-file track along the edge of the transect resulting from the three-monthly recordings. Although it reduced the amount of data from this site, a number of observations were made on species affected by the fire.

114	
115	######## PDF PAGE 4 ########
116	342 Cunninghamia Vol. 1(3): 1985
117	
118	## RESULTS
119	
120	The number of years to first flowering of marked seedlings is shown in Table 2. The time taken for different species ranges from one year for *Poranthera microphylla* to seven to eight years for *Banksia ericifolia*, with many species taking four to six years. Although different species are present, the pattern at each site was similar. Table 3 shows the pattern of flowering at site D for the eight-year period. The first flowering for several species took place within two years of the fire, followed by the gradual addition of other species during the succeeding five years. A similar pattern was recorded for the other three sites at Brisbane Water and that at Glenorie.
121	
122	The onset of flowering rarely included all individuals of a population and commonly only involved a few particularly advanced plants. Figure 1 shows the actual numbers of marked plants for selected species at site D at Brisbane Water and at Glenorie. Here, on the first flowering occasion, between 10 and 40 per cent of individuals of a species were involved, but flowering did not reach a peak for another one to several years. Similar results were obtained for species at the other sites.

202	Figure 1. Flowering periods after fire for selected species at Brisbane Water (site D) (a-e) and Glenorie (f-i), showing total marked seedlings (upper line) and number flowering (hatched bar) for *Actinotus helianthi* (a & f), *Platysace linearifolia* (b & g), *Woollsia pungens* (c), *Boronia ledifolia* (d), *Eriostemon buxifolius* (e & h) and *Petrophile pulchella* (i). For each graph, the vertical axis represents number of plants, and the horizontal axis represents number of years after fire.
203
