205	
206	Fruit set occurred in most species. An exception was *Grevillea sericea* in which marked plants failed to set fruit after first flowering, but did so after subsequent flowering. In many species, notably those of the family Rutaceae, seed is released within a few months of flowering, but some species, particularly those of the woody-fruited Proteaceae, take a year after flowering for the characteristic woody follicles to develop. Examples are *Banksia ericifolia*, *Hakea teretifolia* and *Petrophile pulchella*, the slowest to flower of the species in the study area.
207	
208	A decline in numbers following flowering was recorded for *Mitrasacme polymorpha*, *Poranthera ericifolia* and in particular *Actinotus helianthi*. Individuals of these species had completely disappeared within five years; they may be regarded as early successional species. No further species disappeared from the plots during the recording period except for a number of species represented by only a single marked individual.
209	
210	######## PDF PAGE 7 ########
211	Benson, Fire-sensitive shrub species 345
212	
213	The recorded times to achieve flowering for plants in the vicinity (Table 2) are almost all much shorter than for the marked plants, but do not really indicate the responses of the population as a whole. This is because many recordings are of individuals that were either unaffected or only slightly affected by the fire, as a result of the protection offered by the minor cliff-line, rock-outcrop and moist-soak microhabitats. The results indicate the potential resilience of a system in which considerable topographic variation provides fire refugia, but cannot be extrapolated to sites with less variable topography.
214	
215	The effect of the low intensity fire at site A was interesting — *Poranthera ericifolia* and *Gonocarpus teucrioides*, which had died out before the fire, reappeared. However, individuals of *Platysace linearifolia*, which had appeared only as seedlings after the 1974-75 summer fire, were not killed but resprouted at ground level, indicating that fire-sensitivity in that species may be related to the intensity of the fire.
216	
217	## DISCUSSION
218	
219	Fire-sensitive species may make up a significant component of Australian vegetation. For example, in dry sclerophyll communities near Canberra, of 93 species studied by Purdie & Slatyer (1976), 27 per cent were killed by fire and regenerated only from seed. A similar proportion are present in the scleromorphic flora of Sydney's Hawkesbury Sandstone, particularly on the higher rainfall coastal areas. Of the species recorded in this study 20 are known to be fire-sensitive, and a further 13 are probably so. The only resprouter species to be marked were *Actinotus minor*, *Platysace linearifolia*, *Banksia oblongifolia* and *B. serrata* (neither of the marked *Banksia* species flowered during the recording period). Fire-sensitive species are likely to be severely disadvantaged and possibly eliminated by a series of fires at intervals less than the time taken for seedling regeneration to produce further seed. The results here show that fire-sensitive species may not flower for two to eight years after a fire. Major flowering is not attained for one or two years after that. Similar results were found for all sites at Brisbane Water and also at Glenorie, and are likely to apply to other areas on Sydney's Hawkesbury Sandstone.
220	
221	The results highlight the variability present within most wild populations. For instance, although most individuals may flower simultaneously, there will generally be some individuals flowering out of season.
222	
223	Flowering is an effective indicator of maturity only if it is associated with the development of mature viable seed and leads to the build-up of an adequate seedbank. Some species, particularly those with woody fruits, take up to a year for the fruits to mature, and are vulnerable to fire during this period. Examples are *Banksia ericifolia*, *Hakea teretifolia* and *Petrophile pulchella*. Although fruit formation generally appears to accompany flowering, the percentage viability of the first seeds set by an individual may not be known. In *B. ericifolia*, *B. serrata*, *P. pulchella* and *Isopogon anemonifolius*, first seed set on juvenile plants is normal in terms of viability, i.e. it is comparable to seed viability produced in older plants. However, the number of seeds per cone is often significantly lower in the first and second crops (R. Bradstock, pers. comm.). The density of seedlings at the beginning of this work and the early seedling mortality encountered suggest that some species recruit from a relatively large seedbank either already stored in the soil or available from woody capsules. Certainly, for the survival of each species a minimum seedbank must be present, though the necessary size for most species is unknown.
224	
225	######## PDF PAGE 8 ########
226	346 Cunninghamia Vol. 1(3): 1985
227	
228	Without this seedbank, floristic composition will change to a dominance by resprouter or rhizomatous species, or to annual species, commonly exotics, which seed rapidly. Though rhizomatous species such as *Pteridium esculentum* and monocotyledonous families such as Poaceae and Cyperaceae can spread vegetatively, most dicotyledonous resprouters, with the exception of some which root-sucker, cannot and so rely on seed for the establishment of new individuals. Frequent burning may possibly weaken and eventually kill individual resprouters, so that some seedling establishment is necessary to replace them if the plant community composition is to remain reasonably stable. The critical fire-free period here will be the interval from seedling establishment to the production of an adequate fire-resistant rootstock. However, since seedling recruitment will not be necessary after every fire, the critical fire-free period will not be needed for every fire cycle.
229	
230	Almost all seedlings appear to establish in the first two years after fire, when there is considerable seedling mortality. Similar results were recorded by Purdie (1977) for dry sclerophyll vegetation near Canberra. After this period, with the exception of a few short-lived species (e.g. *Actinotus helianthi*), few of the marked plants died, despite very dry conditions during the latter part of the recording period. Eight years after fire the shrub component of the plant community appears healthy and actively growing, with no sign of senescence. It is likely that such conditions will continue for 15 to 20 years after fire.
231	
232	The localized elimination of the tall woody species *Banksia ericifolia*, *Allocasuarina distyla* and *Hakea teretifolia* by frequent repeated burning has been reported at North Head, Sydney (Siddiqi *et al.*, 1976). Generally, however, the local disappearance of species in bushland has not been recorded. If there has indeed been a loss, the absence of observations could be for two reasons.
233	
234	Firstly, the physiographic and habitat variation within the Hawkesbury Sandstone environment provides an uneven burn pattern with varying local fire intensities and localized fire refuges such as around rocky outcrops, cliff-lines or moist gullies. Our records of flowering within a year of the 1974-75 fire by the fire-sensitive species *Boronia serrulata*, *Eriostemon buxifolius* and *E. australasius* were from unburnt individuals growing amongst rock outcrops, which had provided fire protection. Thus, a plant community may be able to recover from potentially disastrous too-frequent burns by re-invasion from unburnt refuges. However, a succession of frequent burns will greatly increase the chances of losing species.
235	
236	Secondly, the impressive species richness and diversity of plant communities on Hawkesbury Sandstone (426 dicotyledons are recorded for Brisbane Water National Park by Benson & Fallding, 1981) obscures, for most casual observers, changes in the abundance of individual species, particularly the less abundant and less conspicuous species, and particularly where such changes may be taking place gradually over decades. Most of the literature on the effect of fires on fire-sensitive species in the Sydney area concerns *Banksia ericifolia*, one of the most conspicuous and abundant species (e.g. Carpenter & Recher, 1979; Bradstock & Myerscough, 1981). Indeed, it may be the less common species that are more likely to be endangered by too-frequent fires. In their list of rare and restricted species in Brisbane Water National Park, Benson & Fallding (1981) include a number that are probably fire-sensitive. These include *Leucopogon amplexicaulis*, found in areas with low fire frequency, *L. margarodes* in areas not burnt for eight to ten years, *Darwinia procera* on a rocky ridge, and *D. glaucophylla* on rock outcrops that evidently protect it from fire, but it is not known whether these have previously been more abundant and whether frequent burning has endangered them.
237	
238	######## PDF PAGE 9 ########
239	Benson, Fire-sensitive shrub species 347
240	
241	## FIRE MANAGEMENT IN NATURAL AREAS
242	
243	The effects of frequent burning in bushland areas have become particularly important with the increasing use of regular burning as a management tool. Such burning may be "controlled" (and intended only for fuel reduction) or "prescribed" (and sometimes involve biological as well as fuel reduction aims). Both involve the application of regular low-intensity fires, generally at intervals of between two and five years, though planned frequencies often vary widely in reality, to reduce flammable fuel. This is most commonly carried out during cool weather in autumn or spring, in order to keep fire intensities low and manageable. High-intensity prescribed burning is theoretically possible and may be biologically desirable, but there are problems with implementation (for details see Good, 1981; Luke & McArthur, 1978; Foster, 1976).
244	
245	The use of control burning at these frequencies may have the following deleterious effects, which will be particularly undesirable in areas reserved for the protection of native plants.
246	
247	(1) Fire-sensitive species may be eliminated by repeated burning at time intervals that are less than that required to produce seed. For example, burning an area several times in quick succession is reported by Luke & McArthur (1978) to eliminate species of *Acacia* by exhausting their seedbank without allowing it to be replaced.
248	
249	(2) Fruiting in both fire-sensitive and fire-resistant species may be reduced by burning when the plants are in flower or have immature fruits. Though there will generally be some species in flower at any time of the year, many species have a concentrated peak in spring (Timms, 1978), followed by seed maturation and release in summer. This is common in the families Fabaceae and Rutaceae, which are particularly conspicuous in the Hawkesbury Sandstone flora. Thus, a season's potential seed supply may be destroyed by burning when it is immature.
250	
251	(3) Fire-resistant species may be eliminated by continual weakening and death of individuals. For example, Noble (1982) reports that in western New South Wales, mallee eucalypts, generally regarded as having a marked tolerance to periodic fire through their ability to produce epicormic shoots, do die when burnt more than once, especially when one burn closely follows another.
252	
253	(4) Low-intensity fires may not stimulate adequate seedling germination, though allowing rhizomatous regeneration. Gill (1975) noted that for the Australian flora a high burning frequency often leads to dominance by monocotyledonous and fern species in place of shrubs. For example, Bradley (1972) reports on the occurrence of *Pteridium esculentum* and *Culcita dubia* after cool burns in Sydney bushland, while Luke & McArthur (1978) refer to *Imperata cylindrica* as prominent in coastal forests of northern New South Wales that have been burnt extensively.
254	
255	A likely result of these factors is that areas of bush may be simplified both floristically and structurally.
256	
257	For the fire-sensitive species examined, a period of six to seven years is needed to reach regular flowering. In addition, another year is required by some of the slowest-flowering species to develop mature seed. The question of the time needed to establish adequate seedbank reserves, either in the soil or within the plant canopy, has not been determined for many species. It is likely that most species require several seed-bearing seasons for this. Thus, for the communities examined a minimum fire-free period of nine to ten years is needed in a majority of fire cycles. An occasional burn followed quickly by another may be tolerated as seed reserves in the soil may
258	
259	######## PDF PAGE 10 ########
260	348 Cunninghamia Vol. 1(3): 1985
261	
262	not necessarily be exhausted by one fire. However, this is dependent on an adequate seedbank having been built up prior to the first fire.
263	
264	The implications for fire management in natural areas are obvious. Before a long-term burning regime is imposed on an area of native bushland, the consequences of that action should be evaluated. As far as the survival of plant species is concerned, where there are often very little reliable data, it is necessary to err on the conservative side. That is, the time intervals between burns, in a majority of fire cycles, should be longer than the minimum suggested by the present findings.
265	
266	## ACKNOWLEDGMENTS
267	
268	This paper would not have been possible but for the enthusiasm and dedication of Dorothy Darvodelsky, Avril Donovan, Florence Dwight, Marie and John Glass, Marge Gowan, Valerie Jones, Clarice Morris and Peter Price, who germinated interest in the work and have continued with the data collection every three months, in all weathers. The assistance of staff from the Hawkesbury District Office of the National Parks and Wildlife Service is gratefully acknowledged. I would also like to thank Ross Bradstock, Jocelyn Powell, Marilyn Fox, Heidi Fallding and David Keith for commenting on the manuscript.

# MATURATION PERIODS FOR FIRE-SENSITIVE SHRUB SPECIES IN HAWKESBURY SANDSTONE VEGETATION

D. H. BENSON

(Accepted for publication 11.5.1984)

## ABSTRACT

*Benson, D. H. (National Herbarium of New South Wales, Royal Botanic Gardens, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia 2000) 1985. Maturation periods for fire-sensitive shrub species in Hawkesbury Sandstone vegetation. Cunninghamia 1(3), 339-349.* The maturation times (period from germination to flowering) for a number of fire-sensitive shrub species in Hawkesbury Sandstone vegetation at sites in Brisbane Water National Park and at Glenorie near Sydney were recorded from marked seedlings established after hot fires. They range from two to seven years for different species. The implications for fire management, particularly for controlled burning, are discussed. A fire-free period of at least nine to ten years is recommended for similar vegetation if successful flowering and seed set, and continued species survival is to occur.

## INTRODUCTION

Plant species fall into two main groups with regard to their response to fire: some are characterized by vegetative regrowth, where individuals either resprout from epicormic shoots on the trunk and major surviving limbs or, following the death of all above-ground stems, resprout from underground rootstocks, lignotubers or rhizomes (sprouters); others regenerate from seed either stored in the soil before the fire, carried on the plants in woody fruits and released after the fire, or carried in from adjacent unburnt areas (non-sprouters). Adults in the second group are fire-sensitive and generally killed outright (Gill, 1975, 1981; Bradstock, 1981).

The relative proportions of these groups of species appear to be related to the fire frequency in the habitat (Christensen, Recher & Hoare, 1981). In wet sclerophyll forest the proportion of fire-sensitive species is roughly 50 to 60 per cent (Ashton, 1981). In the more frequently burnt dry sclerophyll forests near Canberra, Purdie & Slatyer (1976) found 65 per cent regenerated vegetatively but only 27 per cent of species were fire-sensitive and only regenerated from seed.

The time necessary for reproduction after fire is an important characteristic, especially in fire-sensitive species. Specht, Rayson & Jackman (1958) noted that fires at intervals of five years in heath vegetation are likely to eliminate or reduce numbers of some species that take several years to reach reproductive maturity. Similarly, for bushland north of Sydney, Siddiqi, Carolin & Myerscough (1976) recorded the localized elimination of the woody fire-sensitive species *Banksia ericifolia*, *Allocasuarina distyla* and *Hakea teretifolia* by repeated burning. However, to predict the impact of a series of fires, data on the maturation periods for fire-sensitive species are needed. With some exceptions, e.g. *Banksia ericifolia* (Carpenter & Recher, 1979) and *Leptospermum laevigatum* (Burrell, 1968), such data are not available. The potential effect of frequent burning on fire-sensitive species has become particularly relevant with the increased adoption of "controlled" or "prescribed" burning in bushland areas. Such burning generally involves the application of regular fires of low intensity, commonly at intervals of between two and five years.

This paper documents the time required for a group of fire-sensitive species to reach maturity and discusses the implications for regular, frequent burning programs.

######## PDF PAGE 2 ########
340 Cunninghamia Vol. 1(3): 1985

## METHODS

The main study locality was in Brisbane Water National Park (33° 30'S, 151° 15'E), 40 km north of Sydney. Bushland here is eucalypt-dominated scleromorphic vegetation on low-nutrient Hawkesbury Sandstone. Rainfall is about 1250 mm per annum (Bureau of Meteorology, 1979). The general vegetation is described by Benson & Fallding (1981). A second locality was studied at Glenorie (33° 35'S, 151° 00'E), 15 km north-west of Hornsby, on similar Hawkesbury Sandstone, but with average rainfall of 930 mm per annum, to see whether similar results were obtained in a lower rainfall.

A hot summer (1974-75) fire occurred at the Brisbane Water locality six months before the first observations were made and the size of dead bushes at the time indicated that the area had been unburnt for about 15 years before this. As a result of topographic and drainage features, there was considerable variation in microhabitat; therefore, four sites in generally similar, but slightly different, vegetation were chosen as follows:

- Site A — low-woodland with *Eucalyptus haemastoma* and *E. gummifera* on a gently sloping hillside
- Site B — open-heath on a broad rocky ledge
- Site C — low open-forest of *Banksia serrata* and *Eucalyptus gummifera*
- Site D — woodland of *Eucalyptus piperita* subsp. *piperita* and *E. gummifera* on a sandy ledge below a small cliff-line.

A shrubby understorey characterized all the sites, although site C also had a considerable amount of grassy growth. Sites A and B were poorly drained. All sites were within about 0.5 km of each other.

The Glenorie site was in woodland of *Eucalyptus eximia* and *E. gummifera* on a dry ridgetop and had been burnt in January 1975.

At each site a transect of 10 contiguous 1 m × 1 m plots was established. Each of these plots was subdivided into four 0.5 m × 0.5 m sub-plots and two seedlings within each sub-plot were selected and marked with coloured wires. Seedlings were distinguished from plants regenerating from rootstocks or rhizomes by the presence of cotyledons or by comparison with similar plants that had been dug up and their roots examined. Although restricted to dicotyledonous species, as wide a range of species as possible was chosen, and the most healthy seedlings marked. Table 1 lists the 37 species included in this study, their susceptibility to fire and the total number of seedlings marked ("?" indicates species that are probably fire-sensitive). Initially, 320 seedlings were marked. Many of these died during the first years of recording. Additional plants were marked to replace dead plants during the first two years, after which no additional plants were marked. The occurrence of flowering was recorded four times a year (at Brisbane Water in early March, June, September and December; at Glenorie in early February, May, August and November) for the following eight years.

At the same time all species flowering within about 30 m of the transect were recorded. Because of the range of microhabitats, such as minor cliff-lines, rock platforms and moist soaks, some of which remained unburnt during the fire, flowering recordings may represent as few as one or two individuals of a species.

In July-August 1980 a low-intensity fire burnt part of the Brisbane Water area, including half of the site A transect. There was no canopy scorch and the fire was of

## RESULTS

The number of years to first flowering of marked seedlings is shown in Table 2. The time taken for different species ranges from one year for *Poranthera microphylla* to seven to eight years for *Banksia ericifolia*, with many species taking four to six years. Although different species are present, the pattern at each site was similar. Table 3 shows the pattern of flowering at site D for the eight-year period. The first flowering for several species took place within two years of the fire, followed by the gradual addition of other species during the succeeding five years. A similar pattern was recorded for the other three sites at Brisbane Water and that at Glenorie.

The onset of flowering rarely included all individuals of a population and commonly only involved a few particularly advanced plants. Figure 1 shows the actual numbers of marked plants for selected species at site D at Brisbane Water and at Glenorie. Here, on the first flowering occasion, between 10 and 40 per cent of individuals of a species were involved, but flowering did not reach a peak for another one to several years. Similar results were obtained for species at the other sites.

Fruit set occurred in most species. An exception was *Grevillea sericea* in which marked plants failed to set fruit after first flowering, but did so after subsequent flowering. In many species, notably those of the family Rutaceae, seed is released within a few months of flowering, but some species, particularly those of the woody-fruited Proteaceae, take a year after flowering for the characteristic woody follicles to develop. Examples are *Banksia ericifolia*, *Hakea teretifolia* and *Petrophile pulchella*, the slowest to flower of the species in the study area.

A decline in numbers following flowering was recorded for *Mitrasacme polymorpha*, *Poranthera ericifolia* and in particular *Actinotus helianthi*. Individuals of these species had completely disappeared within five years; they may be regarded as early successional species. No further species disappeared from the plots during the recording period except for a number of species represented by only a single marked individual.

The recorded times to achieve flowering for plants in the vicinity (Table 2) are almost all much shorter than for the marked plants, but do not really indicate the responses of the population as a whole. This is because many recordings are of individuals that were either unaffected or only slightly affected by the fire, as a result of the protection offered by the minor cliff-line, rock-outcrop and moist-soak microhabitats. The results indicate the potential resilience of a system in which considerable topographic variation provides fire refugia, but cannot be extrapolated to sites with less variable topography.

The effect of the low intensity fire at site A was interesting — *Poranthera ericifolia* and *Gonocarpus teucrioides*, which had died out before the fire, reappeared. However, individuals of *Platysace linearifolia*, which had appeared only as seedlings after the 1974-75 summer fire, were not killed but resprouted at ground level, indicating that fire-sensitivity in that species may be related to the intensity of the fire.

## DISCUSSION

Fire-sensitive species may make up a significant component of Australian vegetation. For example, in dry sclerophyll communities near Canberra, of 93 species studied by Purdie & Slatyer (1976), 27 per cent were killed by fire and regenerated only from seed. A similar proportion are present in the scleromorphic flora of Sydney's Hawkesbury Sandstone, particularly on the higher rainfall coastal areas. Of the species recorded in this study 20 are known to be fire-sensitive, and a further 13 are probably so. The only resprouter species to be marked were *Actinotus minor*, *Platysace linearifolia*, *Banksia oblongifolia* and *B. serrata* (neither of the marked *Banksia* species flowered during the recording period). Fire-sensitive species are likely to be severely disadvantaged and possibly eliminated by a series of fires at intervals less than the time taken for seedling regeneration to produce further seed. The results here show that fire-sensitive species may not flower for two to eight years after a fire. Major flowering is not attained for one or two years after that. Similar results were found for all sites at Brisbane Water and also at Glenorie, and are likely to apply to other areas on Sydney's Hawkesbury Sandstone.

The results highlight the variability present within most wild populations. For instance, although most individuals may flower simultaneously, there will generally be some individuals flowering out of season.

Flowering is an effective indicator of maturity only if it is associated with the development of mature viable seed and leads to the build-up of an adequate seedbank. Some species, particularly those with woody fruits, take up to a year for the fruits to mature, and are vulnerable to fire during this period. Examples are *Banksia ericifolia*, *Hakea teretifolia* and *Petrophile pulchella*. Although fruit formation generally appears to accompany flowering, the percentage viability of the first seeds set by an individual may not be known. In *B. ericifolia*, *B. serrata*, *P. pulchella* and *Isopogon anemonifolius*, first seed set on juvenile plants is normal in terms of viability, i.e. it is comparable to seed viability produced in older plants. However, the number of seeds per cone is often significantly lower in the first and second crops (R. Bradstock, pers. comm.). The density of seedlings at the beginning of this work and the early seedling mortality encountered suggest that some species recruit from a relatively large seedbank either already stored in the soil or available from woody capsules. Certainly, for the survival of each species a minimum seedbank must be present, though the necessary size for most species is unknown.

######## PDF PAGE 8 ########
346 Cunninghamia Vol. 1(3): 1985

Without this seedbank, floristic composition will change to a dominance by resprouter or rhizomatous species, or to annual species, commonly exotics, which seed rapidly. Though rhizomatous species such as *Pteridium esculentum* and monocotyledonous families such as Poaceae and Cyperaceae can spread vegetatively, most dicotyledonous resprouters, with the exception of some which root-sucker, cannot and so rely on seed for the establishment of new individuals. Frequent burning may possibly weaken and eventually kill individual resprouters, so that some seedling establishment is necessary to replace them if the plant community composition is to remain reasonably stable. The critical fire-free period here will be the interval from seedling establishment to the production of an adequate fire-resistant rootstock. However, since seedling recruitment will not be necessary after every fire, the critical fire-free period will not be needed for every fire cycle.

Almost all seedlings appear to establish in the first two years after fire, when there is considerable seedling mortality. Similar results were recorded by Purdie (1977) for dry sclerophyll vegetation near Canberra. After this period, with the exception of a few short-lived species (e.g. *Actinotus helianthi*), few of the marked plants died, despite very dry conditions during the latter part of the recording period. Eight years after fire the shrub component of the plant community appears healthy and actively growing, with no sign of senescence. It is likely that such conditions will continue for 15 to 20 years after fire.

The localized elimination of the tall woody species *Banksia ericifolia*, *Allocasuarina distyla* and *Hakea teretifolia* by frequent repeated burning has been reported at North Head, Sydney (Siddiqi *et al.*, 1976). Generally, however, the local disappearance of species in bushland has not been recorded. If there has indeed been a loss, the absence of observations could be for two reasons.

Firstly, the physiographic and habitat variation within the Hawkesbury Sandstone environment provides an uneven burn pattern with varying local fire intensities and localized fire refuges such as around rocky outcrops, cliff-lines or moist gullies. Our records of flowering within a year of the 1974-75 fire by the fire-sensitive species *Boronia serrulata*, *Eriostemon buxifolius* and *E. australasius* were from unburnt individuals growing amongst rock outcrops, which had provided fire protection. Thus, a plant community may be able to recover from potentially disastrous too-frequent burns by re-invasion from unburnt refuges. However, a succession of frequent burns will greatly increase the chances of losing species.

Secondly, the impressive species richness and diversity of plant communities on Hawkesbury Sandstone (426 dicotyledons are recorded for Brisbane Water National Park by Benson & Fallding, 1981) obscures, for most casual observers, changes in the abundance of individual species, particularly the less abundant and less conspicuous species, and particularly where such changes may be taking place gradually over decades. Most of the literature on the effect of fires on fire-sensitive species in the Sydney area concerns *Banksia ericifolia*, one of the most conspicuous and abundant species (e.g. Carpenter & Recher, 1979; Bradstock & Myerscough, 1981). Indeed, it may be the less common species that are more likely to be endangered by too-frequent fires. In their list of rare and restricted species in Brisbane Water National Park, Benson & Fallding (1981) include a number that are probably fire-sensitive. These include *Leucopogon amplexicaulis*, found in areas with low fire frequency, *L. margarodes* in areas not burnt for eight to ten years, *Darwinia procera* on a rocky ridge, and *D. glaucophylla* on rock outcrops that evidently protect it from fire, but it is not known whether these have previously been more abundant and whether frequent burning has endangered them.

## FIRE MANAGEMENT IN NATURAL AREAS

The effects of frequent burning in bushland areas have become particularly important with the increasing use of regular burning as a management tool. Such burning may be "controlled" (and intended only for fuel reduction) or "prescribed" (and sometimes involve biological as well as fuel reduction aims). Both involve the application of regular low-intensity fires, generally at intervals of between two and five years, though planned frequencies often vary widely in reality, to reduce flammable fuel. This is most commonly carried out during cool weather in autumn or spring, in order to keep fire intensities low and manageable. High-intensity prescribed burning is theoretically possible and may be biologically desirable, but there are problems with implementation (for details see Good, 1981; Luke & McArthur, 1978; Foster, 1976).

The use of control burning at these frequencies may have the following deleterious effects, which will be particularly undesirable in areas reserved for the protection of native plants.

(1) Fire-sensitive species may be eliminated by repeated burning at time intervals that are less than that required to produce seed. For example, burning an area several times in quick succession is reported by Luke & McArthur (1978) to eliminate species of *Acacia* by exhausting their seedbank without allowing it to be replaced.

(2) Fruiting in both fire-sensitive and fire-resistant species may be reduced by burning when the plants are in flower or have immature fruits. Though there will generally be some species in flower at any time of the year, many species have a concentrated peak in spring (Timms, 1978), followed by seed maturation and release in summer. This is common in the families Fabaceae and Rutaceae, which are particularly conspicuous in the Hawkesbury Sandstone flora. Thus, a season's potential seed supply may be destroyed by burning when it is immature.

(3) Fire-resistant species may be eliminated by continual weakening and death of individuals. For example, Noble (1982) reports that in western New South Wales, mallee eucalypts, generally regarded as having a marked tolerance to periodic fire through their ability to produce epicormic shoots, do die when burnt more than once, especially when one burn closely follows another.

(4) Low-intensity fires may not stimulate adequate seedling germination, though allowing rhizomatous regeneration. Gill (1975) noted that for the Australian flora a high burning frequency often leads to dominance by monocotyledonous and fern species in place of shrubs. For example, Bradley (1972) reports on the occurrence of *Pteridium esculentum* and *Culcita dubia* after cool burns in Sydney bushland, while Luke & McArthur (1978) refer to *Imperata cylindrica* as prominent in coastal forests of northern New South Wales that have been burnt extensively.

A likely result of these factors is that areas of bush may be simplified both floristically and structurally.

For the fire-sensitive species examined, a period of six to seven years is needed to reach regular flowering. In addition, another year is required by some of the slowest-flowering species to develop mature seed. The question of the time needed to establish adequate seedbank reserves, either in the soil or within the plant canopy, has not been determined for many species. It is likely that most species require several seed-bearing seasons for this. Thus, for the communities examined a minimum fire-free period of nine to ten years is needed in a majority of fire cycles. An occasional burn followed quickly by another may be tolerated as seed reserves in the soil may

######## PDF PAGE 10 ########
348 Cunninghamia Vol. 1(3): 1985

not necessarily be exhausted by one fire. However, this is dependent on an adequate seedbank having been built up prior to the first fire.

The implications for fire management in natural areas are obvious. Before a long-term burning regime is imposed on an area of native bushland, the consequences of that action should be evaluated. As far as the survival of plant species is concerned, where there are often very little reliable data, it is necessary to err on the conservative side. That is, the time intervals between burns, in a majority of fire cycles, should be longer than the minimum suggested by the present findings.

1	## n_pages=15
2	
3	######## PDF PAGE 1 ########
4	*Australian Journal of Ecology* (1988) **13**, 505-518
5	
6	# Demography of woody plants in relation to fire: *Banksia ericifolia* L.f. and *Petrophile pulchella* (Schrad) R.Br.
7	
8	R. A. BRADSTOCK\*
9	*School of Biological Sciences, Macleay Building A12, University of Sydney, Sydney, NSW 2006, Australia*
10	
11	M. A. O'CONNELL
12	*NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, Box N189 Grosvenor St, Sydney, NSW 2000, Australia*
13	
14	## Abstract
15	
16	*Plants of* Banksia ericifolia *and* Petrophile pulchella *are sensitive to fire. Changes in population size under different fire regimes were estimated, based on measurements of post-fire seedling emergence, seedling survival, survival and seed production in established plants of differing ages, survival of seeds held in serotinous cones and seed-release in the periods between fire.*
17	
18	*Seeds were first available at 5 years in* P. pulchella *and 6 years in* B. ericifolia. *Exact replacement would be possible when burnt at these ages, if seedling establishment were very high. Low establishment would delay replacement to 13 years of age in both species. Late summer/autumn fires of high intensity favour high establishment. Such fires at 8-10 year intervals would be tolerated without any sustained decline in numbers. Fires at 10-15 year intervals could occur regardless of season or intensity with little risk of a population decline. Large increases in numbers and density would follow fires spaced at 15-30 years. Enough seeds would be available for replacement up to about 50 years in both species. Viable seed-release in unburnt conditions was sufficient to compensate for deaths in stands over 20 years old, even with very low levels of establishment.*
19	
20	*Two variables accounted for the biggest changes in numbers and density between generations interspersed by fires; namely the age at which a stand is burned and the proportion of seeds which emerge as seedlings. A comparison with other similar species showed similarities in controls on emergence and establishment, lengths of primary juvenile periods and life spans.*
21	
22	## Introduction
23	
24	Plants which rely on seeds for regeneration after fire (obligate seeders) form a prominent part of the vegetation in many fire-prone regions of the world (Gill 1981; Keeley 1981). Some obligate seeders are serotinous as their seeds are retained in the canopy and released by fire (Lotan 1976).
25	
26	The present report presents demographic studies of two species which co-occur in fire-prone vegetation in the Sydney Region of south-eastern Australia: *Banksia ericifolia* L.f. and *Petrophile pulchella* (Schrad) R.Br. These perennial woody shrubs are frequently dominant in shrublands or the understorey of woodlands. Plants of both species are usually killed by fires of most intensities. Seeds (achenes in *P. pulchella*) are stored in woody infructescences, referred to here as cones, within closed follicles (*B. ericifolia*) or bracts (*P. pulchella*). Many other species of shrubs or small trees in these local vegetation types are also serotinous obligate seeders (Beadle 1940; Clemens & Franklin 1981; Benson 1985).
27	
28	Crucial aspects of the demography of serotinous, obligate seeders are: (i) the time taken to first reproduction (primary juvenile period, Gill 1975) which determines the minimum possible interval at which fire may recur without causing extinction (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bond *et al.* 1984; Gill & McMahon 1986) because seeds are usually non-dormant; (ii) seedling establishment post-fire, which is determined by rainfall, tempera-
29	
30	\*Present address: NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, Box N189 Grosvenor St, Sydney, NSW 2000, Australia.
31	
32	######## PDF PAGE 2 ########
33	506 *R. A. Bradstock and M. A. O'Connell*
34	
35	ture, predators and the rate of release of seeds which, in turn, may be influenced by the season and intensity of fire (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bond *et al.* 1984; Cowling & Lamont 1984, 1985; McMahon 1984); (iii) the size of the pre-fire seed-bank, which is dependent on current storage plus new seeds added after each episode of seasonal fruiting minus losses of stored seeds in existing fruits (McMaster & Zedler 1981; Bond 1984; Gill & McMahon 1986); (iv) rates of survival of seedlings, juveniles and adults; (v) any subsequent establishment in unburnt conditions. Survival will be partly determined by density and age (Schlesinger & Gill 1978; Morris & Myerscough 1983, 1988). If establishment is absent in such conditions, the numbers and density in an even-aged post-fire generation will decline to low levels as the time since last fire nears the limit of longevity of the species (Specht *et al.* 1958; Ashton 1976; Gill & McMahon 1986).
36	
37	These factors can be linked in a demographic model to predict population size over successive generations subject to re-occurring fires. Such information would provide a detailed basis for the management of fire-prone plant communities. However, few studies have attempted to relate changes in population size to fire regimes (Zedler 1977; Kruger 1983). At present there is much pressure for repeated burning of the vegetation containing the study species at intervals of less than 10 years for the purpose of fuel reduction. Often such prescribed fires are ignited in the cool months, between April and October. If informed fire-management is to take place it is important to know how these fire regimes and their alternatives may affect these potentially vulnerable, serotinous, obligate seeders. This study aimed to answer the following questions.
38	
39	(1) What is the shortest interval between fires (maximum fire frequency) that either species can withstand for a sustained period (e.g. about 100 years) without suffering a prolonged decrease in population size?
40	
41	(2) How is this maximum tolerable fire frequency affected by differences in the amounts of seedling emergence and survival occurring after different fires?
42	
43	(3) Are variations in seedling emergence and survival related to the seasonal timing and intensity of fires?
44	
45	(4) What are the likely trends in numbers and density of stands when fires occur infrequently?
46	
47	(5) How do these species compare with other serotinous obligate seeders?
48	
49	## Methods
50	
51	### *Study sites*
52	
53	The survival of plants more than 3 years of age, and the sizes of their seed-banks, were studied in seven areas situated within the Brisbane Water National Park, approximately 50 km north of Sydney, from 1980-83. These areas were last burned in 1977, 1976, 1975, 1974, 1973, 1968 and 1960 respectively, determined from fire-history maps and aerial photographs. All were located on ridge-tops of sandy earths derived from Hawkesbury Sandstone. Distance from the coast varied between 3 and 15 km.
54	
55	Observations on the emergence and survival of seedlings (<3 years of age) were made in populations after four unplanned fires and in one experiment, between December 1980 and November 1982. These were located in the same area and had similar site characteristics to those populations used for the study of established plants.
56	
57	### *Seedling emergence and survival*
58	
59	The number of seedlings that emerged after each fire was counted in 40-70 quadrats (0.1 m²) for each species. The number of pre-fire seeds on dead plants was estimated by counting the number of cones held on branches in transects adjacent to the study quadrats, after the fire. The number of seeds per cone and the proportion of stored seeds that were intact and viable were estimated in cones taken from nearby unburnt stands. These procedures are described below.
60	
61	The fate of the seedlings was followed until mid 1983. Two alternative models of survival, the exponential and power function (Silvertown 1982) were fitted. No model is given for Burn IV in *P. pulchella* due to the small numbers of plants which emerged. Indeed, models were fitted only when data for major cohorts of 10 or more seedlings were available.
62	
63	######## PDF PAGE 3 ########
64	*Demography of woody plants in relation to fire* 507
65	
66	Emergence was studied in two experiments (commenced May and November 1982) in which artificial ashbeds were prepared and known quantities of seeds sown. Quadrats (1 m × 1 m) were prepared by removing all plant cover and litter. Heat was applied to the exposed soil using propane burners. Harvested plant material and litter were ashed and placed on the soil after the heating had ceased. Either 50 (May 1982) or 100 (November 1982) seeds of each species were scattered on the quadrats several days later. The number of emerged seedlings was counted on average every month for a year after the starting dates.
67	
68	### *Survival in established plants*
69	
70	Survival was measured in samples of 50 or more plants of both species which were tagged in late 1980-early 1981. Each sample was located within quadrats (1.0 m × 1.0 m or 0.5 m × 0.5 m) on two adjacent lines randomly situated on a 20 m baseline located in thick patches of either species. All tagged plants were assumed to have arisen as seedlings after the previous fire in each area. The initial height of each plant was recorded.
71	
72	Plants of *B. ericifolia* in some areas (burned 1977, 1974) were located solely on shallow soils (depth 0.3-0.4 m) and these were stunted in height and spindly in form compared with populations located on deep soils (depth 1.0-1.5 m; burned 1973, 1968, 1960). One area (burned 1975) contained plants on both soils. One sample was tagged in each area on each available soil type. A second was then established in each of the 1968 and 1960 areas, several hundred metres from the first.
73	
74	Plants of *P. pulchella* were not as common on shallow soils, therefore samples were tagged only on deep soils. These were separate but often close to the *B. ericifolia* samples. No sampling was done in the 1976 or 1973 areas. Two samples were tagged in each of the other areas. A fire in 1982 destroyed a single sample of each species in the 1960 area.
75	
76	Plants were checked twice yearly from the beginning of 1981 until October 1983 and the proportion of deaths was measured for each area to test for differences in mortality between soils in *B. ericifolia* and between populations of differing age in both species using G tests of independence.
77	
78	### *Seed-survival*
79	
80	Ten cones from each of four age classes (1, 5, 9 and 15 years) were harvested from each sample in 1983. These harvests were spread over three to four plants. Ages were estimated either by direct observation (1 and 5 years only) or by position and appearance (9 and 15 years). Cones of 9 and 15 years were those borne nearest the base of plants and presumed to be from the earliest cohort set in the 1968 stand and from the third oldest cohort in the 1960 stand. The latter origin was assumed because some cones in a more advanced state of degradation were found on the ground and these were assumed to be slightly older. In areas where only a single sample was available for each soil type a replicate of ten cones was harvested 50-100 m from the tagged plants. Two samples of cones were also taken from *P. pulchella* plants at the same time as sampling from *B. ericifolia* in the 1973 area.
81	
82	Counts were made, in the laboratory, of total follicles or bracts and the number that was open and empty was recorded. Cones of *B. ericifolia* were heated in an oven at 200°C for 10 min to open follicles and aid seed removal. This treatment had no effect on seed viability (Bradstock 1985). Cones of *P. pulchella* were left unheated for several weeks after which seed extraction was possible.
83	
84	Twenty unopened follicles/bracts were selected randomly and examined and the seeds within were scored as damaged by predators or intact. If intact, seeds were classified as filled, desiccated or aborted. Viability of intact, filled seeds was determined in batches of 50 by germination on filter paper in petri dishes maintained at saturation for 2-3 months. Germination occurred under optimum conditions (12:12 h day:night cycle of 15:5°C; Bradstock 1985) in an environmental cabinet.
85	
86	The relationship between the proportion of seeds per cone surviving (i.e. intact, filled, viable, unreleased seeds) and age was described using various linear and non-linear models. The preferred model was chosen via a comparison of the percentage variances (PV) accounted for. These PV were the differences between the residual and total mean squares expressed as a percentage of the total mean square.
87	
88	######## PDF PAGE 4 ########
89	508 *R. A. Bradstock and M. A. O'Connell*
90	
91	### *Seed-bank estimation*
92	
93	All new cones set in the samples during the study were counted. Cone production during 1984-85 in the 1960 stands was also measured. Collections of 10 cones produced in two flowering seasons between 1981 and 1983 were made from each sample to determine seed-set per cone. A further 10 cones were harvested in areas with only one sample per soil-depth tested. Mean total annual seed production per plant was thus calculated and then described as a function of age by various linear and non-linear models from which a preferred model was chosen by a comparison of PV.
94	
95	Seed-bank at any given age (per plant) was predicted by estimating the number of seeds (one seed per follicle or bract) set in each of the successive annual cohorts produced up to that age, using the preferred seed production model. In each cohort survival was then calculated using the preferred survival model for each species. The numbers of surviving seeds from each cohort at a given age were then summed to give an estimate of total stored viable seeds for that age. This was repeated for all ages between the time of first reproduction and 40 years. The estimates above 25 years were therefore extrapolations beyond the age limit of the samples. Allowance was made for the time between flowering and fruit maturity which is about one year in both species.
96	
97	A further, alternative estimate of seed-bank was made. Seed production was stopped at age 30 years and the attrition of existing seeds was predicted up to an age of 100 years.
98	
99	### *Seed-release between fires*
100	
101	The mean number of viable seeds released annually (per plant) in each sample in unburnt conditions was estimated. Samples of cones of four different ages were marked in the 1968 and 1960 samples in mid 1981. Two age classes of cones (1 and 5 years in 1981, method of ageing similar to that described above) were marked in all other samples. The oldest cones in each sample were also marked and in 1981 these were estimated to be 7 and 13 years old. Follicles (*B. ericifolia*) or bracts (*P. pulchella*) which were open and empty were marked. Cones were rechecked after 2 years and the number of follicles/bracts was counted along with those which had opened and shed seeds. Rates of seed-release were compared between samples and cone ages using analysis of variance.
102	
103	All cones set before 1981 were counted in each sample. The mean number of seeds released per plant was then estimated from the product of the measured annual rate of release per cone age class and the mean number of cones in each class. Cones set before 1981 were allocated to the nearest age class and a correction was made for viability.
104	
105	### *The effect of frequent fires*
106	
107	The effect of three successive fires, separated by intervals of identical length, on the number of plants in a hypothetical stand of each species was estimated. Plants living in the first interval were called first generation and in the second, second generation. The first generation immediate pre-fire number was set at 50 and model stands were assumed to be similar to the sample stands in other respects, such as density. Eleven calculations were done, using values between 5 and 15 years for the 'between-fire' interval.
108	
109	Second generation stand size (*N*) was calculated as a function of the interval (*i*) between fires using:
110	
111	*N* = *B* × *E* × *Ss* × *Se* (1)
112	
113	where *B* = first generation seed-bank size, *E* = proportion of seeds emerging as post-fire seedlings, *Ss* = proportion of seedlings which survive and *Se* = proportion of living plants >3 years old at *i* years of age. Values of *N* were divided by 50 to give estimates of proportional change in numbers. These estimates were plotted against size of gap between fires. Opposing, extreme values of *E* and *Ss* were used to produce high and low estimates of proportional change.
114	
115	## Results
116	
117	### *Seedling emergence and survival*
118	
119	In both species, emergence was spread over periods of up to 9 months after the fires or experiments. The number, density and proportion of seedlings that emerged from seeds were variable (Table 1). Pulses of emergence pro-
120	
121	######## PDF PAGE 5 ########
122	*Demography of woody plants in relation to fire* 509
123

In *B. ericifolia* the power and exponential models were found to be the models of best fit (Table 2) while in *P. pulchella* the power function was the model of best fit (Table 2). In some cases neither model fitted the data well (Table 2).
125	
126	### *Survival in established plants*

199	### *Seed-bank estimation*
200	
201	The age at first flowering was 4 years in *P. pulchella* and 5 years in *B. ericifolia* on deep soils during this study. No cones were set in *B. ericifolia* on shallow soils though a few inflorescences were produced in adjacent untagged plants.
202	
203	Substantial differences occurred between years and samples, in both the numbers of cones produced and the seeds set within them. These produced large variations in seed production (Fig. 4). There was no evidence of any serial correlation between data from successive years for individual samples.
204	
205	In *P. pulchella*, seed-production was very high in the 1960 sample (Fig. 4). Most cones were young which indicated that cone-production may accelerate rapidly between the ages of 15 and 20 years.
206	
207	The preferred models of seed-production per mean plant (*n*) at stand age (*T*) were:
208	
209	*n* = 4.408 (1.116^*T*) (4) *B. ericifolia*: PV = 70.5

212	
213	Predictions of seed-bank size are given in Fig. 5.

218	[Line graph: Proportion surviving (0-1.0) against time, F 1981 to J 1983]

221	
222	### *Seed-release in the interval between fires*
223	
224	A comparison of seed-release rates indicated that two pooled estimates could be made in *B. ericifolia* (1-5 years, 0.021, and 7-13 years, 0.011 seeds/cone per annum) and three in *P. pulchella* (0.009, 0.036 and 0.041, for 1, 5 and 7-13 year old cones respectively). Estimates of mean number of seeds released annually in the four oldest samples are given in Fig. 6.
225	
226	### *The effect of frequent fires*
227	
228	The alternative values of E were set at 0.5 and 0.05. These bounded the range observed in the field (Table 1). In glasshouse studies, levels of emergence in excess of 0.5 were observed in both species (Bradstock 1985), but elsewhere in the field, in *B. ericifolia* only (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981). The survival models from the April 1981 and December 1980 (highest survival), and May 1982 and July 1981 (lowest survival) fires were used to calculate values of Ss in *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella* (Table 2) respectively. Values of Se were estimated from the appropriate mean death rates.
229	
230	The estimates of between-fire intervals at which replacement was possible in second generation stands were (Fig. 7) 5 and 6 years (high E and Ss, *P. pulchella* and *B. ericifolia* respec-
231	
232	######## PDF PAGE 8 ########
233	512 *R. A. Bradstock and M. A. O'Connell*
234	
235	[Bar graphs (i) and (ii): Follicles open; Seeds intact and filled; Intact seeds viable (proportions 0-1.0) against cone age (years) 1, 5, 9, 15 for stands a-d]
236	
237	FIG. 3. Proportions of seeds retained intact and viable in cones of differing ages in (i) *B. ericifolia* and (ii) *P. pulchella*. Times of last fire were: a = 1976, b = 1973, c = 1968, d = 1960.
238	
239	tively) and 13 years (low E and Ss, both species). Fires at longer intervals than these would cause growth in the size of populations under the specified conditions of emergence and survival (Fig. 7).
240	
241	## Discussion
242	
243	### *Effects of frequent fires*
244	
245	The importance of emergence and survival was reflected in the variability of the interval between fires at which stand replacement would be possible (Fig. 7). Burning at an interval close to 13 years could be done with little regard to other factors such as season or intensity of fire without risk of a decline in numbers. The low levels of emergence and survival (Tables 1, 2) used to produce this estimate were the product of a severe drought in the area (Bureau of Meteorology, pers. comm.). It is likely that fires in most years will produce at least a similar or larger number of seedlings. Survival of established plants may also be higher, for this reason.
246	
247	Fire-managers may wish to burn as often as twice a decade, hence it is necessary to know the limit to which fire frequency can be reduced below 13 years without risking a serious decline in numbers. Seasons and intensities of fire may become important in such
248	
249	######## PDF PAGE 9 ########
250	*Demography of woody plants in relation to fire* 513
251	
252	[Scatter plots with fitted lines: Mean annual seed production (log scale) against Age (years) 0-25, *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella*]
253	
254	FIG. 4. Mean annual seed-production per plant as a function of age. Preferred models (highest percentage variance accounted for) are indicated by unbroken lines.
255	
256	[Line graphs: Mean number of seeds per plant (log) against Age (years) 0-90, *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella*]
257	
258	FIG. 5. Mean number of stored viable seeds (seed-bank) per plant, under two regimes of seed production: continuous (——), ceased at 30 years (- - -).
259	
260	circumstances as will year to year variability in rainfall.
261	
262	Bradstock (1985) found that emergence in *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella* varied with rainfall, soil moisture and temperature. High summer temperatures impose a form of exogenous dormancy on seeds (definition of Mott & Groves 1981), restricting emergence to the cooler months. Seeds which lie on the soil over summer lose some viability. The amount of emergence was positively correlated with the period of time the soil surface (0-1.0 cm) remains at field capacity after rain. Seed predation was minimal in burnt areas.
263	
264	Rainfall near the coast in the Sydney Region is highest, on average, from January to July (100-130 mm/month), and lowest from August to December (70-80 mm/month); however, there is great year to year variation. When evaporation is taken into account, the average period of sustained high soil moisture is May-July (early winter). Emergence may therefore be highest after fires which are timed so that most seeds are released in early winter. Seed-release will be most rapid after high intensity fires (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bradstock 1985) and such fires in late summer-autumn will cause most seeds to be released by early winter. In contrast, low inten-
265	
266	######## PDF PAGE 10 ########
267	514 *R. A. Bradstock and M. A. O'Connell*
268	
269	[Bar graphs: Viable seeds released per mean plant per annum against Age (years) 8, 13, 13, 21; *B. ericifolia* (linear scale) and *P. pulchella* (log scale)]
270	
271	FIG. 6. Estimated annual release of viable seeds per plant in samples of differing age.
272	
273	[Line graphs: Proportional change in stand size (log scale, 0.05-30) against Interval between fires (years) 6-15, *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella*]
274	
275	FIG. 7. Proportional changes in sizes of stands over two generations of equal length as a function of interval between fires and seedling establishment (maximum ○; minimum ●). Intersections of estimates with the broken line indicate intervals at which self-replacement is possible (see text).
276	
277	sity fires at this time will prolong seed-release over winter and spring. Late summer-autumn, high intensity fires will therefore, on average, yield optimum emergence. A similar fire regime giving optimum emergence in other species of serotinous Proteaceae has been observed by Specht *et al.* (1958), Specht (1981), Bond *et al.* (1984), Cowling and Lamont (1984a, 1984b, 1985), McMahon (1984). Mechanisms in each case were generally similar to those described here.
278	
279	While mortality of plants older than 100 days was due mainly to drought, younger seedlings died during both short dry spells and heavy rain (Bradstock 1985) when they were broken by raindrop impact or washed away. Bradstock (1985) concluded that the risk of death at the most vulnerable age (<100 days; Table 2) would be minimized when seedlings emerged in early winter. This reinforced the conclusion that late summer fires are optimal in producing seedlings.
280	
281	After successive fires at 8 years, the proportional change in second generation stand size may vary from 9.8 to 0.5 in *B. ericifolia* and from 7.2 to 0.6 in *P. pulchella* (Fig. 7). The daily rainfall patterns for Sydney over 50 years (Bureau of Meterology, pers. comm.) show that a winter containing two successive months of low soil surface moisture occurs on average once every decade whereas very wet winters in which the soil is more or less continually moist occur several times a decade (Bradstock 1985). Thus fires of optimal season and intensity occurring 8 years apart would be followed by a dry winter and a subsequent decline in post-fire numbers, once every 80-100 years. More usually these fires would be followed by wet winters which would permit an increase in numbers. Hence an optimal regime in terms of season and intensity with an 8-10 year interval may cause fluctuations in numbers but is unlikely to send either species into a persistent decline if sustained over a period of up to 100 years. A 6-8 year cycle would be hazardous, due to a lower seed-bank and the increased probability of encountering dry post-fire conditions.
282	
283	Reproduction is delayed in *B. ericifolia* growing on shallow soils and such stands may decline when fires occur less than 15 years apart. Observations indicate that the primary juvenile period may extend to more than 8 years and also that the seed-bank size may be less than on deep soils.
284	
285	There are, therefore, two consecutive phases in which plants are susceptible to recurrent fires: first, during the primary juvenile period and second, the subsequent time up to the age at which exact self-replacement of stands is possible. So far most attention has been given to describing the lengths of primary juvenile periods. Values given here fell within the ranges already reported for these species (Benson 1985) and for other serotinous obligate seeders of the Proteaceae (3-11 years; Kruger 1983; Lamont 1985). Measurements of this second critical phase need to be made if serotinous obligate seeders are to be used as indicator species in fire-prone vegetation. It
286	
287	######## PDF PAGE 11 ########
288	*Demography of woody plants in relation to fire* 515
289	
290	may be useful if correlations exist between this and other demographic characteristics, particularly the length of the primary juvenile period. For example, is first reproduction at an early age always followed by a short interval to the age of self-replacement or vice versa?
291	
292	Replacement ages for the study species were similar, despite differences in seedling-survival, early rates of development of seed-bank and primary juvenile period. Gill and McMahon (1986) reported that in *Banksia ornata*, a serotinous obligate seeder, common in parts of southern Australia, stand replacement may be likely after 16 years of age if post-fire emergence took place from 20% of available seeds. Seeds first become available at about 6 years in *B. ornata* (Gill & McMahon 1986), a figure comparable to that in *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella*. Despite this similarity, populations of *B. ornata* may decline under some repeated cycles of fire less than 15 years apart, whilst *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella* populations may increase or remain stable. This difference was primarily due to a slower rate of accumulation of seed-bank in *B. ornata*, though other possible differences in projected survival rate were also present. Similarly, Kruger and Bigalke (1984) reported that in *Protea repens*, a shrub of the South African fynbos, the primary juvenile period may be 4-5 years (ripe seeds first available), but replacement age may be 10-12 years. It is most prudent to conclude that there is little current evidence of any consistent linkage between these key events. Further demographic studies amongst a wider range of species are needed to confirm this.
293	
294	### *Effects of infrequent fires*
295	
296	The present study was hampered by a lack of old populations (>25 years). This prevented direct measurements of life span and seed-production in very old plants. It was necessary to extrapolate trends from younger populations and anecdotal evidence to describe what happens when fire is excluded for long periods.
297	
298	In the seed-bank models (Fig. 5) seed-production was arbitrarily set to cease at 30 years. However, Bradstock and Myerscough (1981) observed the occurrence of stands of *B. ericifolia* older than this (these also contained *P. pulchella*) in which seeds were still being produced. The modeled storages will therefore underestimate the trend in real stands. Nevertheless, these suggested that enough seeds would be available for replacement for up to about 45 years in *B. ericifolia* and 90 years in *P. pulchella*. The life spans of these species are more likely to be less than 50 years (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981), hence in reality, senescence will hasten the decline of the seed-bank through the death of plants and replacement ages may be much nearer 30 years. The fall of viable seeds onto the litter and soil will increase as a consequence and, if seed-production occurs beyond 30 years, this pool of released seeds will be very large. If these assumptions are correct, changes in number and seed-bank may be quite similar in their pattern to those described by Gill and McMahon 1986 for *B. ornata*. Kruger and Bigalke (1984) also reported a similar decline in numbers after 30 years in some serotinous obligate seeders from South African shrublands, and suggested that life spans for dominant species of this kind fell within the range 20-50 years.
299	
300	In samples that are more than 20 years of age the number of viable seeds released each year (Fig. 6) greatly exceeded the number of plants that died annually (Figs 1, 2). Bradstock (1985) found that the heavy cover of plants and seedling predators restricted establishment from this pool of available seeds. However, a few seedlings are likely to survive in both species. A rough calculation can be done to estimate the number which may establish in a stand of 50 plants. Average conditions of soil moisture in any year will usually be adequate to give 10% emergence of available seeds. If 5% of these survive for 3 years (about eight times lower survival than in burnt conditions; Table 2), then 21-24 year old stands would produce two (*B. ericifolia*) and 12 (*P. pulchella*) seedlings annually. Such recruits would join the ranks of small suppressed plants which are subject to high mortality and would probably have little chance of reproducing (Bradstock 1985).
301	
302	At greater ages, when seed-release and mortality may be high, gaps in the canopy caused by senescence of dominants may appear. Seedling predators may become satiated as a result (e.g. Bond 1984a; O'Dowd & Gill 1984) and these conditions may promote the emergence, growth and reproduction of new plants. The relative abilities of *B. ericifolia*, *P. pulchella*
303	
304	######## PDF PAGE 12 ########
305	516 *R. A. Bradstock and M. A. O'Connell*
306	
307	and other species to exploit gaps and openings may determine whether self-perpetuation in large numbers is possible in the absence of fire. More work is needed to determine regeneration processes in older stands and their scarcity means that some effort needs to be made to preserve unburnt areas in the future.
308	
309	Fires, 20-30 years apart, will create very high density stands and the absence of these in the study area may be due to a history of burning at a higher frequency.
310	
311	### *Effects of density*
312	
313	Fire regimes may be used to increase or decrease the density of stands. For instance, if the relationships in Figs 1-7 hold true for much of the potential range of densities, then it may be possible, for example, to thin very dense stands and then hold them in this state. Several adverse fire-cycles (e.g. low intensity spring fires, less than 10 years apart) followed by a 10 year cycle of high intensity autumn fires would achieve this result.
314	
315	The density of a stand will change with age as plants die and the chronosequence in Table 3 may indicate the approximate trend. Bradstock (1985) found that density had no effect on the survival of seedlings older than 100 days. There were also no obvious effects of density on survival at older ages in either species, including the 1975 samples in *P. pulchella* (Fig. 2; Table 3), although dead plants tended to be small suppressed individuals in both species. Morris and Myerscough (1983, 1988) found evidence for density-dependent mortality in *B. ericifolia* stands of very high density (initial sample: 140 plants m⁻²) between the ages of 4 and 9 years.
316	
317	In both *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella*, the proportion of plants that continues to produce cones declined with age (Bradstock 1985) so that over time the increase in reproductive effort (Fig. 4) came from a small number of dominant individuals (Bradstock 1985). This pattern of reproduction amongst individuals may affect the relationship between density and seed-bank if the survival of dominant reproductive plants is unaffected by the number of suppressed individuals. The number of plants which reproduce and the amount of seeds produced may then be fixed above a moderate threshold of density, as indicated by experimental studies in other single-species populations (Harper 1977; Silvertown 1982). Further evidence of Morris and Myerscough (1988) showed that *B. ericifolia* plants at densities of 27.5 plants m⁻² had set a mean of 345 ± 92 seeds m⁻² at 8 years whereas high density plants (142 m⁻²) produced 225 ± 80 seeds m⁻². If seed-bank size is fixed across the upper range of densities then its prime determinant will be stand age. The perpetuation of very dense stands would then be possible only after longer fire-free intervals than those described here for lower density samples.
318	
319	Density and numbers may also be influenced by pollinators. Paton and Turner (1985) found that introduced bees may double the numbers of seeds set in *B. ericifolia* cones. The introduction of exotic bees may therefore have caused a massive increase in density and numbers in stands containing this species without any concurrent change in fire frequency. Other changes in species composition may have followed.
320	
321	## Conclusions
322	
323	All components of fire regime can influence a change in numbers and density, between generations, of *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella*. However, the largest change was due to differences in the age at which stands were burnt and the proportion of seeds which emerged as seedlings. Seasonal controls on seedling establishment, lengths of primary juvenile periods, effects of seed or seedling predators in unburnt conditions, and changes in structure of old stands and life spans, are generally similar in southern hemisphere species, particularly within the family, Proteaceae. However, demographic behaviour of fire-prone species cannot be predicted solely from any single characteristic such as survival, degree of serotiny (seed-survival in cones), seed-bank size or success of emergence. Any attempt to compare and classify species on their relative ability to withstand specific fire regimes, without a quantitative overview of the life-cycle, could be misleading.
324	
325	There may be little reason to assume that if reproduction commences early, then enough seeds will also be available to ensure replacement at a relatively early age. Quantitative variations in all the important components of the
326	
327	######## PDF PAGE 13 ########
328	*Demography of woody plants in relation to fire* 517
329	
330	life-cycle may exist within a species and correlations between these components and obvious site factors need to be studied (e.g. Cowling & Lamont 1985). Managers concerned with conserving populations at stable numbers should therefore use, as an indicator of the minimum interval between fires, the serotinous obligate seeder within their estate, that is slowest to reach self-replacement.
331	
332	## Acknowledgments

*Australian Journal of Ecology* (1988) **13**, 505-518

# Demography of woody plants in relation to fire: *Banksia ericifolia* L.f. and *Petrophile pulchella* (Schrad) R.Br.

R. A. BRADSTOCK\*
*School of Biological Sciences, Macleay Building A12, University of Sydney, Sydney, NSW 2006, Australia*

M. A. O'CONNELL
*NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, Box N189 Grosvenor St, Sydney, NSW 2000, Australia*

## Abstract

*Plants of* Banksia ericifolia *and* Petrophile pulchella *are sensitive to fire. Changes in population size under different fire regimes were estimated, based on measurements of post-fire seedling emergence, seedling survival, survival and seed production in established plants of differing ages, survival of seeds held in serotinous cones and seed-release in the periods between fire.*

*Seeds were first available at 5 years in* P. pulchella *and 6 years in* B. ericifolia. *Exact replacement would be possible when burnt at these ages, if seedling establishment were very high. Low establishment would delay replacement to 13 years of age in both species. Late summer/autumn fires of high intensity favour high establishment. Such fires at 8-10 year intervals would be tolerated without any sustained decline in numbers. Fires at 10-15 year intervals could occur regardless of season or intensity with little risk of a population decline. Large increases in numbers and density would follow fires spaced at 15-30 years. Enough seeds would be available for replacement up to about 50 years in both species. Viable seed-release in unburnt conditions was sufficient to compensate for deaths in stands over 20 years old, even with very low levels of establishment.*

*Two variables accounted for the biggest changes in numbers and density between generations interspersed by fires; namely the age at which a stand is burned and the proportion of seeds which emerge as seedlings. A comparison with other similar species showed similarities in controls on emergence and establishment, lengths of primary juvenile periods and life spans.*

## Introduction

Plants which rely on seeds for regeneration after fire (obligate seeders) form a prominent part of the vegetation in many fire-prone regions of the world (Gill 1981; Keeley 1981). Some obligate seeders are serotinous as their seeds are retained in the canopy and released by fire (Lotan 1976).

The present report presents demographic studies of two species which co-occur in fire-prone vegetation in the Sydney Region of south-eastern Australia: *Banksia ericifolia* L.f. and *Petrophile pulchella* (Schrad) R.Br. These perennial woody shrubs are frequently dominant in shrublands or the understorey of woodlands. Plants of both species are usually killed by fires of most intensities. Seeds (achenes in *P. pulchella*) are stored in woody infructescences, referred to here as cones, within closed follicles (*B. ericifolia*) or bracts (*P. pulchella*). Many other species of shrubs or small trees in these local vegetation types are also serotinous obligate seeders (Beadle 1940; Clemens & Franklin 1981; Benson 1985).

Crucial aspects of the demography of serotinous, obligate seeders are: (i) the time taken to first reproduction (primary juvenile period, Gill 1975) which determines the minimum possible interval at which fire may recur without causing extinction (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bond *et al.* 1984; Gill & McMahon 1986) because seeds are usually non-dormant; (ii) seedling establishment post-fire, which is determined by rainfall, tempera-
