ture, predators and the rate of release of seeds which, in turn, may be influenced by the season and intensity of fire (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bond *et al.* 1984; Cowling & Lamont 1984, 1985; McMahon 1984); (iii) the size of the pre-fire seed-bank, which is dependent on current storage plus new seeds added after each episode of seasonal fruiting minus losses of stored seeds in existing fruits (McMaster & Zedler 1981; Bond 1984; Gill & McMahon 1986); (iv) rates of survival of seedlings, juveniles and adults; (v) any subsequent establishment in unburnt conditions. Survival will be partly determined by density and age (Schlesinger & Gill 1978; Morris & Myerscough 1983, 1988). If establishment is absent in such conditions, the numbers and density in an even-aged post-fire generation will decline to low levels as the time since last fire nears the limit of longevity of the species (Specht *et al.* 1958; Ashton 1976; Gill & McMahon 1986).

These factors can be linked in a demographic model to predict population size over successive generations subject to re-occurring fires. Such information would provide a detailed basis for the management of fire-prone plant communities. However, few studies have attempted to relate changes in population size to fire regimes (Zedler 1977; Kruger 1983). At present there is much pressure for repeated burning of the vegetation containing the study species at intervals of less than 10 years for the purpose of fuel reduction. Often such prescribed fires are ignited in the cool months, between April and October. If informed fire-management is to take place it is important to know how these fire regimes and their alternatives may affect these potentially vulnerable, serotinous, obligate seeders. This study aimed to answer the following questions.

(1) What is the shortest interval between fires (maximum fire frequency) that either species can withstand for a sustained period (e.g. about 100 years) without suffering a prolonged decrease in population size?

(2) How is this maximum tolerable fire frequency affected by differences in the amounts of seedling emergence and survival occurring after different fires?

(3) Are variations in seedling emergence and survival related to the seasonal timing and intensity of fires?

(4) What are the likely trends in numbers and density of stands when fires occur infrequently?

(5) How do these species compare with other serotinous obligate seeders?

## Methods

### *Study sites*

The survival of plants more than 3 years of age, and the sizes of their seed-banks, were studied in seven areas situated within the Brisbane Water National Park, approximately 50 km north of Sydney, from 1980-83. These areas were last burned in 1977, 1976, 1975, 1974, 1973, 1968 and 1960 respectively, determined from fire-history maps and aerial photographs. All were located on ridge-tops of sandy earths derived from Hawkesbury Sandstone. Distance from the coast varied between 3 and 15 km.

Observations on the emergence and survival of seedlings (<3 years of age) were made in populations after four unplanned fires and in one experiment, between December 1980 and November 1982. These were located in the same area and had similar site characteristics to those populations used for the study of established plants.

### *Seedling emergence and survival*

The number of seedlings that emerged after each fire was counted in 40-70 quadrats (0.1 m²) for each species. The number of pre-fire seeds on dead plants was estimated by counting the number of cones held on branches in transects adjacent to the study quadrats, after the fire. The number of seeds per cone and the proportion of stored seeds that were intact and viable were estimated in cones taken from nearby unburnt stands. These procedures are described below.

The fate of the seedlings was followed until mid 1983. Two alternative models of survival, the exponential and power function (Silvertown 1982) were fitted. No model is given for Burn IV in *P. pulchella* due to the small numbers of plants which emerged. Indeed, models were fitted only when data for major cohorts of 10 or more seedlings were available.

Emergence was studied in two experiments (commenced May and November 1982) in which artificial ashbeds were prepared and known quantities of seeds sown. Quadrats (1 m × 1 m) were prepared by removing all plant cover and litter. Heat was applied to the exposed soil using propane burners. Harvested plant material and litter were ashed and placed on the soil after the heating had ceased. Either 50 (May 1982) or 100 (November 1982) seeds of each species were scattered on the quadrats several days later. The number of emerged seedlings was counted on average every month for a year after the starting dates.

### *Survival in established plants*

Survival was measured in samples of 50 or more plants of both species which were tagged in late 1980-early 1981. Each sample was located within quadrats (1.0 m × 1.0 m or 0.5 m × 0.5 m) on two adjacent lines randomly situated on a 20 m baseline located in thick patches of either species. All tagged plants were assumed to have arisen as seedlings after the previous fire in each area. The initial height of each plant was recorded.

Plants of *B. ericifolia* in some areas (burned 1977, 1974) were located solely on shallow soils (depth 0.3-0.4 m) and these were stunted in height and spindly in form compared with populations located on deep soils (depth 1.0-1.5 m; burned 1973, 1968, 1960). One area (burned 1975) contained plants on both soils. One sample was tagged in each area on each available soil type. A second was then established in each of the 1968 and 1960 areas, several hundred metres from the first.

Plants of *P. pulchella* were not as common on shallow soils, therefore samples were tagged only on deep soils. These were separate but often close to the *B. ericifolia* samples. No sampling was done in the 1976 or 1973 areas. Two samples were tagged in each of the other areas. A fire in 1982 destroyed a single sample of each species in the 1960 area.

Plants were checked twice yearly from the beginning of 1981 until October 1983 and the proportion of deaths was measured for each area to test for differences in mortality between soils in *B. ericifolia* and between populations of differing age in both species using G tests of independence.

### *Seed-survival*

Ten cones from each of four age classes (1, 5, 9 and 15 years) were harvested from each sample in 1983. These harvests were spread over three to four plants. Ages were estimated either by direct observation (1 and 5 years only) or by position and appearance (9 and 15 years). Cones of 9 and 15 years were those borne nearest the base of plants and presumed to be from the earliest cohort set in the 1968 stand and from the third oldest cohort in the 1960 stand. The latter origin was assumed because some cones in a more advanced state of degradation were found on the ground and these were assumed to be slightly older. In areas where only a single sample was available for each soil type a replicate of ten cones was harvested 50-100 m from the tagged plants. Two samples of cones were also taken from *P. pulchella* plants at the same time as sampling from *B. ericifolia* in the 1973 area.

Counts were made, in the laboratory, of total follicles or bracts and the number that was open and empty was recorded. Cones of *B. ericifolia* were heated in an oven at 200°C for 10 min to open follicles and aid seed removal. This treatment had no effect on seed viability (Bradstock 1985). Cones of *P. pulchella* were left unheated for several weeks after which seed extraction was possible.

Twenty unopened follicles/bracts were selected randomly and examined and the seeds within were scored as damaged by predators or intact. If intact, seeds were classified as filled, desiccated or aborted. Viability of intact, filled seeds was determined in batches of 50 by germination on filter paper in petri dishes maintained at saturation for 2-3 months. Germination occurred under optimum conditions (12:12 h day:night cycle of 15:5°C; Bradstock 1985) in an environmental cabinet.

The relationship between the proportion of seeds per cone surviving (i.e. intact, filled, viable, unreleased seeds) and age was described using various linear and non-linear models. The preferred model was chosen via a comparison of the percentage variances (PV) accounted for. These PV were the differences between the residual and total mean squares expressed as a percentage of the total mean square.

### *Seed-bank estimation*

All new cones set in the samples during the study were counted. Cone production during 1984-85 in the 1960 stands was also measured. Collections of 10 cones produced in two flowering seasons between 1981 and 1983 were made from each sample to determine seed-set per cone. A further 10 cones were harvested in areas with only one sample per soil-depth tested. Mean total annual seed production per plant was thus calculated and then described as a function of age by various linear and non-linear models from which a preferred model was chosen by a comparison of PV.

Seed-bank at any given age (per plant) was predicted by estimating the number of seeds (one seed per follicle or bract) set in each of the successive annual cohorts produced up to that age, using the preferred seed production model. In each cohort survival was then calculated using the preferred survival model for each species. The numbers of surviving seeds from each cohort at a given age were then summed to give an estimate of total stored viable seeds for that age. This was repeated for all ages between the time of first reproduction and 40 years. The estimates above 25 years were therefore extrapolations beyond the age limit of the samples. Allowance was made for the time between flowering and fruit maturity which is about one year in both species.

A further, alternative estimate of seed-bank was made. Seed production was stopped at age 30 years and the attrition of existing seeds was predicted up to an age of 100 years.

### *Seed-release between fires*

The mean number of viable seeds released annually (per plant) in each sample in unburnt conditions was estimated. Samples of cones of four different ages were marked in the 1968 and 1960 samples in mid 1981. Two age classes of cones (1 and 5 years in 1981, method of ageing similar to that described above) were marked in all other samples. The oldest cones in each sample were also marked and in 1981 these were estimated to be 7 and 13 years old. Follicles (*B. ericifolia*) or bracts (*P. pulchella*) which were open and empty were marked. Cones were rechecked after 2 years and the number of follicles/bracts was counted along with those which had opened and shed seeds. Rates of seed-release were compared between samples and cone ages using analysis of variance.

All cones set before 1981 were counted in each sample. The mean number of seeds released per plant was then estimated from the product of the measured annual rate of release per cone age class and the mean number of cones in each class. Cones set before 1981 were allocated to the nearest age class and a correction was made for viability.

### *The effect of frequent fires*

The effect of three successive fires, separated by intervals of identical length, on the number of plants in a hypothetical stand of each species was estimated. Plants living in the first interval were called first generation and in the second, second generation. The first generation immediate pre-fire number was set at 50 and model stands were assumed to be similar to the sample stands in other respects, such as density. Eleven calculations were done, using values between 5 and 15 years for the 'between-fire' interval.

Second generation stand size (*N*) was calculated as a function of the interval (*i*) between fires using:

*N* = *B* × *E* × *Ss* × *Se* (1)

where *B* = first generation seed-bank size, *E* = proportion of seeds emerging as post-fire seedlings, *Ss* = proportion of seedlings which survive and *Se* = proportion of living plants >3 years old at *i* years of age. Values of *N* were divided by 50 to give estimates of proportional change in numbers. These estimates were plotted against size of gap between fires. Opposing, extreme values of *E* and *Ss* were used to produce high and low estimates of proportional change.

## Discussion

### *Effects of frequent fires*

The importance of emergence and survival was reflected in the variability of the interval between fires at which stand replacement would be possible (Fig. 7). Burning at an interval close to 13 years could be done with little regard to other factors such as season or intensity of fire without risk of a decline in numbers. The low levels of emergence and survival (Tables 1, 2) used to produce this estimate were the product of a severe drought in the area (Bureau of Meteorology, pers. comm.). It is likely that fires in most years will produce at least a similar or larger number of seedlings. Survival of established plants may also be higher, for this reason.

Fire-managers may wish to burn as often as twice a decade, hence it is necessary to know the limit to which fire frequency can be reduced below 13 years without risking a serious decline in numbers. Seasons and intensities of fire may become important in such

Bradstock (1985) found that emergence in *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella* varied with rainfall, soil moisture and temperature. High summer temperatures impose a form of exogenous dormancy on seeds (definition of Mott & Groves 1981), restricting emergence to the cooler months. Seeds which lie on the soil over summer lose some viability. The amount of emergence was positively correlated with the period of time the soil surface (0-1.0 cm) remains at field capacity after rain. Seed predation was minimal in burnt areas.

Rainfall near the coast in the Sydney Region is highest, on average, from January to July (100-130 mm/month), and lowest from August to December (70-80 mm/month); however, there is great year to year variation. When evaporation is taken into account, the average period of sustained high soil moisture is May-July (early winter). Emergence may therefore be highest after fires which are timed so that most seeds are released in early winter. Seed-release will be most rapid after high intensity fires (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bradstock 1985) and such fires in late summer-autumn will cause most seeds to be released by early winter. sity fires at this time will prolong seed-release over winter and spring. Late summer-autumn, high intensity fires will therefore, on average, yield optimum emergence. A similar fire regime giving optimum emergence in other species of serotinous Proteaceae has been observed by Specht *et al.* (1958), Specht (1981), Bond *et al.* (1984), Cowling and Lamont (1984a, 1984b, 1985), McMahon (1984). Mechanisms in each case were generally similar to those described here.

While mortality of plants older than 100 days was due mainly to drought, younger seedlings died during both short dry spells and heavy rain (Bradstock 1985) when they were broken by raindrop impact or washed away. Bradstock (1985) concluded that the risk of death at the most vulnerable age (<100 days; Table 2) would be minimized when seedlings emerged in early winter. This reinforced the conclusion that late summer fires are optimal in producing seedlings.

After successive fires at 8 years, the proportional change in second generation stand size may vary from 9.8 to 0.5 in *B. ericifolia* and from 7.2 to 0.6 in *P. pulchella* (Fig. 7). The daily rainfall patterns for Sydney over 50 years (Bureau of Meterology, pers. comm.) show that a winter containing two successive months of low soil surface moisture occurs on average once every decade whereas very wet winters in which the soil is more or less continually moist occur several times a decade (Bradstock 1985). Thus fires of optimal season and intensity occurring 8 years apart would be followed by a dry winter and a subsequent decline in post-fire numbers, once every 80-100 years. More usually these fires would be followed by wet winters which would permit an increase in numbers. Hence an optimal regime in terms of season and intensity with an 8-10 year interval may cause fluctuations in numbers but is unlikely to send either species into a persistent decline if sustained over a period of up to 100 years. A 6-8 year cycle would be hazardous, due to a lower seed-bank and the increased probability of encountering dry post-fire conditions.

Reproduction is delayed in *B. ericifolia* growing on shallow soils and such stands may decline when fires occur less than 15 years apart. Observations indicate that the primary juvenile period may extend to more than 8 years and also that the seed-bank size may be less than on deep soils.

There are, therefore, two consecutive phases in which plants are susceptible to recurrent fires: first, during the primary juvenile period and second, the subsequent time up to the age at which exact self-replacement of stands is possible. So far most attention has been given to describing the lengths of primary juvenile periods. Values given here fell within the ranges already reported for these species (Benson 1985) and for other serotinous obligate seeders of the Proteaceae (3-11 years; Kruger 1983; Lamont 1985). Measurements of this second critical phase need to be made if serotinous obligate seeders are to be used as indicator species in fire-prone vegetation. It

may be useful if correlations exist between this and other demographic characteristics, particularly the length of the primary juvenile period. For example, is first reproduction at an early age always followed by a short interval to the age of self-replacement or vice versa?

Replacement ages for the study species were similar, despite differences in seedling-survival, early rates of development of seed-bank and primary juvenile period. Gill and McMahon (1986) reported that in *Banksia ornata*, a serotinous obligate seeder, common in parts of southern Australia, stand replacement may be likely after 16 years of age if post-fire emergence took place from 20% of available seeds. Seeds first become available at about 6 years in *B. ornata* (Gill & McMahon 1986), a figure comparable to that in *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella*. Despite this similarity, populations of *B. ornata* may decline under some repeated cycles of fire less than 15 years apart, whilst *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella* populations may increase or remain stable. This difference was primarily due to a slower rate of accumulation of seed-bank in *B. ornata*, though other possible differences in projected survival rate were also present. Similarly, Kruger and Bigalke (1984) reported that in *Protea repens*, a shrub of the South African fynbos, the primary juvenile period may be 4-5 years (ripe seeds first available), but replacement age may be 10-12 years. It is most prudent to conclude that there is little current evidence of any consistent linkage between these key events. Further demographic studies amongst a wider range of species are needed to confirm this.

### *Effects of infrequent fires*

The present study was hampered by a lack of old populations (>25 years). This prevented direct measurements of life span and seed-production in very old plants. It was necessary to extrapolate trends from younger populations and anecdotal evidence to describe what happens when fire is excluded for long periods.

In the seed-bank models (Fig. 5) seed-production was arbitrarily set to cease at 30 years. However, Bradstock and Myerscough (1981) observed the occurrence of stands of *B. ericifolia* older than this (these also contained *P. pulchella*) in which seeds were still being produced. The modeled storages will therefore underestimate the trend in real stands. Nevertheless, these suggested that enough seeds would be available for replacement for up to about 45 years in *B. ericifolia* and 90 years in *P. pulchella*. The life spans of these species are more likely to be less than 50 years (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981), hence in reality, senescence will hasten the decline of the seed-bank through the death of plants and replacement ages may be much nearer 30 years. The fall of viable seeds onto the litter and soil will increase as a consequence and, if seed-production occurs beyond 30 years, this pool of released seeds will be very large. If these assumptions are correct, changes in number and seed-bank may be quite similar in their pattern to those described by Gill and McMahon 1986 for *B. ornata*. Kruger and Bigalke (1984) also reported a similar decline in numbers after 30 years in some serotinous obligate seeders from South African shrublands, and suggested that life spans for dominant species of this kind fell within the range 20-50 years.

In samples that are more than 20 years of age the number of viable seeds released each year (Fig. 6) greatly exceeded the number of plants that died annually (Figs 1, 2). Bradstock (1985) found that the heavy cover of plants and seedling predators restricted establishment from this pool of available seeds. However, a few seedlings are likely to survive in both species. A rough calculation can be done to estimate the number which may establish in a stand of 50 plants. Average conditions of soil moisture in any year will usually be adequate to give 10% emergence of available seeds. If 5% of these survive for 3 years (about eight times lower survival than in burnt conditions; Table 2), then 21-24 year old stands would produce two (*B. ericifolia*) and 12 (*P. pulchella*) seedlings annually. Such recruits would join the ranks of small suppressed plants which are subject to high mortality and would probably have little chance of reproducing (Bradstock 1985).

At greater ages, when seed-release and mortality may be high, gaps in the canopy caused by senescence of dominants may appear. Seedling predators may become satiated as a result (e.g. Bond 1984a; O'Dowd & Gill 1984) and these conditions may promote the emergence, growth and reproduction of new plants. The relative abilities of *B. ericifolia*, *P. pulchella*

######## PDF PAGE 12 ########
516 *R. A. Bradstock and M. A. O'Connell*

and other species to exploit gaps and openings may determine whether self-perpetuation in large numbers is possible in the absence of fire. More work is needed to determine regeneration processes in older stands and their scarcity means that some effort needs to be made to preserve unburnt areas in the future.

Fires, 20-30 years apart, will create very high density stands and the absence of these in the study area may be due to a history of burning at a higher frequency.

### *Effects of density*

Fire regimes may be used to increase or decrease the density of stands. For instance, if the relationships in Figs 1-7 hold true for much of the potential range of densities, then it may be possible, for example, to thin very dense stands and then hold them in this state. Several adverse fire-cycles (e.g. low intensity spring fires, less than 10 years apart) followed by a 10 year cycle of high intensity autumn fires would achieve this result.

The density of a stand will change with age as plants die and the chronosequence in Table 3 may indicate the approximate trend. Bradstock (1985) found that density had no effect on the survival of seedlings older than 100 days. There were also no obvious effects of density on survival at older ages in either species, including the 1975 samples in *P. pulchella* (Fig. 2; Table 3), although dead plants tended to be small suppressed individuals in both species. Morris and Myerscough (1983, 1988) found evidence for density-dependent mortality in *B. ericifolia* stands of very high density (initial sample: 140 plants m⁻²) between the ages of 4 and 9 years.

In both *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella*, the proportion of plants that continues to produce cones declined with age (Bradstock 1985) so that over time the increase in reproductive effort (Fig. 4) came from a small number of dominant individuals (Bradstock 1985). This pattern of reproduction amongst individuals may affect the relationship between density and seed-bank if the survival of dominant reproductive plants is unaffected by the number of suppressed individuals. The number of plants which reproduce and the amount of seeds produced may then be fixed above a moderate threshold of density, as indicated by experimental studies in other single-species populations (Harper 1977; Silvertown 1982). Further evidence of Morris and Myerscough (1988) showed that *B. ericifolia* plants at densities of 27.5 plants m⁻² had set a mean of 345 ± 92 seeds m⁻² at 8 years whereas high density plants (142 m⁻²) produced 225 ± 80 seeds m⁻². If seed-bank size is fixed across the upper range of densities then its prime determinant will be stand age. The perpetuation of very dense stands would then be possible only after longer fire-free intervals than those described here for lower density samples.

Density and numbers may also be influenced by pollinators. Paton and Turner (1985) found that introduced bees may double the numbers of seeds set in *B. ericifolia* cones. The introduction of exotic bees may therefore have caused a massive increase in density and numbers in stands containing this species without any concurrent change in fire frequency. Other changes in species composition may have followed.

## Conclusions

All components of fire regime can influence a change in numbers and density, between generations, of *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella*. However, the largest change was due to differences in the age at which stands were burnt and the proportion of seeds which emerged as seedlings. Seasonal controls on seedling establishment, lengths of primary juvenile periods, effects of seed or seedling predators in unburnt conditions, and changes in structure of old stands and life spans, are generally similar in southern hemisphere species, particularly within the family, Proteaceae. However, demographic behaviour of fire-prone species cannot be predicted solely from any single characteristic such as survival, degree of serotiny (seed-survival in cones), seed-bank size or success of emergence. Any attempt to compare and classify species on their relative ability to withstand specific fire regimes, without a quantitative overview of the life-cycle, could be misleading.

There may be little reason to assume that if reproduction commences early, then enough seeds will also be available to ensure replacement at a relatively early age. Quantitative variations in all the important components of the

######## PDF PAGE 13 ########
*Demography of woody plants in relation to fire* 517

life-cycle may exist within a species and correlations between these components and obvious site factors need to be studied (e.g. Cowling & Lamont 1985). Managers concerned with conserving populations at stable numbers should therefore use, as an indicator of the minimum interval between fires, the serotinous obligate seeder within their estate, that is slowest to reach self-replacement.

1	## n_pages=10
2	
3	######## PDF PAGE 1 ########
4	35
5	
6	# Post-fire regeneration and growth of *Senecio garlandii* (Asteraceae) — a vulnerable plant of the South Western Slopes, NSW
7	
8	## G.E. Burrows
9	
10	*Burrows, G.E. (Ron Potter Centre, Charles Sturt University – Riverina, PO Box 588, Wagga Wagga, New South Wales, Australia, 2678) 1995. Post-fire regeneration and growth of* Senecio garlandii *(Asteraceae) — a vulnerable plant of the South Western Slopes, NSW. Cunninghamia 4(1): 35–44.* *Senecio garlandii* F. Muell. ex Belcher (Asteraceae) is a perennial subshrub that has been recorded from less than 10 sites, mostly on the South Western Slopes of NSW. In conservation terms *S. garlandii* is currently classified as vulnerable. Its site of greatest abundance is The Rock Nature Reserve (340 ha), 30 km south east of Wagga Wagga. In March 1991 the first major fire in 40 years burnt more than 90% of the reserve and less than 5% of the original *Senecio* population remained in leaf. Over the next 3 years post-fire regeneration was assessed in a permanent quadrat (4 x 5 m) located in an area of pre-fire *Senecio* abundance. Following above-average rainfall during winter 1991, 453 *Senecio* seedlings were recorded in September 1991, ranging in density from 4–45 seedlings/m². After 4 months of below-average rainfall, seedling numbers declined to 171 by February 1992. In comparison to this 62% mortality (average of 2.23 deaths/day), the other 35 species of annuals and herbaceous perennials present in the quadrat had either died or had died back to a rootstock or similar organ at least two months previously. After February 1992 there was a low constant mortality (average 0.07 deaths/day) for the remaining 22 months of the study. By their first summer *S. garlandii* seedlings consisted of a single shoot 8–15 cm height. By the second summer this shoot had senesced to be replaced by 1–5 shoots (mean = 2.2, average height 65 cm) and by the third summer these shoots also senesced to be replaced by 1–12 shoots (mean = 3.9, average height 92 cm). No seedlings of *S. garlandii* flowered in their first summer, while 44% of the surviving 143 seedlings flowered in their second year and over 95% of the surviving 122 plants flowered in their third year. A small number of plants survived the fire and resprouted from rootstocks. This study indicates that the conservation status of *S. garlandii* has not been harmed by the fire.
11	
12	## Introduction
13	
14	*Senecio garlandii* F. Muell. ex Belcher (Asteraceae) is a perennial subshrub, usually up to one metre in height. The stems and lower leaf surfaces are densely lanate, which explains the common name of 'Woolly Ragwort'. The first known collection of *S. garlandii* was made in 1890 by J. R. Garland who sent his material to Ferdinand von Mueller. Mueller prepared a manuscript description of this material under the specific epithet 'garlandii' but never published this species name. The name was formally published almost 100 hundred years later (Belcher 1986).
15	
16	######## PDF PAGE 2 ########
17	36 Cunninghamia Vol. 4(1): 1995
18	
19	Belcher (1986) describes the distribution of *S. garlandii* as 'Very local along the 147° E. meridian on the western slopes of the Dividing Range between West Wyalong and Albury.' Belcher lists five localities for the herbarium specimens he examined: i) The Rock Hill, ii) Tabletop Range, iii) a site '15 miles' ESE of The Rock, iv) Gidginbung and v) 'near Albury'. In addition, *S. garlandii* has been recorded at Flowerpot Hill (4 km S of The Rock), Ulandra Nature Reserve (7 km SE of Bethungra) and Benambra State Forest (20 km W of Holbrook)(personal observation). *Senecio garlandii* is classified as a 3V (vulnerable) species (Endangered Flora Network for the Australian & New Zealand Environment and Conservation Council 1993) as its range is greater than 100 km but it only occurs in small populations that are mostly restricted to highly specific habitats.
20	
21	At only 340 ha, The Rock Nature Reserve (lat. 35° 16' S, long. 147° 05' E) is a small island of remnant native vegetation, surrounded by extensive agricultural lands. The Rock Nature Reserve is an important area for the protection of *S. garlandii* as it supports the largest known population of the species (personal observation) and is one of the few formally protected areas within which the species grows. While *S. garlandii* has a restricted geographical distribution, it also has a restricted distribution within The Rock Nature Reserve. It occurs almost exclusively on the exposed upper slopes and ridges of the reserve and thus occupies only a small percentage of a small reserve. The same habitat requirements are evident at Tabletop and Ulandra Nature Reserves and Benambra State Forest.
22	
23	After less than 75 mm of rain during November 1990 to March 1991 (average 208 mm for this period) the first major fire (15–17 March 1991) in 40 years burnt more than 90% of The Rock Nature Reserve (personal observation). Personal estimates indicated that pre-fire there were several thousand *S. garlandii* plants in the reserve but post-fire there were probably less than 100 plants in leaf and these were confined to inaccessible rock ledges on the eastern cliff.
24	
25	Given: i) the restricted distribution of *S. garlandii*, ii) the importance of The Rock Nature Reserve to this species' formal protection and iii) the major reduction in plant numbers in the reserve due to the March 1991 fire, it was considered useful to study the post-fire regeneration and subsequent growth of *S. garlandii*. In addition two other aspects of the biology of *S. garlandii* were investigated to help understand seedling establishment and survival. Firstly, *S. garlandii* possesses large leaves of mesophytic appearance while all other perennial species at The Rock Nature Reserve that stay in leaf during summer have smaller xerophytic leaves. Thus leaf anatomy was studied to better understand seedling survival during summer. Secondly, a study of seed viability was conducted as prior tests indicated that a period of dry heat was needed to overcome dormancy. A similar response has only been described in a small number of native species (Bell et al. 1993).
26	
27	######## PDF PAGE 3 ########
28	Burrows, *Senecio garlandii* and fire 37
29	
30	## Materials and methods
31	
32	An area 50 m to the east of the main cliff was selected for the establishment of a permanent quadrat, 4 x 5 m. This area was chosen as it supported, excluding the herbaceous stratum, an almost monospecific stand of *S. garlandii* prior to the fire and thus was considered favourable for regeneration. The quadrat was 250 m above the surrounding plains and was on the easterly facing scree slopes of a north–south ridge. The quadrat had a slope of 30° and consisted of about 80% bare soil and 20% rock and was divided into 20 1 x 1 m contiguous sub-quadrats. The site was well-drained and was shaded from the early afternoon onwards by a 100 m high cliff to the west. Rainfall and temperature data were obtained from the Bureau of Meteorology's station at Forest Hill, Wagga Wagga, about 35 km NE of the study site.
33	
34	The quadrat was assessed for a total of 28 months, usually at six-weekly intervals. At each trip the following parameters were assessed: i) number of seedlings and rootstocks of *S. garlandii*/m², ii) average height and number of basal shoots of seedlings and rootstocks of *S. garlandii*, iii) reproductive stage of seedlings and rootstocks of *S. garlandii* and iv) presence/absence and reproductive stage of species other than *S. garlandii*.
35	
36	Mature seed of *S. garlandii* was collected from plants that recovered from rootstocks and 30 month old plants in late December 1993 and stored dry at ambient temperature. Seed viability was tested (3 replicates of 50 seeds) at about one month intervals by direct germination on filter paper supported on moistened vermiculite in petri dishes subject to a 16 hr photoperiod (45 µmol/m²/sec) at 23° C and 8 hrs dark at 20° C. For light microscopy leaves were fixed in glutaraldehyde, processed using standard procedures for plastic embedding and transverse sectioned at 1–2 µm and stained with toluidine blue (O'Brien & McCully 1981).
37	
38	## Results
39	
40	### Seed germination
41	
42	The seeds were roughly cylindrical (about 2.5 mm length, 0.6 mm diameter), averaged 0.29 mg in weight and had a thin seed coat. Immediately upon wetting the acheneal hairs released several intertwined spiral bodies and within 24 hrs the seeds were surrounded by a mucilaginous sheath. Seed tested within one week of collection exhibited low (< 6%) germination. After 1.5, 2.5 and 3.5 months dry storage at ambient temperatures average germination percentages of 69, 90 and 92%, respectively, were recorded.
43	
44	### Leaf anatomy
45	
46	In cross-section the leaves showed typical dorsiventral anatomy with a layer of palisade mesophyll, a layer of spongy mesophyll and a layer of mesophyll intermediate between the palisade and the spongy mesophyll in position and cell arrangement (Fig. 1). A large proportion of the leaf was intercellular air space and little or no sclerenchyma was present. Xerophytic modifications to this basically mesophytic
47	
48	######## PDF PAGE 4 ########
49	38 Cunninghamia Vol. 4(1): 1995
50	
51	structure included: i) the large diameter upper epidermal cells possessed a thick (10–15 µm) outer cell wall, with a thin cuticle, ii) all stomata were restricted to the lower leaf surface, and iii) the lower surface had numerous single-celled trichomes that formed a dense mat about 200 µm thick (Fig. 1).
52	
53	## Field assessment
54	
55	### i) Species other than *Senecio garlandii*
56	
57	The overstorey surrounding the quadrat consisted of *Eucalyptus macrorhyncha*, with some *E. polyanthemos*, *E. albens* and *Brachychiton populneus*, but these species were not recorded in the quadrat. A total of 35 species, excluding *S. garlandii*, were recorded in the quadrat over the assessment period. In terms of origin 22 species (63%) were naturalised and 13 (37%) were native species. In terms of life cycle and growth form 26 (74%) were annual herbs and 9 (26%) were perennial herbs.
58	
59	[Micrograph: leaf transverse section, labels pm and sm, panel 1]
60	
61	**Fig. 1.** Transverse section of a mature leaf of *Senecio garlandii*. Note the thick outer epidermal cell walls, the large adaxial epidermal cells, the palisade (pm) and spongy mesophyll (sm) layers, the stoma (arrowed) and the abaxial trichome layer. Scale = 50 µm.
62	
63	######## PDF PAGE 5 ########
64	Burrows, *Senecio garlandii* and fire 39
65	
66	### ii) Survival of *Senecio garlandii*
67	
68	While the fire killed many of the existing *Senecio* plants some survived by resprouting from a rootstock. Survivors could be identified by their greater shoot growth compared with *Senecio* seedlings and often by the presence of the charred stumps of the previous year's growth. By early September 1991 at least 2 rootstocks had not resprouted in the quadrat, 2 rootstocks both had a single shoot 3 cm in height and one rootstock had 7 shoots all about 8 cm high. Six weeks later one of the smaller rootstocks had died, while of the two remaining, one had a shoot 28 cm high and the other five shoots 50–75 cm high, all with flower primordia. This represents a rapid elongation of 1–1.5 cm/day over the intervening 6 weeks for many of the rootstock shoots. These two plants remained alive for the duration of the study.
69	
70	### iii) *Senecio garlandii* seedling establishment and mortality
71	
72	In early September 1991, 5 months after the fire and with average or above average rainfall in the preceding 3 months (Fig. 2), 453 *S. garlandii* seedlings were recorded in the 20 m² quadrat (Fig. 3), ranging from 4–45 seedlings/m², at an average of 22.7 seedlings/m². The seedlings were no greater than 2 cm in height and most were 1 cm or less. Seedling numbers remained largely unchanged over the next 6 weeks (Fig. 3). Several annual species, e.g. *Carduus tenuiflorus*, *Daucus glochidiatus*, *Parietaria debilis*, *Ranunculus sessiliflorus* and *Stellaria media*, were more abundant and vigorous than the *Senecio* seedlings and tended to smother the smaller individuals. By late November 1991, a relatively small 7.3% reduction in seedling numbers had occurred (Fig. 3), although rainfall had been well below average for October and November (Fig. 2). Seedlings that had germinated in thin, loose ash on the top of boulders had died and many of the smaller individuals appeared to be water-stressed. Well-developed seedlings had 5–8 fully expanded leaves, were 10–15 cm high and did not elongate further. All the annual species that had previously overgrown the smaller, slower growing *Senecio* were dead and the perennial herbs died back to some form of rootstock or bulb by mid-summer. At mid-January 1992 the preceding 6 weeks had been relatively dry with only 31 mm of rainfall recorded. Combined with the excellent drainage and warmer temperatures this resulted in the most rapid rate of seedling mortality during the study (Fig. 3) with a 44% reduction in numbers, at an average of 4 deaths/day. In late February 1992, a further 27% reduction in numbers from the previous assessment period (average of 1.5 deaths/day) was recorded. The second half of summer 1991/1992 was relatively wet (93.4 mm of rainfall) and cool (January and February mean monthly maxima were about 2 degrees below average). These conditions had allowed hundreds of *Carduus tenuiflorus* seedlings to germinate in the quadrat, but a new cohort of *Senecio* seedlings did not germinate. During the winter and spring of 1992 no new *Senecio* seedlings germinated, even in the organic material and soil on top of the rocks where suitable germination conditions occurred without competition from existing plants. In spring 1992, as per the previous year, the *Senecio* seedlings were partially smothered by annuals but given their greater size and greater competitive ability the effects were not as pronounced. After the high mortality rate recorded during summer 1991/1992 seedling mortality was low during the remainder of the study (Fig. 3) even during the summer of
73	
74	######## PDF PAGE 6 ########
75	40 Cunninghamia Vol. 4(1): 1995
76	
77	1992/1993 when there were 10 consecutive weeks where only 33.4 mm of rainfall was recorded and there were 11 consecutive days with maxima greater than 35° C.
78	
79	In spring 1991 there were about 450 *Senecio* seedlings in the quadrat, ranging in density from 4–45/m². In December 1993, 28 months later, there were 122 *Senecio* seedlings, ranging in density from 1–14/m². This represents an overall mortality of 73%, ranging from a high of 89–94% in 3 sub-quadrats, to a low of 44% in one sub-quadrat.
80	
81	### iv) Growth form
82	
83	In their first year of growth the *Senecio* seedlings developed a single upright shoot but by early winter this shoot had usually senesced and axillary buds at its base began to slowly elongate. Rapid elongation of the new basal shoots commenced in mid-August 1992 and by late September most shoots had increased in average height by 8 cm in the preceding 6 weeks. This elongation was greatest during October (about 4.5 cm/week) and began to slow in December when plants reached their average maximum height of 65 cm. Seedlings averaged 2.2 shoots in their second year, and some plants had up to 5 equal-sized shoots. In early May 1993 the shoots produced during the previous spring and summer began to senesce and, as in the previous year, the shoot system was gradually replaced by new shoots which were initiated in the basal leaf axils of the existing shoots. These shoots were often initiated just below ground level and grew horizontally for a short distance before becoming upright, thus giving a single individual the appearance of several plants growing in close proximity. In December 1993 most plants were at full adult-size (average plant height 92 cm), with an average of 3.9 shoots per plant (range 1–12). These main shoots were unbranched for most of their length but near the apex several axillary buds had elongated and initiated flowers to form a corymbose inflorescence.
84	
85	### v) Flowering
86	
87	In their first year no seedlings in the quadrat flowered or had formed flower primordia, while the two rootstocks had finished flowering by late November but fruits had not been released. In September 1992 many *Senecio* plants had initiated flower primordia and by early November the primordia had developed into large flower buds. In mid-December 1992, 44% of the 143 remaining *Senecio* plants were flowering or had finished flowering and in late January 1993 flowering had finished. However December 1992 was unusually moist (Fig. 2) and cool, and in January 1993 the lower axillary buds in some plants had rapidly elongated and initiated new flower primordia. In mid-March 1993, after a dry finish to summer (Fig. 2), the flower buds that had been initiated in mid-January had been aborted. In December 1993 more than 95% of the 122 plants surviving their third summer had flowered or were flowering.
88	
89	General observations throughout the reserve revealed that *S. garlandii* had: i) re-established monospecific thickets where they existed pre-fire, ii) increased plant density where previously only scattered plants had been present, and iii) a limited increase in range but was still restricted to the ridge areas.
90	
91	######## PDF PAGE 7 ########
92	Burrows, *Senecio garlandii* and fire 41
93	
94	[Bar graph: rainfall (mm/month), 0-140, monthly 1991-1993, with long-term average line]
95	
96	**Fig. 2.** Monthly rainfall during the study period with long-term average (■ – ■) values. Values are for Forest Hill, Wagga Wagga (35 km NE from site). Arrow indicates time of the fire.
97	
98	[Line graph: seedling no., 0-500, D J 1992 D J 1993 D]
99	
100	**Fig. 3.** Number of *Senecio garlandii* seedlings in the permanent quadrat during the study period.
101	
102	## Discussion
103	
104	The principal finding of this study is that *Senecio garlandii*, a vulnerable species reduced to a few individuals after the 1991 fire at The Rock Nature Reserve, has regenerated successfully from seed and, to a lesser extent, from rootstocks. It has maintained its almost monospecific stands in its areas of pre-fire dominance, has increased in density where previously only scattered individuals existed and has expanded its distribution but is still principally restricted to the upper ridge areas. Several *Senecio* species are known as fire ephemerals or 'fire weeds' (Gill 1993). While *S. garlandii* shares with these species the ability to successfully regenerate after fire it would not be considered a fire weed because: i) seeds do not need a heat treatment to germinate, ii) individual plants appear to be relatively long lived through their annual resprouting habit, i.e. they do not have the short life span of a fire
105	
106	######## PDF PAGE 8 ########
107	42 Cunninghamia Vol. 4(1): 1995
108	
109	ephemeral, and iii) populations can persist in low fire frequency conditions, e.g. plants on cliff ledges.
110	
111	Lawrence (1985) investigated the reproductive biology of 32 mainly native species of *Senecio*, with *S. garlandii* listed as *Senecio* species A (Belcher 1986). Lawrence noted, as in the present study, that *S. garlandii* is a perennial, is early flowering, produces lightweight seeds, the seeds produce a mucilaginous sheath upon wetting and that these seeds can have high germination percentages. From observations on pollen-ovule ratios and inflorescence morphology it was possible for Lawrence to deduce that *S. garlandii* was self-incompatible. Lawrence noted that stable environments favour outbreeding perennials but only 5 of the 15 self-incompatible perennials she investigated were usually restricted to comparatively stable environments. Three of the five, including *S. garlandii*, are found on rocky outcrops of drier inland areas.
112	
113	The most common criterion for classifying a species response to fire is whether persistence is by seed ('seeders') or by vegetative means ('sprouters') (Gill & Bradstock 1992). This study indicates that *S. garlandii* is principally a seeder although some plants function as sprouters after a low-intensity fire. Gill & Bradstock (1992) list three categories of seed regeneration: i) from viable canopy-stored seed, ii) from soil-stored seed, and iii) from seed brought in, because no propagules remain on site after fire. In *S. garlandii* the mature achenes are easily dislodged from the head's receptacle with little force, therefore no seed-store exists on the plant. Many species of the Asteraceae have small air-borne fruits and are capable of recolonising burnt areas with seed blown in from unburnt areas (Purdie & Slatyer 1976). However, because the fire eliminated almost the complete *Senecio* population, except for some isolated individuals on cliff ledges, there were no seeds on unburnt plants to be used for recolonisation of burnt areas. In addition, while the achenes of *S. garlandii* have numerous slender pappus bristles they are not persistent (Belcher 1986), and thus long-distance wind dispersal of the fruits would not be expected. Thus it is most probable that the re-establishment of *S. garlandii* was from a seed-store in the soil, as were the 7 composites described by Purdie & Slatyer (1976). Purdie (1977) noted that seeds in litter are often destroyed in fires, while many seeds in the soil survive. Purdie (1977) noted that germination of herbaceous species, including *Senecio quadridentatus* and *Hypochoeris* spp., was lower in burnt than unburnt areas. She suggests that the seed may not be stored for long periods in the soil or are trapped in the litter by their pappus and thus destroyed by fire.
114	
115	Studies by Hobbs & Atkins (1991) and Purdie & Slatyer (1976) found, as did the present study, that germination of perennial species occurred in the first year after the fire, but not in subsequent years. Hobbs & Atkins (1991) also found that seedlings of perennial species that survived their first summer generally continued to survive or, conversely, mortality is greatest in the seedling phase (Fig. 3).
116	
117	Bell et al. (1993) noted that obligate re-seeding species tend to grow vertically initially then produce an 'umbrella shape', while resprouting species have more of an 'urn shape'. *Senecio garlandii* combines these two strategies as initially it produces a vertically growing shoot that only branches near the apex; however, after plants have become established they branch from near the base and form a more spreading canopy.
118	
119	######## PDF PAGE 9 ########
120	Burrows, *Senecio garlandii* and fire 43
121	
122	While *S. garlandii* operates as a resprouter in its annual growth cycle, the shoots originate above or close to ground level and a specialised rootstock or similar organ does not appear to be present. Thus fire-induced mortality of mature plants is to be expected. The degree of water-stress experienced by shrubs at and following the time of fire may be an important factor in determining the proportion of shrubs that resprout (Hodgkinson & Griffin 1982). This suggests that a low fire intensity, combined with more than the about 25 mm of rainfall received in the 2.5 months after the March fire (Fig. 2), then more *Senecio* rootstocks may have resprouted.
123	
124	Over 200 vascular plant species have been recorded at The Rock Nature Reserve (Benson & Melrose 1993) but only about 50 species remain in leaf over summer. Most (> 90%) of these species possess small leaves and/or pronounced xerophytic modifications to their leaf anatomy. Thus it is remarkable that *S. garlandii* has the largest leaves of any species at The Rock Nature Reserve (personal observation) and possesses a mesophytic dorsiventral leaf anatomy that appears unsuited to the semi-arid conditions. The thickening of the outer epidermal cell wall, the restriction of stomata to the abaxial surface and the extremely dense abaxial trichome covering are probably effective in controlling water loss, in both seedlings and adults. This contributes to a relatively low mortality rate for a mesophytic species growing in semi-arid conditions and allows the seedlings a competitive advantage as they are able to continue vegetative and reproductive growth when the other species are dead or dormant. The lack of sclerenchyma results in wilting of leaves during times of pronounced water-stress.
125	
126	After more than 70 mm of rainfall in early February 1992, combined with 13 consecutive days with temperature maxima below the monthly mean, there was an extensive germination of *Carduus* seedlings but no *Senecio garlandii* seedlings were observed. All the thistle seedlings died of water-stress before flowering. This observation, combined with the germination tests, suggests that the *Senecio garlandii* seeds may possess some mechanism to prevent germination after periods of wet weather in summer. A period of after-ripening, consisting of several months of dry heat has been described for a small number of Australian species of the Asteraceae and Poaceae (Mott & Groves 1981, Bell et al. 1993).
127	
128	From a conservation viewpoint it is of concern that 22 weed species were present in the quadrat. General observation and the findings of other studies (Purdie & Slatyer 1976, Hobbs & Atkins 1991) indicate that the abundance and diversity of weeds should progressively be reduced as the *S. garlandii* re-establishes. *Senecio garlandii* is able to reach reproductive maturity relatively quickly as shown by 45% of the surviving seedlings flowering in their second summer and greater than 95% flowering in their third summer. This indicates that this species would not be eliminated at this site even if the fire frequency increased, although further study is required to determine what length of time and conditions are required to establish an effective seed-store in the soil. In summary, it appears that *S. garlandii* could tolerate a wide variation in fire frequency and no specific fire management practices are needed to maintain the population at The Rock Nature Reserve.
129

# Post-fire regeneration and growth of *Senecio garlandii* (Asteraceae) — a vulnerable plant of the South Western Slopes, NSW

## G.E. Burrows

*Burrows, G.E. (Ron Potter Centre, Charles Sturt University – Riverina, PO Box 588, Wagga Wagga, New South Wales, Australia, 2678) 1995. Post-fire regeneration and growth of* Senecio garlandii *(Asteraceae) — a vulnerable plant of the South Western Slopes, NSW. Cunninghamia 4(1): 35–44.* *Senecio garlandii* F. Muell. ex Belcher (Asteraceae) is a perennial subshrub that has been recorded from less than 10 sites, mostly on the South Western Slopes of NSW. In conservation terms *S. garlandii* is currently classified as vulnerable. Its site of greatest abundance is The Rock Nature Reserve (340 ha), 30 km south east of Wagga Wagga. In March 1991 the first major fire in 40 years burnt more than 90% of the reserve and less than 5% of the original *Senecio* population remained in leaf. Over the next 3 years post-fire regeneration was assessed in a permanent quadrat (4 x 5 m) located in an area of pre-fire *Senecio* abundance. Following above-average rainfall during winter 1991, 453 *Senecio* seedlings were recorded in September 1991, ranging in density from 4–45 seedlings/m². After 4 months of below-average rainfall, seedling numbers declined to 171 by February 1992. In comparison to this 62% mortality (average of 2.23 deaths/day), the other 35 species of annuals and herbaceous perennials present in the quadrat had either died or had died back to a rootstock or similar organ at least two months previously. After February 1992 there was a low constant mortality (average 0.07 deaths/day) for the remaining 22 months of the study. By their first summer *S. garlandii* seedlings consisted of a single shoot 8–15 cm height. By the second summer this shoot had senesced to be replaced by 1–5 shoots (mean = 2.2, average height 65 cm) and by the third summer these shoots also senesced to be replaced by 1–12 shoots (mean = 3.9, average height 92 cm). No seedlings of *S. garlandii* flowered in their first summer, while 44% of the surviving 143 seedlings flowered in their second year and over 95% of the surviving 122 plants flowered in their third year. A small number of plants survived the fire and resprouted from rootstocks. This study indicates that the conservation status of *S. garlandii* has not been harmed by the fire.

## Introduction

*Senecio garlandii* F. Muell. ex Belcher (Asteraceae) is a perennial subshrub, usually up to one metre in height. The stems and lower leaf surfaces are densely lanate, which explains the common name of 'Woolly Ragwort'. The first known collection of *S. garlandii* was made in 1890 by J. R. Garland who sent his material to Ferdinand von Mueller. Mueller prepared a manuscript description of this material under the specific epithet 'garlandii' but never published this species name. The name was formally published almost 100 hundred years later (Belcher 1986).

######## PDF PAGE 2 ########
36 Cunninghamia Vol. 4(1): 1995

Belcher (1986) describes the distribution of *S. garlandii* as 'Very local along the 147° E. meridian on the western slopes of the Dividing Range between West Wyalong and Albury.' Belcher lists five localities for the herbarium specimens he examined: i) The Rock Hill, ii) Tabletop Range, iii) a site '15 miles' ESE of The Rock, iv) Gidginbung and v) 'near Albury'. In addition, *S. garlandii* has been recorded at Flowerpot Hill (4 km S of The Rock), Ulandra Nature Reserve (7 km SE of Bethungra) and Benambra State Forest (20 km W of Holbrook)(personal observation). *Senecio garlandii* is classified as a 3V (vulnerable) species (Endangered Flora Network for the Australian & New Zealand Environment and Conservation Council 1993) as its range is greater than 100 km but it only occurs in small populations that are mostly restricted to highly specific habitats.

At only 340 ha, The Rock Nature Reserve (lat. 35° 16' S, long. 147° 05' E) is a small island of remnant native vegetation, surrounded by extensive agricultural lands. The Rock Nature Reserve is an important area for the protection of *S. garlandii* as it supports the largest known population of the species (personal observation) and is one of the few formally protected areas within which the species grows. While *S. garlandii* has a restricted geographical distribution, it also has a restricted distribution within The Rock Nature Reserve. It occurs almost exclusively on the exposed upper slopes and ridges of the reserve and thus occupies only a small percentage of a small reserve. The same habitat requirements are evident at Tabletop and Ulandra Nature Reserves and Benambra State Forest.

After less than 75 mm of rain during November 1990 to March 1991 (average 208 mm for this period) the first major fire (15–17 March 1991) in 40 years burnt more than 90% of The Rock Nature Reserve (personal observation). Personal estimates indicated that pre-fire there were several thousand *S. garlandii* plants in the reserve but post-fire there were probably less than 100 plants in leaf and these were confined to inaccessible rock ledges on the eastern cliff.

Given: i) the restricted distribution of *S. garlandii*, ii) the importance of The Rock Nature Reserve to this species' formal protection and iii) the major reduction in plant numbers in the reserve due to the March 1991 fire, it was considered useful to study the post-fire regeneration and subsequent growth of *S. garlandii*. In addition two other aspects of the biology of *S. garlandii* were investigated to help understand seedling establishment and survival. Firstly, *S. garlandii* possesses large leaves of mesophytic appearance while all other perennial species at The Rock Nature Reserve that stay in leaf during summer have smaller xerophytic leaves. Thus leaf anatomy was studied to better understand seedling survival during summer. Secondly, a study of seed viability was conducted as prior tests indicated that a period of dry heat was needed to overcome dormancy. A similar response has only been described in a small number of native species (Bell et al. 1993).

######## PDF PAGE 3 ########
Burrows, *Senecio garlandii* and fire 37

## Materials and methods

An area 50 m to the east of the main cliff was selected for the establishment of a permanent quadrat, 4 x 5 m. This area was chosen as it supported, excluding the herbaceous stratum, an almost monospecific stand of *S. garlandii* prior to the fire and thus was considered favourable for regeneration. The quadrat was 250 m above the surrounding plains and was on the easterly facing scree slopes of a north–south ridge. The quadrat had a slope of 30° and consisted of about 80% bare soil and 20% rock and was divided into 20 1 x 1 m contiguous sub-quadrats. The site was well-drained and was shaded from the early afternoon onwards by a 100 m high cliff to the west. Rainfall and temperature data were obtained from the Bureau of Meteorology's station at Forest Hill, Wagga Wagga, about 35 km NE of the study site.

The quadrat was assessed for a total of 28 months, usually at six-weekly intervals. At each trip the following parameters were assessed: i) number of seedlings and rootstocks of *S. garlandii*/m², ii) average height and number of basal shoots of seedlings and rootstocks of *S. garlandii*, iii) reproductive stage of seedlings and rootstocks of *S. garlandii* and iv) presence/absence and reproductive stage of species other than *S. garlandii*.

Mature seed of *S. garlandii* was collected from plants that recovered from rootstocks and 30 month old plants in late December 1993 and stored dry at ambient temperature. Seed viability was tested (3 replicates of 50 seeds) at about one month intervals by direct germination on filter paper supported on moistened vermiculite in petri dishes subject to a 16 hr photoperiod (45 µmol/m²/sec) at 23° C and 8 hrs dark at 20° C. For light microscopy leaves were fixed in glutaraldehyde, processed using standard procedures for plastic embedding and transverse sectioned at 1–2 µm and stained with toluidine blue (O'Brien & McCully 1981).

## Results

### Seed germination

The seeds were roughly cylindrical (about 2.5 mm length, 0.6 mm diameter), averaged 0.29 mg in weight and had a thin seed coat. Immediately upon wetting the acheneal hairs released several intertwined spiral bodies and within 24 hrs the seeds were surrounded by a mucilaginous sheath. Seed tested within one week of collection exhibited low (< 6%) germination. After 1.5, 2.5 and 3.5 months dry storage at ambient temperatures average germination percentages of 69, 90 and 92%, respectively, were recorded.

### Leaf anatomy

In cross-section the leaves showed typical dorsiventral anatomy with a layer of palisade mesophyll, a layer of spongy mesophyll and a layer of mesophyll intermediate between the palisade and the spongy mesophyll in position and cell arrangement (Fig. 1). A large proportion of the leaf was intercellular air space and little or no sclerenchyma was present. Xerophytic modifications to this basically mesophytic

######## PDF PAGE 4 ########
38 Cunninghamia Vol. 4(1): 1995

structure included: i) the large diameter upper epidermal cells possessed a thick (10–15 µm) outer cell wall, with a thin cuticle, ii) all stomata were restricted to the lower leaf surface, and iii) the lower surface had numerous single-celled trichomes that formed a dense mat about 200 µm thick (Fig. 1).

## Field assessment

### i) Species other than *Senecio garlandii*

The overstorey surrounding the quadrat consisted of *Eucalyptus macrorhyncha*, with some *E. polyanthemos*, *E. albens* and *Brachychiton populneus*, but these species were not recorded in the quadrat. A total of 35 species, excluding *S. garlandii*, were recorded in the quadrat over the assessment period. In terms of origin 22 species (63%) were naturalised and 13 (37%) were native species. In terms of life cycle and growth form 26 (74%) were annual herbs and 9 (26%) were perennial herbs.

[Micrograph: leaf transverse section, labels pm and sm, panel 1]

**Fig. 1.** Transverse section of a mature leaf of *Senecio garlandii*. Note the thick outer epidermal cell walls, the large adaxial epidermal cells, the palisade (pm) and spongy mesophyll (sm) layers, the stoma (arrowed) and the abaxial trichome layer. Scale = 50 µm.

######## PDF PAGE 5 ########
Burrows, *Senecio garlandii* and fire 39

### ii) Survival of *Senecio garlandii*

While the fire killed many of the existing *Senecio* plants some survived by resprouting from a rootstock. Survivors could be identified by their greater shoot growth compared with *Senecio* seedlings and often by the presence of the charred stumps of the previous year's growth. By early September 1991 at least 2 rootstocks had not resprouted in the quadrat, 2 rootstocks both had a single shoot 3 cm in height and one rootstock had 7 shoots all about 8 cm high. Six weeks later one of the smaller rootstocks had died, while of the two remaining, one had a shoot 28 cm high and the other five shoots 50–75 cm high, all with flower primordia. This represents a rapid elongation of 1–1.5 cm/day over the intervening 6 weeks for many of the rootstock shoots. These two plants remained alive for the duration of the study.

### iii) *Senecio garlandii* seedling establishment and mortality

In early September 1991, 5 months after the fire and with average or above average rainfall in the preceding 3 months (Fig. 2), 453 *S. garlandii* seedlings were recorded in the 20 m² quadrat (Fig. 3), ranging from 4–45 seedlings/m², at an average of 22.7 seedlings/m². The seedlings were no greater than 2 cm in height and most were 1 cm or less. Seedling numbers remained largely unchanged over the next 6 weeks (Fig. 3). Several annual species, e.g. *Carduus tenuiflorus*, *Daucus glochidiatus*, *Parietaria debilis*, *Ranunculus sessiliflorus* and *Stellaria media*, were more abundant and vigorous than the *Senecio* seedlings and tended to smother the smaller individuals. By late November 1991, a relatively small 7.3% reduction in seedling numbers had occurred (Fig. 3), although rainfall had been well below average for October and November (Fig. 2). Seedlings that had germinated in thin, loose ash on the top of boulders had died and many of the smaller individuals appeared to be water-stressed. Well-developed seedlings had 5–8 fully expanded leaves, were 10–15 cm high and did not elongate further. All the annual species that had previously overgrown the smaller, slower growing *Senecio* were dead and the perennial herbs died back to some form of rootstock or bulb by mid-summer. At mid-January 1992 the preceding 6 weeks had been relatively dry with only 31 mm of rainfall recorded. Combined with the excellent drainage and warmer temperatures this resulted in the most rapid rate of seedling mortality during the study (Fig. 3) with a 44% reduction in numbers, at an average of 4 deaths/day. In late February 1992, a further 27% reduction in numbers from the previous assessment period (average of 1.5 deaths/day) was recorded. The second half of summer 1991/1992 was relatively wet (93.4 mm of rainfall) and cool (January and February mean monthly maxima were about 2 degrees below average). These conditions had allowed hundreds of *Carduus tenuiflorus* seedlings to germinate in the quadrat, but a new cohort of *Senecio* seedlings did not germinate. During the winter and spring of 1992 no new *Senecio* seedlings germinated, even in the organic material and soil on top of the rocks where suitable germination conditions occurred without competition from existing plants. In spring 1992, as per the previous year, the *Senecio* seedlings were partially smothered by annuals but given their greater size and greater competitive ability the effects were not as pronounced. After the high mortality rate recorded during summer 1991/1992 seedling mortality was low during the remainder of the study (Fig. 3) even during the summer of

######## PDF PAGE 6 ########
40 Cunninghamia Vol. 4(1): 1995

1992/1993 when there were 10 consecutive weeks where only 33.4 mm of rainfall was recorded and there were 11 consecutive days with maxima greater than 35° C.

In spring 1991 there were about 450 *Senecio* seedlings in the quadrat, ranging in density from 4–45/m². In December 1993, 28 months later, there were 122 *Senecio* seedlings, ranging in density from 1–14/m². This represents an overall mortality of 73%, ranging from a high of 89–94% in 3 sub-quadrats, to a low of 44% in one sub-quadrat.

### iv) Growth form

In their first year of growth the *Senecio* seedlings developed a single upright shoot but by early winter this shoot had usually senesced and axillary buds at its base began to slowly elongate. Rapid elongation of the new basal shoots commenced in mid-August 1992 and by late September most shoots had increased in average height by 8 cm in the preceding 6 weeks. This elongation was greatest during October (about 4.5 cm/week) and began to slow in December when plants reached their average maximum height of 65 cm. Seedlings averaged 2.2 shoots in their second year, and some plants had up to 5 equal-sized shoots. In early May 1993 the shoots produced during the previous spring and summer began to senesce and, as in the previous year, the shoot system was gradually replaced by new shoots which were initiated in the basal leaf axils of the existing shoots. These shoots were often initiated just below ground level and grew horizontally for a short distance before becoming upright, thus giving a single individual the appearance of several plants growing in close proximity. In December 1993 most plants were at full adult-size (average plant height 92 cm), with an average of 3.9 shoots per plant (range 1–12). These main shoots were unbranched for most of their length but near the apex several axillary buds had elongated and initiated flowers to form a corymbose inflorescence.

### v) Flowering

In their first year no seedlings in the quadrat flowered or had formed flower primordia, while the two rootstocks had finished flowering by late November but fruits had not been released. In September 1992 many *Senecio* plants had initiated flower primordia and by early November the primordia had developed into large flower buds. In mid-December 1992, 44% of the 143 remaining *Senecio* plants were flowering or had finished flowering and in late January 1993 flowering had finished. However December 1992 was unusually moist (Fig. 2) and cool, and in January 1993 the lower axillary buds in some plants had rapidly elongated and initiated new flower primordia. In mid-March 1993, after a dry finish to summer (Fig. 2), the flower buds that had been initiated in mid-January had been aborted. In December 1993 more than 95% of the 122 plants surviving their third summer had flowered or were flowering.

General observations throughout the reserve revealed that *S. garlandii* had: i) re-established monospecific thickets where they existed pre-fire, ii) increased plant density where previously only scattered plants had been present, and iii) a limited increase in range but was still restricted to the ridge areas.

######## PDF PAGE 7 ########
Burrows, *Senecio garlandii* and fire 41

[Bar graph: rainfall (mm/month), 0-140, monthly 1991-1993, with long-term average line]

**Fig. 2.** Monthly rainfall during the study period with long-term average (■ – ■) values. Values are for Forest Hill, Wagga Wagga (35 km NE from site). Arrow indicates time of the fire.

[Line graph: seedling no., 0-500, D J 1992 D J 1993 D]

**Fig. 3.** Number of *Senecio garlandii* seedlings in the permanent quadrat during the study period.

## Discussion

The principal finding of this study is that *Senecio garlandii*, a vulnerable species reduced to a few individuals after the 1991 fire at The Rock Nature Reserve, has regenerated successfully from seed and, to a lesser extent, from rootstocks. It has maintained its almost monospecific stands in its areas of pre-fire dominance, has increased in density where previously only scattered individuals existed and has expanded its distribution but is still principally restricted to the upper ridge areas. Several *Senecio* species are known as fire ephemerals or 'fire weeds' (Gill 1993). While *S. garlandii* shares with these species the ability to successfully regenerate after fire it would not be considered a fire weed because: i) seeds do not need a heat treatment to germinate, ii) individual plants appear to be relatively long lived through their annual resprouting habit, i.e. they do not have the short life span of a fire

######## PDF PAGE 8 ########
42 Cunninghamia Vol. 4(1): 1995

ephemeral, and iii) populations can persist in low fire frequency conditions, e.g. plants on cliff ledges.

Lawrence (1985) investigated the reproductive biology of 32 mainly native species of *Senecio*, with *S. garlandii* listed as *Senecio* species A (Belcher 1986). Lawrence noted, as in the present study, that *S. garlandii* is a perennial, is early flowering, produces lightweight seeds, the seeds produce a mucilaginous sheath upon wetting and that these seeds can have high germination percentages. From observations on pollen-ovule ratios and inflorescence morphology it was possible for Lawrence to deduce that *S. garlandii* was self-incompatible. Lawrence noted that stable environments favour outbreeding perennials but only 5 of the 15 self-incompatible perennials she investigated were usually restricted to comparatively stable environments. Three of the five, including *S. garlandii*, are found on rocky outcrops of drier inland areas.

The most common criterion for classifying a species response to fire is whether persistence is by seed ('seeders') or by vegetative means ('sprouters') (Gill & Bradstock 1992). This study indicates that *S. garlandii* is principally a seeder although some plants function as sprouters after a low-intensity fire. Gill & Bradstock (1992) list three categories of seed regeneration: i) from viable canopy-stored seed, ii) from soil-stored seed, and iii) from seed brought in, because no propagules remain on site after fire. In *S. garlandii* the mature achenes are easily dislodged from the head's receptacle with little force, therefore no seed-store exists on the plant. Many species of the Asteraceae have small air-borne fruits and are capable of recolonising burnt areas with seed blown in from unburnt areas (Purdie & Slatyer 1976). However, because the fire eliminated almost the complete *Senecio* population, except for some isolated individuals on cliff ledges, there were no seeds on unburnt plants to be used for recolonisation of burnt areas. In addition, while the achenes of *S. garlandii* have numerous slender pappus bristles they are not persistent (Belcher 1986), and thus long-distance wind dispersal of the fruits would not be expected. Thus it is most probable that the re-establishment of *S. garlandii* was from a seed-store in the soil, as were the 7 composites described by Purdie & Slatyer (1976). Purdie (1977) noted that seeds in litter are often destroyed in fires, while many seeds in the soil survive. Purdie (1977) noted that germination of herbaceous species, including *Senecio quadridentatus* and *Hypochoeris* spp., was lower in burnt than unburnt areas. She suggests that the seed may not be stored for long periods in the soil or are trapped in the litter by their pappus and thus destroyed by fire.

Studies by Hobbs & Atkins (1991) and Purdie & Slatyer (1976) found, as did the present study, that germination of perennial species occurred in the first year after the fire, but not in subsequent years. Hobbs & Atkins (1991) also found that seedlings of perennial species that survived their first summer generally continued to survive or, conversely, mortality is greatest in the seedling phase (Fig. 3).

Bell et al. (1993) noted that obligate re-seeding species tend to grow vertically initially then produce an 'umbrella shape', while resprouting species have more of an 'urn shape'. *Senecio garlandii* combines these two strategies as initially it produces a vertically growing shoot that only branches near the apex; however, after plants have become established they branch from near the base and form a more spreading canopy.

######## PDF PAGE 9 ########
Burrows, *Senecio garlandii* and fire 43

While *S. garlandii* operates as a resprouter in its annual growth cycle, the shoots originate above or close to ground level and a specialised rootstock or similar organ does not appear to be present. Thus fire-induced mortality of mature plants is to be expected. The degree of water-stress experienced by shrubs at and following the time of fire may be an important factor in determining the proportion of shrubs that resprout (Hodgkinson & Griffin 1982). This suggests that a low fire intensity, combined with more than the about 25 mm of rainfall received in the 2.5 months after the March fire (Fig. 2), then more *Senecio* rootstocks may have resprouted.

Over 200 vascular plant species have been recorded at The Rock Nature Reserve (Benson & Melrose 1993) but only about 50 species remain in leaf over summer. Most (> 90%) of these species possess small leaves and/or pronounced xerophytic modifications to their leaf anatomy. Thus it is remarkable that *S. garlandii* has the largest leaves of any species at The Rock Nature Reserve (personal observation) and possesses a mesophytic dorsiventral leaf anatomy that appears unsuited to the semi-arid conditions. The thickening of the outer epidermal cell wall, the restriction of stomata to the abaxial surface and the extremely dense abaxial trichome covering are probably effective in controlling water loss, in both seedlings and adults. This contributes to a relatively low mortality rate for a mesophytic species growing in semi-arid conditions and allows the seedlings a competitive advantage as they are able to continue vegetative and reproductive growth when the other species are dead or dormant. The lack of sclerenchyma results in wilting of leaves during times of pronounced water-stress.

After more than 70 mm of rainfall in early February 1992, combined with 13 consecutive days with temperature maxima below the monthly mean, there was an extensive germination of *Carduus* seedlings but no *Senecio garlandii* seedlings were observed. All the thistle seedlings died of water-stress before flowering. This observation, combined with the germination tests, suggests that the *Senecio garlandii* seeds may possess some mechanism to prevent germination after periods of wet weather in summer. A period of after-ripening, consisting of several months of dry heat has been described for a small number of Australian species of the Asteraceae and Poaceae (Mott & Groves 1981, Bell et al. 1993).

From a conservation viewpoint it is of concern that 22 weed species were present in the quadrat. General observation and the findings of other studies (Purdie & Slatyer 1976, Hobbs & Atkins 1991) indicate that the abundance and diversity of weeds should progressively be reduced as the *S. garlandii* re-establishes. *Senecio garlandii* is able to reach reproductive maturity relatively quickly as shown by 45% of the surviving seedlings flowering in their second summer and greater than 95% flowering in their third summer. This indicates that this species would not be eliminated at this site even if the fire frequency increased, although further study is required to determine what length of time and conditions are required to establish an effective seed-store in the soil. In summary, it appears that *S. garlandii* could tolerate a wide variation in fire frequency and no specific fire management practices are needed to maintain the population at The Rock Nature Reserve.
