## **Flowering, seed dispersal, seed predation and seedling recruitment in two pyrogenic flowering resprouters**

*Andrew J*. *Denham*<sup>A</sup> *and Tony D*. *Auld*

Biodiversity Research Group, NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, PO Box 1967, Hurstville, NSW 2220, Australia.

ACorresponding author; email: andrew.denham@npws.nsw.gov.au

*Abstract.* A few resprouting plants in fire-prone environments have no local seed bank (soil or canopy) when a fire occurs. These species rely on post-fire flowering and the production of non-dormant seeds to exploit favourable post-fire establishment and growth conditions. For two such pyrogenic flowering species (*Doryanthes excelsa* Correa and *Telopea speciosissima* (Smith) R.Br.), we examined the timing of seed release, patterns of fruit production, seed dispersal, seed predation and seedling establishment following a fire in the Sydney region of southeastern Australia. Both species took some 19 months after the fire to flower and the first seeds were released 2 years after the fire. *D*. *excelsa* flowered and fruited only once after the fire. For *T*. *speciosissima*, plants also flowered at least once more in the subsequent 5 years, but produced seed in only the first three post-fire flowering years. Fruit production differed between species, with fruiting individuals of *D*. *excelsa* producing fewer infructescences, similar numbers of follicles, but many more seeds per follicle than fruiting individuals of *T*. *speciosissima*. Ultimately, *D*. *excelsa* produced approximately six times as many seeds per m2 and four times as many seeds per adult in one flowering season than *T*. *speciosissima* did after four flowering (three successful fruiting) seasons.

Seeds were passively dispersed from fruits borne 3–4 m (*D*. *excelsa*) or 1–2 m (*T*. *speciosissima*) above the ground. Most seeds were found within 5 m (*D*. *excelsa*) or 3 m (*T*. *speciosissima*) of parent plants. The primary seed shadow of both species was a poor predictor of the distribution of seedlings, with more seedlings occurring further from the adults than expected from the distribution of seeds. Seed loss to predators was high in both species in exclusion experiments where mammals had access to clumps of seeds (77–88%). It was variable and generally lower (8–65%) in experiments where seeds were not locally clumped. However, for *T*. *speciosissima*, at one site, some 65% of seeds were lost to mammals and invertebrates in these latter experiments. At this site, these losses appeared to influence subsequent recruitment levels, as very low seedling densities were observed.

For both species, germination of seedlings first occurred some 2.5–3 years after the passage of the fire. The percentage of seeds produced to seedlings successfully established was low in *D*. *excelsa* (2–3%) and more variable across sites and years in *T*. *speciosissima* (0–18%). Resultant post-fire seedling densities of *D*. *excelsa* (two sites) and *T*. *speciosissima* at one site were similar, but they were much lower at the *T*. *speciosissima* site that had high levels of seed predation. Both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* are amongst the slowest woody resprouting species to recruit seedlings after fire in south-eastern Australia and lag years behind species with soil or canopy seed banks.

#### **Introduction**

In fire-prone habitats, recruitment in plant species is frequently linked to the passage of a fire (Tyler 1995). This results from at least two main mechanisms. First, in species with soil seed banks, seed dormancy may be broken by the passage of fires (e.g. via heat, smoke, charred wood: Keeley 1991; Brown 1993; or interactions of these factors: Keith 1997; Morris 2000). Examples include many legumes (Jeffery *et al.* 1988; Auld and O'Connell 1991) and nonleguminous species (Brown 1993; Dixon *et al.* 1995). Second, in species with canopy seed banks, fires result in the mass opening of fruits and the release of seeds (Bond *et al.* 1984; Lamont *et al.* 1991).

However, a number of species have no available seed storage in either the soil or canopy at the time of the passage of a fire (Keith 1996). A few may rely on dispersal from unburnt areas, but most have mechanisms that allow established plants to survive fire via buried lignotubers, rhizomes or buds (protected meristems). These species usually flower soon after fire and then release seeds (Gill 1981; Frost 1984; Johnson *et al.* 1994; Bond and van Wilgen 1996; Carrington 1999). For species dependant on post-fire flowering for recruitment (pyrogenic flowering resprouters), 

{2}

######## PDF PAGE 4 ########
the timing and magnitude of this flowering will influence opportunities for post-fire seedling establishment. The longer the interval between the passage of a fire and seedling recruitment, the more of the available resources such as light, nutrients and space, are likely to have been captured by other resprouting species or by those species with soil or canopy seed banks that can recruit in the immediate post-fire period.

Many individuals of pyrogenic flowering resprouting species in south-eastern Australia appear to have a single post-fire flowering (e.g. *Angophora hispida*, Auld 1986; *Blandfordia nobilis*, Johnson *et al.* 1994; *Lomatia silaifolia*, Denham and Whelan 2000; *Xanthorrhoea australis*, Gill and Ingwersen 1976, but see; *X*. *fulva*, Taylor *et al.* 1998). In such cases, this represents the only opportunity for recruitment between fires. For other species, flowering may extend over several years following a fire (e.g. *T*. *speciosissima*, Pyke 1983; Bradstock 1995; Goldingay 2000; *Xanthorrhoea australis*, Curtis 1998). However, the timing of recruitment in pyrogenic flowering resprouting species has been little studied and the degree to which each post-fire flowering event contributes to recruitment is unexplored.

In the post-fire environment, the impact of seed predation may be reduced due to lower predator abundance and also via predator satiation, in the case of serotinous seed release (Whelan 1995; Bond and van Wilgen 1996; Myerscough *et al.* 2000). However, the seeds of pyrogenic flowering resprouters are likely to be released after most seeds from serotinous species have germinated and, consequently, would not benefit from any predator satiation effects from serotinous seed release. In addition, populations of predators may have recovered by this time. All pyrogenic flowering resprouters are thought to release seeds in a non-dormant state (Bell *et al.* 1993; Bond and van Wilgen 1996) and hence form transient soil seed banks (*sensu* Parker and Kelly 1989).

In this study, we assessed post-fire reproduction and the patterns of seedling recruitment after a wildfire in 1994, in two resprouting species reliant on post-fire flowering for seed production (*Doryanthes excelsa* and *Telopea speciosissima*), from the Sydney area of south-eastern Australia. We examined (i) the timing of flowering and magnitude of seed production over 5 years after the fire; (ii) the pattern of seed and seedling dispersal; (iii) the level of post-dispersal seed predation; and (iv) the proportion of seeds released that resulted in successful establishment of new plants.

#### **Methods**

#### *Study species*

*Doryanthes excelsa* Correa (Gymea lily—Doryanthaceae) is a large perennial rosette plant with a bulbous rhizome and long broad linear leaves up to 3 m long. It is apparently capable of asexual reproduction by branching of the rhizome (Nash 1996). It grows in dry sclerophyll forests and woodlands on soils derived from sandstone containing some clay and is restricted to the Sydney Basin in south-eastern Australia, with three outlying populations in northern New South Wales (Harden 1990–1993). The species survives fire by having apical buds protected in underground leaf bases. It flowers in a large, red inflorescence held up to 5 m above the foliage of the plant (Harden 1990–1993). Fire appears to stimulate flowering, although sporadic flowering does occur in the absence of fire (Nash 1996). The mechanism determining flowering is unknown (Beeh 1996; Nash 1996).

*Telopea speciosissima* (Smith) R.Br. (waratah—Proteaceae) is a tall shrub, generally 2–4 m, which is also known for its striking red blooms that emerge above the resprouting shrubby vegetation in the post-fire environment. It is common in dry sclerophyll forest and woodlands on the central coast and central and southern tablelands of New South Wales (Harden 1990–1993). The species survives fire by having dormant buds protected in an underground lignotuber (Bradstock 1995). Aerial stems are completely regrown after each fire.

#### *Sites*

Three sample sites within a 10-km radius were chosen in Royal National Park, about 35 km south of Sydney (34°03′S, 151°03′E). All sites occurred on soils derived from the Triassic Hawkesbury Sandstone Formation, although Site 1 (with an ironstone influence) and Site 2 (with an alluvial influence) were on soils slightly more fertile than Site 3. At Site 1, both study species occurred in ironstone woodland vegetation (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with an overstorey of *Eucalyptus sieberi*, *Corymbia gummifera*, *Banksia serrata*, *Xylomelum pyriforme* and *Ceratopetalum gummiferum*. The shrubby understorey included *Grevillea diffusa*, *Banksia spinulosa*, *Lissanthe strigosa*, *Prostanthera* sp., *Isopogon anemonifolius*, *Acacia myrtifolia*, *Xanthorrhoea media*, *Lomandra* spp. and *Dianella* sp. The vegetation at Site 2 (*D*. *excelsa* only) is Sandstone Gully Forest (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with an overstorey of *Angophora costata*, *Banksia serrata*, *Ceratopetalum gummiferum*, *Eucalyptus piperita* and *E*. *sieberi* and a shrubby understorey that included *Boronia pinnata*, *Grevillea mucronulata*, *Acacia terminalis*, *Lomandra longifolia* and *Caustis flexuosa*. At Site 3 (*T*. *speciosissima* only) the vegetation is Sandstone Heath (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with a short overstorey of *Corymbia gummifera*, *Eucalyptus obstans*, *E*. *sclerophylla* and *Banksia serrata* and a shrubby understorey that included *Lambertia formosa*, *Lissanthe strigosa* and sedges including *Xanthorrhoea media*, *Restio dimorpha* and *Cyathochaeta diandra*. Plant nomenclature follows Harden (1990–1993).

All sites were burnt in January 1994. Before 1994, there was variation in fire history across sites. The eastern part of Site 1 (sampled for *D*. *excelsa*) and Site 3 were burnt in 1988. The western part of Site 1, separated by a road from the eastern part (sampled for both study species), and Site 2 were burnt in the early 1980s (NPWS fire records; D. Keith, pers. comm.).

#### *Timing of flowering and seed release*

The three study sites were monitored to observe flowering after the January 1994 fire for both species up until December 2000. As both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* flower in July–October, this involved seven potential flowering seasons (1994–2000). General observations were also made throughout Royal National Park to determine whether the pattern of the study sites was representative of the general response of the study species to fire in this area. The timing of fruit development and seed release was recorded for the first four flowering seasons after the 1994 fire.

#### *Estimates of seed production and seedling establishment*

Six 30 × 30-m plots were established as follows: *D*. *excelsa*, two plots at each of Sites 1 and 2; *T*. *speciosissima*, one plot at each of Sites 1 and 3. For both study species, within each plot at each site, the numbers of infructescences and follicles on all plants were scored each year (1994–2000). To estimate the number of seeds per follicle, intact

{3}

######## PDF PAGE 5 ########
follicles were collected in autumn 1996, prior to dehiscence, for each species from each site. For *T*. *speciosissima*, samples of 23 and 25 follicles were collected from Sites 1 and 3, respectively, while for *D*. *excelsa*, samples of 15 and 29 follicles were collected from Sites 1 and 2, respectively. Seeds within these follicles were scored after dehiscence in the laboratory. For *T*. *speciosissima*, only those seeds judged as 'filled' (i.e. likely to be viable) were included in this assessment (see also Bradstock 1995; Denham and Whelan 2000). For *D*. *excelsa*, no assessment was made, although Nash (1996) found that the average viability of seeds collected from a number of locations (not including Royal National Park) was 86% (±6.2 s.e.). The individuals used to estimate numbers of seeds per follicle were sampled from outside the plots to avoid impacts on primary seed dispersal and seedling recruitment. The density of seeds per plot was estimated by multiplying the number of intact follicles by the estimate of the mean number of seeds per follicle and dividing this value by the area of each plot (900 m2 ).

To estimate the magnitude of post-fire seedling recruitment for both study species, five randomly allocated transects each 1 × 30 m were searched for seedlings in spring 1998, within each of the 30 × 30-m plots. For *T*. *speciosissima*, we assessed the probable fruiting year from which seedlings were established, by comparisons with other seedlings of known age within the sites.

#### *Primary seed dispersal*

The seeds of *D*. *excelsa* are disc-like, about 15 mm in diameter, 2 mm thick, have a dry spongy texture and weigh approximately 43 mg (Westoby *et al.* 1990; Nash 1996; A. J. Denham, pers. obs.). The seeds of *T*. *speciosissima* are winged and weigh approximately 72 mg (Westoby *et al.* 1990). Westoby *et al.* (1990) considered *T*. *speciosissima* to be adapted for wind dispersal, but could only suggest that the spongy texture of *D*. *excelsa* seed could serve for wind or water dispersal. Initial seed fall from dehisced follicles in both species is passive and movement in the air appears likely to be the main means of dispersal away from the infructescence.

The spatial pattern of initial seed fall was estimated by counting seeds found on the ground in four orthogonal transects along compass bearings from each of five isolated plants at Site 1 for *D*. *excelsa* and Sites 1 and 3 for *T*. *speciosissima*. Because of time constraints, this was not done at Site 2 for *D*. *excelsa*. Searches were done in June–August of 1996, when most seeds had fallen from the follicles. Some further redistribution of seeds along the soil surface by wind and rain after this time is likely (Lamont *et al.* 1993; Hammill *et al.* 1998). The transects for *D*. *excelsa* started approximately 0.25 m from the centre of each clump, because of the space occupied by the leaf bases of the plants. Counts of numbers of seeds were made every 0.1 m along each transect. Transects were 0.5 m wide and limited to 7.25 m long as there were no seeds seen in initial searches beyond 7.15 m. For *T*. *speciosissima*, the area occupied by the stems was included in the transects. In preliminary searches around *T*. *speciosissima* adults, no seeds were found more than 3 m from adults at Site 1 and 2 m from adults at Site 3, so the transect lengths were reduced to 3.5 and 2.5 m, respectively.

#### *Seed predation*

The fates of recently released seeds on the ground were examined during the initial seed release after the 1994 fire (i.e. in 1996), in two trials. First, an exclusion experiment was used to investigate the agents responsible for and the degree of post-dispersal predation at each site. It was assumed that no secondary dispersal of seeds by invertebrates such as ants was likely, since neither species have lipid bodies attached to their seeds. Westoby *et al.* (1990) suggested that neither species is myrmecochorous and field observations supported this. A block design was used with two treatments and 10 seeds per treatment per block. This experiment was set up for *D*. *excelsa* at Sites 1 and 2 and for *T*. *speciosissima* at Sites 1 and 3 as follows:

(a) caged: cages (15 × 15 cm × 5 cm high with 1-cm<sup>2</sup> mesh size) were used to exclude vertebrate predators, while still allowing access to most invertebrates. To prevent seeds from washing away in heavy rain, a PVC ring sawn from pipe 10 cm in diameter and about 1 cm tall was placed on the ground. This ring was pushed into the soil leaving only the top 0.5 cm protruding. The cage was placed over the ring and fastened down with wire stakes.

(b) uncaged: where only the PVC ring was used. This allowed access to both invertebrates and vertebrates.

Ten blocks consisting of a caged and an uncaged treatment, were used for each species, at each site. The blocks were placed about 5 m apart along a transect through the site, with separate transects for each species at Site 1.

The number of seeds remaining in each treatment block was recorded every day for the first week and approximately every second day for the following 10 weeks. Additionally, any information concerning the condition of seeds (such as whether chewed or germinated) or the presence of testa remains was recorded at each visit.

Second, for both study species, a trial was established to examine the level of predation on seeds that were placed singly at random locations throughout the plots, rather than clumped as above (see Auld and Denham 1999, 2001). These trials were established for *D*. *excelsa* in two plots at Site 1 and in one plot at Site 2 and for *T*. *speciosissima* in one plot at each of Sites 1 and 3. A single seed was placed at each of 10 randomly located positions according to the 30 × 30-m grid established at each site, with the location marked by a steel stake 0.2 m away. Additional batches of 10 seeds were similarly placed in new random locations each week for the following 3 weeks. The fate of these seeds was followed for the next 10 weeks, with details recorded as for the exclusion experiment. Only 'filled' seeds were used in these experiments.

#### *Seedling dispersal*

The following two different estimates were made of the dispersal pattern of seedlings around adult plants:

(a) the ground was searched for seedlings up to a distance of 10 m from fruiting plants around five isolated plants of *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1. The distance of each seedling from the centre of the adult was measured. The adults included two of those used to sample primary seed dispersal. Sufficient seedlings were not available at the other three adults sampled for primary seed dispersal. For *T*. *speciosissima*, this technique was not used as adults continued to flower after the first year.

(b) for *D*. *excelsa* at Sites 1 and 2 and *T*. *speciosissima* at Sites 1 and 3, the distance of each seedling from the centre of the nearest parent was measured for all seedlings observed in the transects used for estimating seedling establishment (above). Because of the overall low number of seedlings observed for *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 3, the entire 30 × 30-m plot was surveyed. This estimate included overlapping seed shadows from adult plants, as typically occurs in the field.

#### *Analyses*

To test the hypothesis that fruit and seed production varied across sites and years within the study area, estimates of infructescence and follicle production per fruiting plant were compared in *D*. *excelsa* by a nested 2-factor ANOVA with plots nested within sites and in *T*. *speciosissima* across sites and years when fruit was produced, by a 2-factor ANOVA without replication. Estimates of seed production per m2 were compared in *D*. *excelsa* across sites by a 1-factor ANOVA with plots as replicates and in *T*. *speciosissima* across sites and fruiting years by a 2-factor ANOVA without replication (Zar 1996).

To test the hypothesis that vertebrate seed predators had an impact on the number of seeds available for germination (the seed predation

exclusion experiment), the proportions of seeds remaining in each replicate treatment within the 10 blocks after 75 days were compared by a 3-factor ANOVA (factors were treatment, site and block, with blocks nested within sites) for each species separately. The hypothesis that the two species suffered different levels of predation at Site 1, where both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* were sampled, was tested by a 3-factor ANOVA with species and caging treatment (with blocks nested within species) as factors.

At lower seed densities than in the seed predation exclusion experiment (the single seeds trial) we tested the hypothesis that predation varied across sites. For *T*. *speciosissima*, the proportions of seeds remaining in each weekly cohort of 10 seeds at the end of the study (after 9 weeks) were compared across sites by a 1-factor ANOVA. Data for *D*. *excelsa* were similarly analysed, using both plots at Site 1 and the single plot at Site 2 as three levels in a 'location' factor. Again, it was possible to test the hypothesis that the two species suffered different levels of predation at Site 1 at this lower seed density. Here, only the western of the two *D*. *excelsa* plots was used, as it was adjacent to the *T*. *speciosissima* plot (1-factor ANOVA).

We tested the hypothesis that seedling establishment varied across sites in both species and across years for *T*. *speciosissima*. In *D*. *excelsa*, the number of seedlings per transect was compared across sites by a nested 2-factor ANOVA with plots nested in sites. For *T*. *speciosissima*, the number of seedlings per transect was compared across sites and fruiting year of origin by a 2-factor ANOVA.

For each ANOVA, homogeneity of variances was tested by Cochran's test. Where variances were significantly heterogeneous an arcsine transformation was applied to proportion data and a square-root transformation was applied to count data. If variances were still heterogeneous, the analysis was carried out on the raw data with a conservative approach to rejection of the null hypothesis (Underwood 1981).

To test the hypothesis that the distributions of seedlings around plants were the same as the distributions of seeds around plants, a number of Kolmogorov–Smirnov goodness-of-fit tests were done.

(i) For *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1, seed and seedling data from the isolated plants were placed into 0.1-m classes and frequency counts of seeds or seedlings were obtained from each distance class for all five individuals. The proportions of seeds or seedlings per distance class were then determined. Seedling data for distances less than 0.25 m from the adult were omitted, since data for seed distribution were not obtained at this distance, due to the occupation of most of the available space by the parent plants. Similarly, seedling distances greater than 7.15 m were omitted since this was distance of the furthest observed seed. A Kolmogorov–Smirnov test was used to determine the goodnessof-fit of the seedling distribution (observed) with the seed distribution (predicted) (Zar 1996).

(ii) For *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1 and *T*. *speciosissima* at Sites 1 and 3, estimations were made of the goodness-of-fit of the seedling distributions from the plot transect sampling (observed) with the seed distributions from the isolated individuals (expected). Restriction of seedling data to the greatest distance observed for seeds (7.15 m) was as above for *D*. *excelsa*, and to 3.75 m for *T*. *speciosissima*. There was no restriction on the least distance for *T*. *speciosissima*. This test enabled the determination of whether the distribution of seeds around isolated adults adequately explained the distribution of seedlings around adults that were contagiously distributed (a more typical situation) and thus had overlapping seed shadows.

(iii) For *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1, the seedling distribution from the five isolated plants ('expected') was compared with that obtained from the plot transect sampling ('observed'). This test assessed how well the distribution of seedlings around isolated plants of *D*. *excelsa* represented the more typical situation of contagiously distributed individuals.

#### **Results**

#### *Timing of flowering and seed release*

For both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*, the first flowering after the January 1994 fires occurred in late winter (August) of 1995, some 19 months after the January 1994 fire. This pattern was found at all study sites and more generally across Royal National Park. Fruits matured in the following autumn (March–June 1996), with *D*. *excelsa* first releasing seeds in March 1996 and *T*. *speciosissima* in April 1996. Consequently, seeds were not released into the post-fire habitat until some 25–26 months after the passage of the January 1994 fire. Seed fall was quite prolonged with some seeds still in fruits in June (both species). *D. excelsa* plants in the study plots did not flower in any of the subsequent 5 years, while most *T*. *speciosissima* individuals flowered again the following year and a few in three of the subsequent 4 years (Table 1), with a similar timing of flowering and fruiting to that observed in 1995–1996.

#### *Fruit and seed production*

In *D*. *excelsa*, the number, and hence density, of flowering plants varied considerably between plots within sites, ranging from six at Site 1, plot 1 (0.2 m–2) to 39 at Site 2, plot 2 (1.3 m–2) (Table 1). There were no significant differences between sites in the mean numbers of infructescences (*F*1,2 = 0.86, *P* = 0.45) or follicles (*F*1,2 = 9.94, *P* = 0.09) produced per fruiting plant, although there were almost twice as many follicles produced at Site 1, plot 1, than at Site 2, plot 2 (Table 1). For *T*. *speciosissima*, the total number of individuals that flowered between 1995 and 2000 varied from 14 at Site 1 to 24 at Site 3 (Table 1). There was no significant difference in the mean number of infructescences (*F*1,2 = 0.4, *P* = 0.59) or follicles (*F*1,2 = 0.003, *P* = 0.96) per fruiting plant between sites across the 1995–1997 flowering seasons. *D. excelsa* had greater seed production per follicle than *T*. *speciosissima* (104, 105 *v.* 11 seeds per follicle, respectively, Table 2). There were no significant differences in the number of seeds per follicle between sites for *T*. *speciosissima* (*F*1,46 = 0.43, *P* = 0.52) or *D*. *excelsa* (*F*1,42 = 0.08, *P* = 0.93) (Table 2). The estimated density of seeds produced by *D*. *excelsa* varied greatly, although not significantly (*F*1,2 = 4.76, *P* = 0.16) across sites, with Site 1 producing 9.9 (±0.4 s.e.) seeds per m<sup>2</sup> and Site 2 producing 17.7 (±3.6 s.e.) (Table 3). The lack of significance in this comparison is likely to be a result of the considerable variation between plots at Site 2, with one plot producing approximately 1.5 times as many seeds as the other. This in turn was largely because of the much higher density of flowering and fruiting plants in plot 2 than in plot 1 of Site 2 (Table 1). There were no significant differences in seed density of *T*. *speciosissima* between sites (*F*1,2 = 1.11, *P* = 0.40) or among years (*F*2,2 = 4.19, *P* = 0.19). In the first post-fire fruiting year (1996), the estimated density of seeds

Despite the lack of significance of a year effect in the analysis, at both sites seed production declined dramatically by the third fruiting year (1997) and no seeds were produced in subsequent years (Table 1). Seed dispersal approximated an exponential decay curve (see also Janzen 1970; Okubo and Levin 1989; Willson 1992). Most seeds fell within 5 m of adults for *D*. *excelsa* and within 3 m of adults for *T*. *speciosissima* (Fig. 1).

2	
3	######## PDF PAGE 1 ########
4	Canopy Seed Bank Dynamics and Optimum Fire Regime for the Highly Serotinous Shrub, Banksia Hookeriana
5	Author(s): N. J. Enright, Byron B. Lamont and Ralf Marsula
6	Source: Journal of Ecology, Vol. 84, No. 1 (Feb., 1996), pp. 9-17
7	Published by: British Ecological Society
8	Stable URL: http://www.jstor.org/stable/2261695
9	Accessed: 07-05-2016 01:46 UTC
10	
11	Your use of the JSTOR archive indicates your acceptance of the Terms & Conditions of Use, available at http://about.jstor.org/terms
12	
13	JSTOR is a not-for-profit service that helps scholars, researchers, and students discover, use, and build upon a wide range of content in a trusted digital archive. We use information technology and tools to increase productivity and facilitate new forms of scholarship. For more information about JSTOR, please contact support@jstor.org.
14	
15	Wiley, British Ecological Society are collaborating with JSTOR to digitize, preserve and extend access to Journal of Ecology
16	
17	######## PDF PAGE 2 ########
18	*Journal of Ecology* 1996, **84**, 9-17
19	
20	# Canopy seed bank dynamics and optimum fire regime for the highly serotinous shrub, *Banksia hookeriana*
21	
22	N.J. ENRIGHT,\*† BYRON B. LAMONT† and RALF MARSULA‡
23	
24	\*Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, University of Melbourne, Parkville, 3052, Australia, †School of Environmental Biology, Curtin University of Technology, GPO Box U1987 Perth, 6001, Australia and ‡Sektion Ökosystemanalyse, UFZ-Umweltforschungszentrum, Leipzig-Halle GmbH, Permoserstr. 15, PF 2, O-7050 Leipzig, Germany
25	
26	## Summary
27	
28	1 *Banksia hookeriana* is a serotinous nonsprouting shrub restricted to the fire-prone northern sandplain scrub-heaths of Western Australia. Evidence of the natural fire frequency to which the species is best adapted was sought through analysis of its seed demography using a computer model of canopy seed bank dynamics based on field data.
29	
30	2 Plants began flowering at 3-4 years of age but storage of viable seeds in the canopy was rare for plants < 5 years. Infructescences (cones) contained a mean of 12 follicles, holding two seeds of which 62% were estimated to be viable.
31	
32	3 Cone (and seed) production increased with plant age to 15 years, but then fluctuated widely around a mean of 17 cones per year. By this time the average plant had an estimated canopy seed bank of 700 viable seeds comprising seeds 1–10 years old.
33	
34	4 Seeds were lost from the canopy seed bank through spontaneous follicle rupture (i.e. in the absence of fire), granivory by insect larvae, and decay. Most follicles remained closed for at least 5 years and up to 50% of follicles were still closed after 10 years. Insect granivores destroyed 18% of seeds in 1-year-old cones, and continued to destroy seeds in older cones at a rate of 2-3% per year.
35	
36	5 The seed bank model predicted continued seed accumulation in the canopy to at least age 25 years (1400 seeds), but by this time more viable seeds (~ 2200) had been lost to spontaneous opening, granivory and decay than were then stored on the plant.
37	
38	6 Shannon–Weiner diversity (H′) of seed ages in the canopy seed bank increased with plant age, while evenness (V′) decreased at first (to plant age 17 years) and then increased.
39	
40	7 On a time-scale of many generations, the likelihood of successful recruitment of individuals in the next generation (on average), occurs for a fire frequency of 15-18 years. At this frequency resource wastage in this low-nutrient environment would be minimized.
41	
42	8 Recent fires have recurred within 7-11 years and indicate a human impact on the natural fire regime which may ultimately threaten the species.
43	
44	*Keywords*: *Banksia*, fire frequency, seed bank model, seed demography, serotiny
45	
46	*Journal of Ecology* (1996) **84**, 9-17
47	
48	## Introduction
49	
50	Serotiny refers to the retention of seeds in closed fruits within the plant canopy for more than one year, and can be contrasted with two alternative fates of seeds: storage in a soil seed bank, or release of short-lived seeds upon maturity (no seed storage) (Lamont *et al.* 1991a). # Canopy seed bank dynamics and optimum fire regime for the highly serotinous shrub, *Banksia hookeriana*

N.J. ENRIGHT,\*† BYRON B. LAMONT† and RALF MARSULA‡

\*Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, University of Melbourne, Parkville, 3052, Australia, †School of Environmental Biology, Curtin University of Technology, GPO Box U1987 Perth, 6001, Australia and ‡Sektion Ökosystemanalyse, UFZ-Umweltforschungszentrum, Leipzig-Halle GmbH, Permoserstr. 15, PF 2, O-7050 Leipzig, Germany

## Summary

1 *Banksia hookeriana* is a serotinous nonsprouting shrub restricted to the fire-prone northern sandplain scrub-heaths of Western Australia. Evidence of the natural fire frequency to which the species is best adapted was sought through analysis of its seed demography using a computer model of canopy seed bank dynamics based on field data.

2 Plants began flowering at 3-4 years of age but storage of viable seeds in the canopy was rare for plants < 5 years. Infructescences (cones) contained a mean of 12 follicles, holding two seeds of which 62% were estimated to be viable.

3 Cone (and seed) production increased with plant age to 15 years, but then fluctuated widely around a mean of 17 cones per year. By this time the average plant had an estimated canopy seed bank of 700 viable seeds comprising seeds 1–10 years old.

4 Seeds were lost from the canopy seed bank through spontaneous follicle rupture (i.e. in the absence of fire), granivory by insect larvae, and decay. Most follicles remained closed for at least 5 years and up to 50% of follicles were still closed after 10 years. Insect granivores destroyed 18% of seeds in 1-year-old cones, and continued to destroy seeds in older cones at a rate of 2-3% per year.

5 The seed bank model predicted continued seed accumulation in the canopy to at least age 25 years (1400 seeds), but by this time more viable seeds (~ 2200) had been lost to spontaneous opening, granivory and decay than were then stored on the plant.

6 Shannon–Weiner diversity (H′) of seed ages in the canopy seed bank increased with plant age, while evenness (V′) decreased at first (to plant age 17 years) and then increased.

7 On a time-scale of many generations, the likelihood of successful recruitment of individuals in the next generation (on average), occurs for a fire frequency of 15-18 years. At this frequency resource wastage in this low-nutrient environment would be minimized.

8 Recent fires have recurred within 7-11 years and indicate a human impact on the natural fire regime which may ultimately threaten the species.

*Keywords*: *Banksia*, fire frequency, seed bank model, seed demography, serotiny

*Journal of Ecology* (1996) **84**, 9-17

## Introduction

Serotiny refers to the retention of seeds in closed fruits within the plant canopy for more than one year, and can be contrasted with two alternative fates of seeds: storage in a soil seed bank, or release of short-lived seeds upon maturity (no seed storage) (Lamont *et al.* 1991a). Seed release in serotinous species is normally triggered by fire and seeds are short-lived after release, germinating during the first favourable period (Cowling & Lamont 1987). Species can range from weakly serotinous, where most seeds are released within a few years of production, to strongly serotinous, where seeds are held in the canopy for many years. The

ecological significance of serotiny seems clear: where conditions for seedling recruitment are best immediately following fire (i.e. competition for light, moisture and nutrients are probably at their minimum), cued release of canopy-stored seeds after fire maximizes the age, and therefore canopy seed store, of the population by the time of the next fire. Any seedlings that establish later during the interfire period have a low probability of survival due to competition with their parents and other established plants (Cowling & Lamont 1987; Lamont & Barker 1988). They will be much younger and, on average, will have a smaller canopy seed bank when fire recurs and so are less fit (*sensu* Stearns 1992).

The dynamics of seed production, storage and loss in relation to plant age determines the range of fire frequencies for which population maintenance is possible. If fire occurs either before the onset of reproductive maturity, or before a sufficient canopy seed bank has accumulated, then a population is threatened with extinction.

In the absence of fire some seeds are released by the spontaneous opening of old fruits, but the likelihood of plant recruitment and survival to reproductive age is extremely low. Seed release is hastened by the death of stem tissue due to drought stress and plant senescence (Witkowski *et al.* 1991). This means that the canopy seed bank may be completely lost where plant death occurs before the next fire, a fate not shared by most soil seed bank species where seeds may survive for many years after the death of parent plants (Baker 1989). Because dry plant biomass is more readily consumed by fire, any seeds held in the canopy of dead plants at the time of fire are also likely to perish (Lamont & Barker 1988).

*Banksia hookeriana* Meissn. (Proteaceae) is a highly serotinous, fire-killed (nonsprouting) woody shrub to 2.5 m high which is restricted to the northern sandplain scrub-heaths of south-western Australia about 250-330 km north of Perth (George 1981; Taylor & Hopper 1988). While new inflorescences may be damaged and removed from plants by birds, mature cones normally remain attached to the plant throughout its life. Some seeds abort during development, while others are either released gradually or (especially after fire) are consumed by insects, lose viability and decay, or remain viable. Once released seeds germinate with the onset of winter rains or perish as there is no persistent soil seed bank (Enright & Lamont 1989).

The geographical extent (80 × 30 km) of the low nutrient, noncalcareous, sandplain defines the distribution of this species, which is further limited by its specific preference for the deeper sands of low dune crests (Enright & Lamont 1989; Lamont *et al.* 1989). In addition, its attractive orange inflorescences are harvested in large numbers for the commercial wildflower trade, so reducing seed production in exploited populations (Witkowski *et al.* 1994).

This paper describes seed production and availability, and a computer model of seed bank dynamics in *Banksia hookeriana* in relation to plant age (= time since last fire) for sites near Mt Adams. The following questions were posed:

1 What is the pattern of seed production with plant age, and what factors influence the rate of seed accumulation in the crown (e.g. level of serotiny, granivory, seed abortion and longevity)?

2 Does the analysis of seed demography reveal the optimum fire frequency to which the species is adapted, and the range of fire frequencies compatible with population survival?

Mean annual rainfall at the two closest climate stations is 513 mm (Eneabba; 55 km to the south) and 471 mm (Dongara; 25 km to the north), respectively. There is a pronounced winter maximum with almost no rain (median 20 mm) in the five summer months from December to April. Temperature regimes are similar for both climate stations: mean maximum temperature in the hottest month (January) is 35.8 °C, mean minimum temperature in the coolest month (July) is 9.2 °C. Soils vary from acidic, leached sands on low dunes to sandy clays in intervening depressions (Hnatiuk & Hopkins 1981). The vegetation of the low dunes is a diverse scrub-heath usually dominated by two *Banksia* species, *Banksia hookeriana* and *Banksia attenuata* R. Br., although up to six banksias may co-occur (Beard 1984; Enright & Lamont 1989).

## Materials and methods

Seven sample plots, each 400 m² in area and ranging in age since last fire from 1 to 3 and 14-16 years, were established in 1986 and monitored for 6-8 years. They were on the crests and slopes of low, sandy dunes in scrub-heath along the edge of a 2-km section of Mt Adams Road within the Yardanogo Nature Reserve. Sites covering a broader range of *Banksia hookeriana* stand ages could not be located.

The onset and level of flower head (inflorescence) and cone (infructescence) production were recorded within five replicate 25-m² subplots per plot for each year until 1991 (four plots) or 1993 (one plot).

For the two plots where plant age was 14-16 years in 1986, the total number of plants and total number of cones per plant was determined. 13	# Summary
14	
15	0 A comprehensive data set on age\ survival and reproduction for the non!sprouting "\_re!killed# shrub Banksia hookeriana\ encompassing 02years of measurements at 04 sites in south!western Australia\ and including 09 \_res\ was used to parameterize a computer model to investigate optimum plant life!history strategies in a \_re!prone environment[ Parameter ranges encompassed life!history information for other non! sprouting Banksia species from the same region[

21	3 Changes to biological attributes associated with timing of reproduction and lon! gevity shifted the optimum \_re interval and estimated rate of population growth\ but did not alter the conclusions concerning serotiny[ Although shorter seed longevity and increased rates of predation and:or decay reduced the value of serotiny\ even very low levels of canopy seed storage increased species \_tness under intermediate \_re frequencies "09Ð19 years#[
22	
23	4 If the probability of inter!\_re recruitment and survival was increased\ optimum growth shifted from strong serotiny under a regime of frequent \_re "³19 year inter! val#\ to weak "or no# serotiny where the interval between successive \_res was long "×39 year interval#[

34	# Introduction
35	
36	Plants in \_re!prone environments are often char! acterized by biological attributes that increase the probability of survival and:or recruitment following disturbance by \_re[ Among these are the ability of individuals to regrow from protected buds either above! or below!ground "resprouting#\ \_re!stimu! lated ~owering and seed production\ and \_re!trig! gered germination of seeds stored either in the soil or in the plant canopy "Gill 0870#[ Since species that resprout after \_re commonly co!exist in \_re!prone environments "e[g[ mediterranean!type shrublands# with those that are killed by \_re "non!sprouters#\ a frequent question concerns the circumstances under which one or other strategy is favoured "e[g[ Keeley + Zedler 0867^ Keeley 0875^ Hilbert 0876#[ Beyond this simple dichotomous division into resprouters and non!sprouters\ \_re!prone communities may con! tain an array of "sometimes congeneric# species showing consistent variation in the amount of resprouting after \_re\ the extent to which seeds are stored in the soil or on the plant\ and in other biological attributes "e[g[ longevity\ age to repro! duction\ level of seed production#[
37	
38	It is important to determine the biological attri! butes that in~uence demographic behaviour and to establish which attributes confer the greatest \_tness advantage on a species in relation to particular \_re regimes[ As well as revealing information on the selective pressures acting on species in \_re!prone environments\ the answers aid conservation and management of species in relation to human! imposed \_re regimes[
39	
40	This paper presents a computer model of popu! lation dynamics for a non!sprouting woody per! ennial in a \_re!prone environment\ and the results of simulations which sought to reveal the optimum level of on!plant seed storage "serotiny# in relation to \_re interval[ Serotiny refers to the retention of seeds in closed fruits or cones within the crown for more than 0 year and is common in species from a number of important families in \_re!prone areas of Australia "Proteaceae\ Myrtaceae\ Cupressaceae\ Casuarinaceae#\ South Africa "Proteaceae\ Bru! niaceae# and North America "Pinaceae# "Lamont et al[ 0880a#[ It can be contrasted with two alter! native fates of seeds] storage in a soil seed bank\ or release of short!lived seeds once mature "no seed storage#[ Seed release in serotinous species is nor! mally triggered by \_re and seeds are short!lived after release\ germinating during the \_rst favourable period "Cowling + Lamont 0876#[ Species can range from weakly serotinous\ where most seeds are released spontaneously "in the absence of \_re# within a few years of production\ to strongly serotinous\ where most seeds are held in the canopy for many years "e[g[ <sup>×</sup>09 years in some species of Pinus and Banksia#[
41	
42	The ecological and evolutionary signi\_cance of serotiny seems clear] where \_re is the most common cause of ecosystem disturbance\ cued release of canopy!stored seeds by \_re "and their germination in the \_rst growing season after \_re# maximizes plant age and therefore seed available for the next generation by the time of the next \_re[ Seeds released\ and seedlings established\ later during the inter!\_re period have a lower probability of survival due to competition with their parents and other established plants "Cowling + Lamont 0876#[ They will be younger and will thus have a smaller canopy seed bank when \_re recurs\ and so are less \_t "sensu Stearns 0881#[ It would therefore appear that very strong serotiny should represent the optimum strat! egy for perennial plants in \_re!prone environments[ However\ a range of degrees of serotiny may be encountered within the same plant community "e[g[ Cowling et al[ 0876^ Enright + Lamont 0878a\b# or even within the same species[ In the latter case\ variations have been found in relation to environ! mental gradients\ e[g[ lower serotiny in less \_re! prone parts of the species| geographical range for Banksia attenuata in Australia "Cowling + Lamont 0874#\ and in relation to time since last \_re\ e[g[ inter!\_re recruits show lower serotiny than immediate post!\_re recruits of Pinus banksiana in boreal forests of southern Quebec "Gautier et al[ 0885#[ Lamont et al[ "0880a# note that some \_re regimes and growth forms apparently foster incom! plete serotiny\ but that {degree of serotiny has received little formal treatment\ and the empirical subtleties of such relationships remain largely unex! plored|[
43	
44	The model described here is based on \_eld data collected over 02 years from 04 sites and including 09 di}erent \_res "up to two at the same site# for B[ hookeriana Meissn[ "Proteaceae#\ a non!sprouting woody shrub of mediterranean!type shrublands in south!western Australia "Enright + Lamont 0878a\ 0881a\b^ Enright et al[ 0885#[ Nevertheless\ the model is likely to have a more general application since parameter values can readily be changed to match the known life!history attributes of other serotinous\ non!sprouting perennial plants[ By basing the model and its parameter values on those measured over an extended period of time "and at a number of sites# for a real plant species the model described here avoids many of the criticisms levelled at population models[ For example\ Cousens "0884# argues that the results of simulation studies for hypothetical species are often determined largely by the structure of the models themselves and provide little insight into real population dynamic behaviour and\ further\ that many models based on real data are ~awed since the data are derived from glasshouse experiments or from density studies that exclude stochastic year!to! year variations in factors unrelated to density "e[g[ weather#[

49	FIELD DATA COLLECTION
50	
51	Banksia hookeriana is a highly serotinous\ \_re!killed "non!sprouting# woody shrub that grows up to 1[4 m in height\ which is restricted to the northern sandplain heaths of south!western Australia "centred on 18>29?S\ 004>04?E# about 149Ð229 km north of Perth "George 0870^ Taylor + Hopper 0877#[ Seed pro! duction and plant survivorship were estimated for sample populations of di}erent ages "i[e[ time since last \_re#[ Sites covering the whole range of possible plant ages could not be located\ and \_res during the course of remeasurements returned some sites to zero age[ Fifteen sample plots\ each 399 m1 in area\ and ranging in age from 0 to 05 years at the start of the study\ were established and censused annually in June "i[e[ at the end of the summerÐautumn period of peak plant mortality# from 0875 to 0885[
52	
53	The onset and level of ~owering "in~orescence# and cone "infructescence# production were recorded for all individuals within \_ve replicate 14 m1 subplots per plot for stands <sup>³</sup>7 years old\ and annual cone pro! duction followed for a random sample of 09 indi! viduals for older stands[ Fertile cones typically carry 4Ð04 woody follicles arranged around a central rachis\ each follicle holding two seeds[ Cones arise terminally at the beginning of each growing season\ and node scars and branching pattern clearly mark the bound! ary between successive years of vegetative growth[ Thus plant age and individual cone age can be deter! mined with only a small likelihood of error[ Complete cone crops were harvested from 19 randomly chosen 05!year!old plants in 0875\ and cones were aged so that the entire history of reproduction could be deter! mined for each plant[ The numbers of \_rm\ aborted\ eaten and decayed seeds in closed follicles were deter! mined by cone age\ and viability of \_rm seeds was assessed by germination testing "full details are pro! vided in Enright et al[ 0885#[ Degree of serotiny was based on the proportion of follicles per cone age class that remained closed in the absence of \_re "following Lamont et al[ 0880a#[

63	Seed production typically commences when plants are 4 years old and ~uctuates widely around a mean of about 199 viable seeds per year from 04 years onwards "Enright et al[ 0885#[ While new in~orescences may be damaged and removed from plants by birds\ mature cones normally remain attached to the plant through! out their life[ Few seeds are released except when \_re causes the follicles on cones to open[ Once released\ seeds either germinate with the onset of winter rains or perish "Enright + Lamont 0878a#[ Enright et al[ "0885# describe in detail the mean rate of accumu! lation of viable seeds in the canopy in relation to plant age[ On average\ 06) of embryos abort^ seed losses due to spontaneous release in the absence of \_re aver! age 3) per annum^ while predation and decay of seeds stored in closed follicles increases by 3) per annum from the \_rst year[

72	Seed release is hastened by the death of stem tissues due to drought stress and plant senescence\ but is incomplete relative to seed release after \_re "Wit! kowski et al[ 0880#[ The canopy seed bank may be completely lost where plant death occurs before the next \_re\ both because even if seeds are released they will have a low probability of establishment\ and because dead plants are usually completely incin! erated by \_re so that any seeds still held in the crown will perish "Lamont + Barker 0877#[ The woody stems and cones on living shrubs burn less intensely due to a higher moisture content\ and although the stems are killed they remain standing and the cones are opened but not consumed[ If \_re occurs either before the onset of reproductive maturity\ or before a su.cient canopy seed bank has accumulated\ a population is threatened with local extinction[

78	Summer weather conditions are important in deter! mining levels of seedling survival in the \_rst year fol! lowing \_re[ Survivorship of seedlings is highest in wet summers and lowest in dry summers "Enright + Lamont 0881a#[ There was no relationship between rainfall in the previous summer and subsequent in~orescence production for plants <sup>×</sup>04 years old[ However\ there was a signi\_cant positive relationship between total rainfall in one year and in~orescence production in the next "log09 cones 4[34 × log09 annual rainfall Ð 02[79^ d[f[ 05\ F 09[49\ P <sup>³</sup> 9[94\ r 1 9[25#[ This non!linear relationship sug! gests reduced in~orescence production following years of lower than average rainfall\ but little increase above average levels of production following wet years[

84	### THE MODEL
85	
86	The computer model\ written in C¦¦\ describes the population dynamics of a serotinous\ non!sprouting woody perennial that is subject to disturbance by \_re[ We chose an age!based approach to characterize the population] the model traces the number of x!year! old plants\ N"x#\ and the number of seeds stored on an x!year!old plant\ S"x#\ for each age x[ Changes in N"x# and S"x# are caused by plant death\ seed production\ seed loss\ seed release\ germination and establishment of seedlings[ These processes are described by the functional relationships detailed below\ and illustrated conceptually in Fig[ 0[ The model begins with a post!\_re population of 099 viable seeds and calculates their survivorship and repro! duction in relation to age until \_re causes plant death and seed release[ Fire kills all individuals\ and recruit! ment following \_re is solely from seeds[

# The ecological signi\_cance of canopy seed storage in \_re!prone environments] a model for non!sprouting shrubs

NEAL J[ ENRIGHT\$\ RALF MARSULA%\ BYRON B[ LAMONT\$ and CHRISTIAN WISSEL%

Department of Geography and Environmental Studies\ University of Melbourne\ Parkville 2941\ Australia^ \$School of Environmental Biology\ Curtin University of Technology\ GPO Box U0876 Perth 5990\ Australia^ and %Department of Ecological Modelling\ UFZ Centre for Environmental Research\ Leipzig!Halle\ Permoserstr[ 04\ PF 1\ D!93290 Leipzig\ Germany

# Summary

0 A comprehensive data set on age\ survival and reproduction for the non!sprouting "\_re!killed# shrub Banksia hookeriana\ encompassing 02years of measurements at 04 sites in south!western Australia\ and including 09 \_res\ was used to parameterize a computer model to investigate optimum plant life!history strategies in a \_re!prone environment[ Parameter ranges encompassed life!history information for other non! sprouting Banksia species from the same region[

1 The relationship between \_re interval and level of canopy seed storage "serotiny# was analysed to identify the circumstances under which serotiny is favoured\ and what degree of serotiny maximizes potential population growth rate[ In addition to deterministic versions of the model\ stochasticity in \_re interval and conditions for recruitment were analysed[

2 The deterministic model indicated a maximum \_nite rate of natural increase "l0[04# when the \_re interval was 05 years and all seeds were retained on the plant until \_re occurred[ Although the model failed to predict the intermediate degrees of serotiny present in nature\ it supported the optimum \_re interval predicted from canopy seed bank dynamics[

3 Changes to biological attributes associated with timing of reproduction and lon! gevity shifted the optimum \_re interval and estimated rate of population growth\ but did not alter the conclusions concerning serotiny[ Although shorter seed longevity and increased rates of predation and:or decay reduced the value of serotiny\ even very low levels of canopy seed storage increased species \_tness under intermediate \_re frequencies "09Ð19 years#[

4 If the probability of inter!\_re recruitment and survival was increased\ optimum growth shifted from strong serotiny under a regime of frequent \_re "³19 year inter! val#\ to weak "or no# serotiny where the interval between successive \_res was long "×39 year interval#[

5 Stochasticity around mean \_re interval resulted in intermediate to strong "but not complete# serotiny being predicted as optimal once the CV for \_re interval approached 099)[ This result is interpreted as a bet!hedging strategy whereby spontaneous release of some seeds during the inter!\_re period permits recruitment on rare occasions where \_re interval approaches or exceeds the species longevity[

Keywords] Banksia\ computer models\ \_re regime\ optimum life!history strategies\ serotiny\ stochastic e}ects\ woody plants

Journal of Ecolo`y "0887# 75\ 835Ð848

{1}

######## PDF PAGE 3 ########
# Introduction

Plants in \_re!prone environments are often char! acterized by biological attributes that increase the probability of survival and:or recruitment following disturbance by \_re[ Among these are the ability of individuals to regrow from protected buds either above! or below!ground "resprouting#\ \_re!stimu! lated ~owering and seed production\ and \_re!trig! gered germination of seeds stored either in the soil or in the plant canopy "Gill 0870#[ Since species that resprout after \_re commonly co!exist in \_re!prone environments "e[g[ mediterranean!type shrublands# with those that are killed by \_re "non!sprouters#\ a frequent question concerns the circumstances under which one or other strategy is favoured "e[g[ Keeley + Zedler 0867^ Keeley 0875^ Hilbert 0876#[ Beyond this simple dichotomous division into resprouters and non!sprouters\ \_re!prone communities may con! tain an array of "sometimes congeneric# species showing consistent variation in the amount of resprouting after \_re\ the extent to which seeds are stored in the soil or on the plant\ and in other biological attributes "e[g[ longevity\ age to repro! duction\ level of seed production#[

It is important to determine the biological attri! butes that in~uence demographic behaviour and to establish which attributes confer the greatest \_tness advantage on a species in relation to particular \_re regimes[ As well as revealing information on the selective pressures acting on species in \_re!prone environments\ the answers aid conservation and management of species in relation to human! imposed \_re regimes[

This paper presents a computer model of popu! lation dynamics for a non!sprouting woody per! ennial in a \_re!prone environment\ and the results of simulations which sought to reveal the optimum level of on!plant seed storage "serotiny# in relation to \_re interval[ Serotiny refers to the retention of seeds in closed fruits or cones within the crown for more than 0 year and is common in species from a number of important families in \_re!prone areas of Australia "Proteaceae\ Myrtaceae\ Cupressaceae\ Casuarinaceae#\ South Africa "Proteaceae\ Bru! niaceae# and North America "Pinaceae# "Lamont et al[ 0880a#[ It can be contrasted with two alter! native fates of seeds] storage in a soil seed bank\ or release of short!lived seeds once mature "no seed storage#[ Seed release in serotinous species is nor! mally triggered by \_re and seeds are short!lived after release\ germinating during the \_rst favourable period "Cowling + Lamont 0876#[ Species can range from weakly serotinous\ where most seeds are released spontaneously "in the absence of \_re# within a few years of production\ to strongly serotinous\ where most seeds are held in the canopy for many years "e[g[ <sup>×</sup>09 years in some species of Pinus and Banksia#[

The ecological and evolutionary signi\_cance of serotiny seems clear] where \_re is the most common cause of ecosystem disturbance\ cued release of canopy!stored seeds by \_re "and their germination in the \_rst growing season after \_re# maximizes plant age and therefore seed available for the next generation by the time of the next \_re[ Seeds released\ and seedlings established\ later during the inter!\_re period have a lower probability of survival due to competition with their parents and other established plants "Cowling + Lamont 0876#[ They will be younger and will thus have a smaller canopy seed bank when \_re recurs\ and so are less \_t "sensu Stearns 0881#[ It would therefore appear that very strong serotiny should represent the optimum strat! egy for perennial plants in \_re!prone environments[ However\ a range of degrees of serotiny may be encountered within the same plant community "e[g[ Cowling et al[ 0876^ Enright + Lamont 0878a\b# or even within the same species[ In the latter case\ variations have been found in relation to environ! mental gradients\ e[g[ lower serotiny in less \_re! prone parts of the species| geographical range for Banksia attenuata in Australia "Cowling + Lamont 0874#\ and in relation to time since last \_re\ e[g[ inter!\_re recruits show lower serotiny than immediate post!\_re recruits of Pinus banksiana in boreal forests of southern Quebec "Gautier et al[ 0885#[ Lamont et al[ "0880a# note that some \_re regimes and growth forms apparently foster incom! plete serotiny\ but that {degree of serotiny has received little formal treatment\ and the empirical subtleties of such relationships remain largely unex! plored|[

The model described here is based on \_eld data collected over 02 years from 04 sites and including 09 di}erent \_res "up to two at the same site# for B[ hookeriana Meissn[ "Proteaceae#\ a non!sprouting woody shrub of mediterranean!type shrublands in south!western Australia "Enright + Lamont 0878a\ 0881a\b^ Enright et al[ 0885#[ Nevertheless\ the model is likely to have a more general application since parameter values can readily be changed to match the known life!history attributes of other serotinous\ non!sprouting perennial plants[ By basing the model and its parameter values on those measured over an extended period of time "and at a number of sites# for a real plant species the model described here avoids many of the criticisms levelled at population models[ For example\ Cousens "0884# argues that the results of simulation studies for hypothetical species are often determined largely by the structure of the models themselves and provide little insight into real population dynamic behaviour and\ further\ that many models based on real data are ~awed since the data are derived from glasshouse experiments or from density studies that exclude stochastic year!to! year variations in factors unrelated to density "e[g[ weather#[

{2}

######## PDF PAGE 4 ########
FIELD DATA COLLECTION

Banksia hookeriana is a highly serotinous\ \_re!killed "non!sprouting# woody shrub that grows up to 1[4 m in height\ which is restricted to the northern sandplain heaths of south!western Australia "centred on 18>29?S\ 004>04?E# about 149Ð229 km north of Perth "George 0870^ Taylor + Hopper 0877#[ Seed pro! duction and plant survivorship were estimated for sample populations of di}erent ages "i[e[ time since last \_re#[ Sites covering the whole range of possible plant ages could not be located\ and \_res during the course of remeasurements returned some sites to zero age[ Fifteen sample plots\ each 399 m1 in area\ and ranging in age from 0 to 05 years at the start of the study\ were established and censused annually in June "i[e[ at the end of the summerÐautumn period of peak plant mortality# from 0875 to 0885[

The onset and level of ~owering "in~orescence# and cone "infructescence# production were recorded for all individuals within \_ve replicate 14 m1 subplots per plot for stands <sup>³</sup>7 years old\ and annual cone pro! duction followed for a random sample of 09 indi! viduals for older stands[ Fertile cones typically carry 4Ð04 woody follicles arranged around a central rachis\ each follicle holding two seeds[ Cones arise terminally at the beginning of each growing season\ and node scars and branching pattern clearly mark the bound! ary between successive years of vegetative growth[ Thus plant age and individual cone age can be deter! mined with only a small likelihood of error[ Complete cone crops were harvested from 19 randomly chosen 05!year!old plants in 0875\ and cones were aged so that the entire history of reproduction could be deter! mined for each plant[ The numbers of \_rm\ aborted\ eaten and decayed seeds in closed follicles were deter! mined by cone age\ and viability of \_rm seeds was assessed by germination testing "full details are pro! vided in Enright et al[ 0885#[ Degree of serotiny was based on the proportion of follicles per cone age class that remained closed in the absence of \_re "following Lamont et al[ 0880a#[

The total number of cones per plant was quanti\_ed for all plants in plots a}ected by wild \_res during the course of the \_eld study[ The number of follicles opened by \_re was enumerated for a random sample of 09 cones on each of 09 plant skeletons per plot\ and the number of viable seeds released per plant estimated using data for seeds from harvested cones[

Plant survivorship was recorded annually for 09 randomly chosen individuals within each subplot where plant age was <sup>³</sup>7 years\ and in the whole plot for older stands[ The number of seeds released fol! lowing \_re\ the number of seedlings established in the \_rst winter\ and number of survivors at each age was used to produce survivorship trajectories[ These tra!

Data for three other non!sprouting Banksia species "B[ prionotes Lindley\ B[ leptophylla A[S[ George and B[ lanata A[S[ George# provided information on ranges for parameter values for modelling purposes[ Up to six Banksia species "a mixture of resprouters and non!sprouters# co!occurred in some of the \_eld sites[ The biological attributes of these species are described in Cowling et al[ "0876#\ Enright + Lamont "0878a# and Enright + Lamont "0881a#[

#### SPECIES ATTRIBUTES

Seed production typically commences when plants are 4 years old and ~uctuates widely around a mean of about 199 viable seeds per year from 04 years onwards "Enright et al[ 0885#[ While new in~orescences may be damaged and removed from plants by birds\ mature cones normally remain attached to the plant through! out their life[ Few seeds are released except when \_re causes the follicles on cones to open[ Once released\ seeds either germinate with the onset of winter rains or perish "Enright + Lamont 0878a#[ Enright et al[ "0885# describe in detail the mean rate of accumu! lation of viable seeds in the canopy in relation to plant age[ On average\ 06) of embryos abort^ seed losses due to spontaneous release in the absence of \_re aver! age 3) per annum^ while predation and decay of seeds stored in closed follicles increases by 3) per annum from the \_rst year[

From 2) to 16) of seeds released following \_res in the period 0874Ð82 produced seedlings in the \_rst winter "Enright + Lamont 0878a^ N[ J[ Enright\ unpublished data#[ Plant survivorship is lowest in the \_rst year and quickly increases such that there is little mortality "³0) year−0# in plants older than 7 years[ While no plants older than 14 years have been observed in the \_eld\ the continuing survival of most individuals in our oldest study site "N[ J[ Enright\ unpublished data# indicates that longevity may be 29Ð 39 years in the absence of \_re[ Large\ old plants may succumb to drought over summer\ and are prone to collapse due to the heavy load of seed!bearing cones on old branches\ and this suggests an increased mor! tality rate for old plants[

In the absence of \_re\ some seeds are released by the spontaneous opening of old fruits\ but the prob! ability of germination and survival of recruits to reproductive age is extremely low[ Seedlings are occasionally encountered in stands <sup>×</sup>04 years old\ but so far no such recruits have been recorded to survive to reproductive age[ Nevertheless\ it is reason! able to assume that occasionally these inter!\_re recruits might grow to maturity and contribute to future generations[ The low chance of establishment\ combined with low rates of seed release when the degree of serotiny is high\ means that very few recruits are likely via this pathway[

{3}

######## PDF PAGE 5 ########
Seed release is hastened by the death of stem tissues due to drought stress and plant senescence\ but is incomplete relative to seed release after \_re "Wit! kowski et al[ 0880#[ The canopy seed bank may be completely lost where plant death occurs before the next \_re\ both because even if seeds are released they will have a low probability of establishment\ and because dead plants are usually completely incin! erated by \_re so that any seeds still held in the crown will perish "Lamont + Barker 0877#[ The woody stems and cones on living shrubs burn less intensely due to a higher moisture content\ and although the stems are killed they remain standing and the cones are opened but not consumed[ If \_re occurs either before the onset of reproductive maturity\ or before a su.cient canopy seed bank has accumulated\ a population is threatened with local extinction[

### WEATHER AND FIRE

Mediterranean!type climate regions are characterized by cool\ moist winters and hot\ dry summers[ In the northern sandplain heaths of south!western Australia\ winter rains are highly predictable and will almost always provide su.cient moisture to allow seedling establishment after \_re[ However\ the extent of summer drought is more variable[ One!hundred and ten years of rainfall records for nearby Dongara "Western Australian Bureau of Meteorology climate station 7933^ 18>04?S\ 003>45?E\ mean annual rainfall of 360 mm for the period 0773Ð0882# show that about 79) of summers have the typical mediterranean!type pattern of low to very low rainfall[ In the other 19) of years\ tropical storms punctuate the summer with heavy rainfall events and drought stress on plants is greatly reduced "Enright + Lamont 0881a#[

Summer weather conditions are important in deter! mining levels of seedling survival in the \_rst year fol! lowing \_re[ Survivorship of seedlings is highest in wet summers and lowest in dry summers "Enright + Lamont 0881a#[ There was no relationship between rainfall in the previous summer and subsequent in~orescence production for plants <sup>×</sup>04 years old[ However\ there was a signi\_cant positive relationship between total rainfall in one year and in~orescence production in the next "log09 cones 4[34 × log09 annual rainfall Ð 02[79^ d[f[ 05\ F 09[49\ P <sup>³</sup> 9[94\ r 1 9[25#[ This non!linear relationship sug! gests reduced in~orescence production following years of lower than average rainfall\ but little increase above average levels of production following wet years[

Risk of \_re is high every summer and there is no obvious relationship between rainfall and \_re] of nine wild \_res recorded in the vicinity of the \_eld area since 0856\ four occurred in wetter than average years\ and four in years with very dry summers "one of which followed a wet winter#[ However\ the timing of \_re in relation to rainfall in the \_rst few years after \_re "especially unusually wet or dry summers# is impor! tant since seedling mortality is highest during this period "Enright + Lamont 0878a\ 0881a#[ Stands burned within the last 4 years are unlikely to have accumulated su.cient biomass to carry a \_re[ The shortest recorded \_re interval in relation to the nine \_res noted above was 6 years[

# Methods

### THE MODEL

The computer model\ written in C¦¦\ describes the population dynamics of a serotinous\ non!sprouting woody perennial that is subject to disturbance by \_re[ We chose an age!based approach to characterize the population] the model traces the number of x!year! old plants\ N"x#\ and the number of seeds stored on an x!year!old plant\ S"x#\ for each age x[ Changes in N"x# and S"x# are caused by plant death\ seed production\ seed loss\ seed release\ germination and establishment of seedlings[ These processes are described by the functional relationships detailed below\ and illustrated conceptually in Fig[ 0[ The model begins with a post!\_re population of 099 viable seeds and calculates their survivorship and repro! duction in relation to age until \_re causes plant death and seed release[ Fire kills all individuals\ and recruit! ment following \_re is solely from seeds[

Germination\ establishment and survivorship of plants depend on the growing conditions "especially summer rainfall#\ and the model uses the \_ts derived from \_eld data on survivorship\ and illustrated in Fig[ 1\ to describe these rates[ The probability of ger! mination of seeds and establishment of seedlings in the \_rst year is the inverse of the observed number of seeds required for self!replacement of a 0!year!old plant[ In the same way\ the probability p"x# that a plant survives until it is x years old is the inverse of the number of seeds required for self!replacement of a plant at age x[ Thus\ the probability p"x\ x ¦ 0# to survive from year x to year x ¦ 0 can be calculated

At each time step the plants get 0 year older[ The model calculates the age class distribution of the indi! viduals as well as their seed production in that year and accumulated seed storage in the plant canopy[ Plants have an increased risk of mortality once an age of 14 years is exceeded[ This mortality rate increases from 9 to 9[0 by steps of 9[90 per year such that <sup>³</sup>19) of plants alive at age 14 years are still alive at age 39 years[ Maximum plant longevity is described by the parameter A3 "Table 0#[

Juvenile plants commence seed production at plant age A1 years[ Seed production increases linearly up to age A2\ after which it remains constant at Fm seeds per year[ Most seeds are stored in the plant canopy\ but the seeds in a proportion\ Lv\ of follicles are lost each year due to predation and rotting\ while a further proportion\ r\ open each year in the absence of \_re and release their seeds "inter!\_re release#[ 0:r "the inverse of r# describes the degree of serotiny[ Thus\ a value of 0 for serotiny means that all seeds are released by the end of the year in which they were produced "i[e[ the plant is not serotinous#\ while a value of 0999 means that\ on average\ only 9[0) of the seed crop is released per year and nearly all of the seed crop "regardless of seed age# is held on the plant until \_re triggers seed release[ This de\_nition of serotiny follows that proposed by Lamont "0880#[ The degree of serotiny can theoretically range from 0 "9) ser! otiny# to in\_nity "099) serotiny# but most recorded values "e[g[ for Banksia species# fall between 09 and 099 "Table 1#[

Seeds have a longevity of Vm years on the plant[ Seeds released during the inter!\_re period have a lower probability of germination and establishment than seeds released in response to \_re "post!\_re release#[ The model takes this into account] the prob! ability of germination and establishment for seeds released in any inter!\_re year is only Postint of that of the post!\_re released seeds[ For a given released seed\ we estimate the probability of inter!\_re recruit! ment "expressed as a proportion# to be c[ 9[94 that of post!\_re recruitment[ When a plant dies during the inter!\_re period all seeds stored on that plant are lost[ When a \_re occurs all remaining plants are killed\ and all of their stored seeds are released[

The mean \_tness of the population "sensu Stearns 0881# in relation to any set of life!history parameters and environmental factors is estimated using the \_nite rate of natural increase "l#[ This is calculated as]
