{1}

######## PDF PAGE 3 ########
in fire-prone landscapes (Harrison et al. [2021;] Schwilk and Ackerly [2001]). However, with ongoing climate change, fire is projected to occur with greater frequency and intensity in many regions (Jones et al. [2022]), thereby imposing altered fire regimes on biota which may threaten their persistence (Bowman et al. [2014;] Enright et al. [2015]; Le Breton et al. [2022]). Fire intervals, in particular, are considered to have a strong influence on species persistence, especially in ecosystems characterised by high severity or stand-replacing fire regimes (Bowman et al. [2014;] Enright et al. [2015;] Gallagher et al. [2021\)]. Land management agencies tasked with conserving fire-prone ecosystems often include minimum fire-free intervals in their planning to maximise species persistence (Bradstock and Kenny [2003;] Burrows and McCaw [2013]).

Plant species which inhabit fire-prone environments are generally characterised as one of two major fire response types: (1) fire-killed (or obligate seeders), which are killed by complete canopy scorch and rely on soil or canopy-stored seeds for post-fire recovery; and (2) resprouters, which primarily survive fire and regrow from buds protected from the heat of fire, but can often also recruit new individuals from seed (Clarke et al. [2015;] Pausas and Keeley [2014]). Plants of both types face two key threats in relation to fire interval: immaturity risk and senescence risk. Immaturity risk occurs when intervals between lethal fires are shorter than the time required to reach reproductive maturity, establish a seed bank and/or develop resprouting capacity (Keeley, Ne'eman, and Fotheringham [1999\)], whereas senescence risk occurs when fire intervals exceed the lifespan of mature plants and their seed bank or stock of live buds (Enright et al. [2011]; Gosper, Prober, and Yates [2013\)]. Tolerable fire intervals, defined by minimum and maximum inter-fire periods that avoid species loss through immaturity and senescence risk respectively, are widely used in planning fire management with conservation objectives (Gosper et al. [2022\)]. Immaturity risk and shortened fire intervals arguably pose the greatest risk to species persistence, with fire-killed species particularly vulnerable to decline or local extinction if they are slow maturing and require an ample fire-free period to flower and produce seeds (Bowman et al. [2014;] Enright et al. [2014\)]. Resprouters, while generally considered to be more resilient to short fire intervals, may be vulnerable to unusually short intervals due to the depletion of resources required for resprouting and reduced recruitment probability from seed (Enright et al. [2014], [2011;] Fairman, Nitschke, and Bennett [2016\)].

Defining potential immaturity or senescence risks in a population or species is often achieved using demographic or reproductive information such as the timing of post-fire reproductive maturity, long-term trajectories of reproductive output and adult lifespans (Enright, Lamont, and Marsula [1996;] Gosper, Prober, and Yates [2013]; Kraaij et al. [2013]). The juvenile period approach for quantifying post-fire reproductive maturity and estimating minimum tolerable fire intervals originates from a concept by Gill and Nicholls ([1989\)] and has been applied to a variety of woody plant species in Australia and South Africa (Gill and McMahon [1986]; Gosper et al. [2022;] Harvey et al. [2017;] Kraaij et al. [2013;] McCaw [2008;] Muir, Vesk, and Hepworth [2014]). The juvenile period can be defined in a number of ways, including the time to first flowering or fruiting after fire in the most

precocious individual, or the time to flowering or fruiting in a certain portion of the population, often 50% (Gosper et al. [2022;] Kraaij et al. [2013\)]. While the first signs of reproduction may indicate the minimum time to maturity, several years of flowering and subsequent successful seed set may be required to accumulate a seed bank large enough for population replacement after fire, particularly for fire-killed species (Burrows, Wardell-Johnson, and Ward [2008;] Burrows and Wardell-Johnson [2003\)]. A suggested rule of thumb, therefore, is that a fire interval equal to two times (or three times for particularly sensitive species) the juvenile period is the minimum period required for population persistence under average growing conditions (e.g., average post-fire rainfall) (Burrows and Wardell-Johnson [2003;] Gill and Nicholls [1989]). A rule of thumb applied in South African shrublands is that at least half a population must have flowered at least three times (Kraaij et al. [2013\)]. The juvenile period approach is specifically designed for fire-killed species where there is no persistence via resprouting, all individuals are normally killed by fire (i.e., fire is not patchy), there is little or no inter-fire seedling recruitment and seed banks are exhausted by fire (i.e., no residual seed bank) (Bell [2001\)]. While this approach is supported by a few single- or multi-species studies on post-fire maturation rates (Burrows and Wardell-Johnson [2003]; Treurnicht et al. [2016\)], it was only originally intended to provide guidance until more detailed assessments were available (Gill and Nicholls [1989]), and there has been little critical evaluation of whether the 2×rule of thumb is appropriate across a wide range of species.

Maximum tolerable fire intervals are not commonly defined, but can be identified from adult longevity (e.g., evidence of senescence) or a decline in reproductive output in the long absence of fire, where there is little or no inter-fire seedling recruitment to maintain populations in the absence of fire (Bond [1980]; Gosper, Prober, and Yates [2013]). Maximum tolerable intervals for resprouters probably even precede adult senescence as the stock of live buds required for resprouting declines with plant age such that plants approaching the end of their lifespan have decreasing probability of survival through fire (Enright et al. [2011\)].

Variation in post-fire juvenile periods at least partly depends on the mode of plant regeneration (Burrows, Wardell-Johnson, and Ward [2008;] Harvey et al. [2017]). The juvenile period for plants regenerating from seed after fire (termed the primary juvenile period) tends to be longer than that for plants resprouting or recovering vegetatively after fire (termed the secondary juvenile period) (Bradstock and Kenny [2003]; Zammit and Westoby [1987\)]. Given that fire-killed species typically recover entirely from seed, only the primary juvenile period is relevant, whereas postfire populations of resprouting species may contain a mix of resprouting individuals and post-fire seedlings so that both primary and secondary juvenile periods can be defined. In practice, reported juvenile periods for resprouting species are generally a composite value of both primary and secondary juvenile periods, but since new recruits are often infrequent, such estimates are best regarded as estimates of the secondary juvenile period (Enright and Goldblum [1999]). Estimates of the primary juvenile period for resprouter species are rare due to sample size constraints associated with low rates of recruitment, and the usually much longer times to first reproduction (Keeley, Fotheringham, and Baer-Keeley [2006;] Zammit and Westoby [1987]). While the juvenile period approach largely focusses on fire-killed species, as 

{2}

######## PDF PAGE 4 ########
these are considered to be most sensitive to fire interval impacts (Bowman et al. [2014]; Enright et al. [2014]; Harvey et al. [2017\)], successful reproduction and seedling recruitment are also required for the long-term persistence of resprouting species (Enright et al. [2014\)].

Despite global applicability of the juvenile period approach for assessing immaturity risk and estimating minimum tolerable fire intervals, including widespread use in some regions, including southern Australia and South Africa, there has been limited evaluation of the relationship between the onset of flowering and seed bank accumulation for different species, or of the consequences of variation in environmental conditions or population size structure for sensitivities to shortened fire intervals (Gosper et al. [2022;] McCaw [2008;] Treurnicht et al. [2016]; von Takach Dukai, Lindenmayer, and Banks [2018]; Wooller, Wooller, and Brown [2002\)]. Variation in climate, herbivory and other environmental factors which affect plant growth and population structure can alter reproductive trajectories such that a single species-level juvenile period value may over- or under-estimate the fire-free period required for different populations (Gosper et al. [2022;] Kraaij et al. [2013;] McCaw [2008]; Morgan, McCarthy, and Willocks [2021]). Longer juvenile periods are often associated with low-productivity environments, including sites with low average rainfall, or low rainfall in the few years following fire (Burrows, Wardell-Johnson, and Ward [2008;] McCaw [2008\)]. Low environmental productivity can act to delay maturation, reduce growth, flowering and seed set, and increase the seedbank required for replacement after subsequent fires (Enright et al. [2015\)]. High herbivore pressure may also delay or reduce flowering and seed production by reducing the size of plants and altering the resources available for reproduction, although these effects are less well documented (Brown, Paczkowska, and Gibson [2016\)]. While variation in reproductive attributes across sites or years will always be a confounding factor in defining tolerable fire intervals, understanding the causal relationships behind variation in reproductive trajectories is particularly important for the management of contemporary landscapes with warming and drying climates alongside ongoing fragmentation and other human disturbances.

In this study, we used field data to model post-fire reproductive trajectories across varying environmental conditions for six woody plant species in fire-prone Banksia woodlands of southwestern Australia. Increasing understanding of fire intervalrelated population dynamics offers the opportunity to manage fire regimes for species conservation. We employed a space-fortime sampling approach to quantify reproduction (flowering rate, flower counts, and cone counts per plant) in co-occurring fire-killed and resprouting species along a post-fire chronosequence of 1–35 years since the last fire and across sites with varying rainfall and herbivory. Vegetation in this region regularly experiences fire, and native species exhibit a variety of firerelated traits and adaptation syndromes which we anticipate would be reflected in varying post-fire reproductive trajectories. Objectives for risk reduction through prescribed burning (managed fire intervals) indicate fire intervals of 13–33 years (Ritchie et al. [2021]). Recent data show post-fire ages ranging from 1 to 56 years since the last fire, with some areas potentially older (Tangney et al. [2022\)]. During the period 1970–2009, median fire intervals (prescribed burns and wildfires combined) across the northern (drier) part of our study area was 9 years with an average of 37% of area burnt attributed to wildfires (Wilson et al. [2014]).

We aim to quantify post-fire juvenile periods (defined here as time to 50% flowering), estimate minimum tolerable fire intervals based on the '2 × juvenile period' rule of thumb guideline, explore whether this rule of thumb reflects sufficient flowering and canopy seed bank accumulation and quantify reproduction in the long absence of fire. We also aim to quantify reproductive patterns under varying rainfall and herbivory conditions and how this affects minimum tolerable fire interval estimates. Populations of fire-killed and resprouting species may also be multi-cohort (Hobbs and Atkins [1990\)] which can complicate reproductive dynamics; therefore, we also aim to evaluate models of reproduction relative to plant size (as a surrogate for age or cohort) to investigate the causal relationship between size and reproduction and test the strength of time since fire as a predictor of reproduction commonly used to inform fire management.

#### **2   |   Methods**

## **2.1   |   Study Area**

This study was conducted in urban and peri-urban reserves in the Swan Coastal Plain bioregion of southwestern Australia. Low open Banksia woodlands are the dominant vegetation type in this region, with an estimated 50%–60% of their original extent having been cleared in recent decades for the rapid urbanisation of Western Australia's capital city of Perth (Ritchie et al. [2021\)]. Most remaining vegetation is restricted to a few large conservation areas on the city margins, and small urban and peri-urban reserves, but even in these areas, there is projected ongoing species loss associated with time-delayed effects of habitat loss and fragmentation (Fowler et al. [2023]). In 2016, Banksia woodlands were recognised as a Threatened Ecological Community under Australia's national environmental law, and smaller portions have conservation listings at the state level (Commonwealth of Australia [2016;] Ramalho et al. [2014]; Ritchie et al. [2021\)].

Banksia woodlands are characterised by a low (4–8m height), open canopy of *Banksia* (Proteaceae) trees (predominantly the resprouters *B. attenuata* and *B. menziesii*, and fire-killed *B. prionotes*) and a species-rich understorey dominated by sclerophyllous shrubs in the plant families Dilleniaceae, Ericaceae, Fabaceae, Myrtaceae and Proteaceae (Dodd and Griffin [1989;] Ritchie et al. [2021]). The nutrient-poor, deep sandy soils of the Swan Coastal Plain are comprised largely of two major Pleistocene dune complexes (Bassendean and Spearwood), distinguished by their age of origin (Spearwood sands: 120k—500ka old, Bassendean sands: ~2ma old) and nutrient content (particularly nitrogen and phosphorus, declining with age) (Turner, Hayes, and Laliberté [2018]). The region has a Mediterranean-type climate, with cool, wet winters and hot, dry summers, making vegetation highly fire-prone during the dry season (austral summer and autumn; December–May). Average annual precipitation ranges from approximately 800mm in the south to 550mm in the north, 80% of which falls between May and October (Tangney et al. [2022\)] (Figure [S1\)].

{3}

######## PDF PAGE 5 ########
Fire is a regular occurrence on the Swan Coastal Plain, including low-moderate severity prescribed burning for risk reduction and conservation purposes during autumn and spring periods, and high severity wildfires mostly from human-caused ignitions during the hot, dry summer period (Densmore and Clingan [2019;] Enright and Fontaine [2014;] Howard et al. [2020]; Plucinski [2014\)]. The proximity of urban and peri-urban Banksia woodlands to human homes and infrastructure has placed substantial attention and importance on fire management in this ecosystem. While there are no direct estimates of historical or long-term fire intervals in Banksia woodlands that might suggest lower or upper limits to their adaptations, they share attributes (e.g., key plant functional types, surface and elevated fuel types) with surrounding vegetation types, including shrublands to the north and eucalypt forests to the east and south, where typical fire intervals have been estimated at 10–40+ years (shrublands) and 5–20 years (low severity, forest) or 20–100 years (high severity, forest) (Burrows, Ward, and Robinson [1995]; Enright et al. [2012;] Enright and Thomas [2008]; Murphy et al. [2013\)]. Indigenous use of fire was widespread in the region prior to European colonisation but specific information regarding burning in Banksia woodlands is not clear (Lullfitz et al. [2020;] Rodrigues et al. [2022]).

## **2.2   |   Study Species**

To explore fire interval effects on reproduction, we chose six woody plant species with a range of growth forms, fire response traits and seed bank storage modes across four common plant families (Table [1]). All species are native, common and widespread in Banksia woodlands and considered indicators of the vegetation type; although varying in their abundance and distribution within the landscape (Gibson et al. [1994]). Serotinous (canopy seed bank) species typically accumulate woody fruits containing seeds (hereafter cones) in the canopy over multiple years, therefore allowing assessment

of cumulative reproductive output. In the study area, the two selected *Banksia* species are known to be weakly serotinous, with most seeds released from woody fruits (hereafter cones) within 1–2 years of cone maturity (Cowling and Lamont [1985]). The dioecious shrub species *Allocasuarina humilis* is moderately serotinous with female plants retaining seeds in cones for up to 5 years (personal obs.). By pairing serotinous species with species with other seed storage modes, here specifically soil seed banks, we aim to gain an insight into the response of the broader plant community.

## **2.3   |   Site Selection**

To assess varying fire intervals, we employed a space-for-time approach and selected sites with a broad range of recent fire histories (time since fire, TSF). We first interrogated fire history data for remnant vegetation in urban and peri-urban reserves across the study region to identify a set of candidate sites with a wide range of fire ages, suitable access (with permission from land managers) and appropriate vegetation type (i.e., not wetland, riparian, or limestone vegetation). Year of last fire for each site was determined from spatial data layers maintained by the Western Australian Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA-060, <https://catalogue.data.wa.gov.au/dataset/dbca-fire-history>); historical satellite and aerial imagery (Landgate, [https://map](https://map-viewer-plus.app.landgate.wa.gov.au/index.html)[viewer-plus.app.landgate.wa.gov.au/index.html](https://map-viewer-plus.app.landgate.wa.gov.au/index.html)); and local government records. Given limitations in fire history records and satellite and aerial imagery, we were unable to confirm exact ages for some sites beyond 35 years (occurring before approximately 1986). Sites with no assignable post-fire age are referred to here as long unburnt (LUB), and for analysis are given a notional age of 35 years.

We visited candidate sites to confirm the above criteria as well as the presence of the study species and the absence of

This produced a total of 34 sites across a fire interval chronosequence from 1 to 35years (or more), with each site containing one to five study species. The number of sites surveyed for each species ranged from 11 to 17, all spanning a similar post-fire chronosequence (Table [1\)]. Some sites were surveyed over two successive years, creating two nonindependent TSF samples.

Sites were mostly (91%) located on Spearwood sands across a 100 km north–south extent of the Swan Coastal Plain (Figure [1]). Mean annual rainfall ranged from 698 mm in the north (Muchea, 1971–2000) to 843 mm in the south (Halls Head, 1971–2000; Australian Bureau of Meteorology [2020]) (Figure [S1\)]. All species except *B. prionotes* were sampled across the full extent of this rainfall gradient. *Banksia prionotes* was only found across a very narrow (negligible) range (30 mm mean annual rainfall difference) in the sampled study area, but occur more broadly in the region, as do the other study species. The presence (*n* = 19) or absence (*n* = 15) of kangaroos (western grey kangaroo, *Macropus fuliginosus*) as major herbivores was assessed at each site based on sightings of individuals or their scats as well as local knowledge and records (City of Joondalup [2015]; City of Nedlands [2014;] Ecoscape (Australia Pty Ltd) [2008;] Government of Western Australia [2000;] Natural Area Consulting [2012]). Where present in urban reserves, kangaroos (or signs of their presence) are easily observed, and populations often achieve high density. There was no discernible change in kangaroo abundance over the study period.

#### **2.4   |   Field Surveys**

At each site, data were collected on reproductive and size attributes for live individuals. Seedlings less than 1–2 years old in sites older than 4years since fire (inter-fire seedlings) were excluded as these individuals can have a low survival rate and therefore have little consequence for the reproductive status of populations. Data on the abundance of inter-fire seedlings from the same sites are presented in Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [\(2024]). Seedlings were distinguished by the presence of cotyledons, lack of signs of current or past reproduction, and were generally <10–20 cm tall for shrub species or <30 cm tall for tree species. Estimates of seedling age were confirmed by observations of seedlings of known age in post-fire sites.

Data were mostly collected within plots positioned to include as many of the target species as possible and ranging in size from 25 to 150 m2 as necessary to suit different species and plant densities, and to ensure sampling of at least 30 individuals. Plant densities were calculated from the number of individuals in each plot and scaled to the number of plants per hectare. Smaller plots were used for shrub species (density range 0.1–4.6 plants m−2), and larger plots for tree species (0.03–1.58 plants m−2). At least two plots were established at each site, but where plant density was particularly low, measurements were taken based on a nearest-neighbour search until a minimum of 30 plants were recorded. For some plotbased surveys, additional nearest plants outside of plots were measured to fulfil sample size criterion. Field surveys were undertaken from 2016 to 2018 during peak flowering times for each species (Table [1\)].

Measurements recorded for each individual included: (1) number of flowers (or inflorescences; all species), (2) number of mature cones with unopened follicles (canopy seed bank species only) and (3) size (all species). *Allocasuarina humilis* is a dioecious species and we identified and recorded attributes of male and female plants separately (only female plants produce cones). The number of cones recorded represents the cumulative canopy seed bank from all previous reproductive seasons excluding seed loss from seed predation, disease and spontaneous follicle opening, among other factors. Size was recorded as aboveground plant height (*Gompholobium tomentosum* and *Acacia pulchella*), canopy volume (*Hibbertia hypericoides* and *Allocasuarina humilis*) or stem diameter at breast height (DBH, 1.37m above the ground; *Banksia attenuata, B. prionotes*). These measurements were chosen to best represent how size relates to reproductive performance given each species' growth form.

Some reserves contained multiple sites of various fire ages (some points obscured by other points). Green shading indicates extant native vegetation, grey shading indicates urban areas and the solid red line indicates the boundary of the Swan Coastal Plain region (also shown on inset map).

#### **2.5   |   Data Analysis**

## **2.5.1   |   Post-Fire Reproductive Trajectories**

To analyse post-fire reproductive trajectories, we evaluated generalised additive mixed models (GAMMs) of TSF, herbivory and mean annual rainfall as a priori predictors of each of three population-level reproductive attributes: flowering rate (% individuals flowering), mean number of flowers per plant and mean number of closed cones per plant (for the three serotinous species only). Population-level attributes were calculated from all individuals surveyed, including resprouting and young (nonreproductive) plants, where present. We employed a model selection approach whereby we constructed a set of plausible models from subsets of the a priori predictors and compared these using Akaike's Information Criterion corrected for small sample size (AICc) and AICc model weights (ωAICc) which represent the probability or weight of evidence for each model (Burnham, Anderson, and Huyvaert [2011]; Hurvich and Tsai [1989\)]. Models with ΔAICc <5 generally represented a cumulative ωAICc of ≥0.95 and therefore are presented here as part of the 95% confidence set, following Symonds and Moussalli ([2011\)]. Models with ΔAICc<2 are considered to have substantial support (Burnham and Anderson [2002\)]. We conducted this analysis in *R* (version 4.0.3) (R Core Team [2020\)] using the *FSSgam* package (Fisher et al. [2018\)] which enables an all subsets approach and uses the *gam()* function from the *mgcv* package (Wood [2017\)].

Flowering rate, presented as proportions, was modelled using a binomial error distribution (logit link function) with data weighted by the number of individuals recorded per site. Mean number of flowers and cones per plant were modelled using a tweedie error distribution (log link function) to account for many zero values (i.e., non-flowering/non-fruiting individuals). TSF was logtransformed for analysis as responses are expected to change most rapidly in the first few years after fire, and to optimise the distribution of values across the predictor range. TSF was included as a continuous smoother in the model set to allow for non-linear relationships with time. In all models, the smoothing parameter was limited to a simple spline (k=3) to avoid overfitting. Mean annual rainfall was included as a linear predictor in all models, and any effects were presented as predictions at the 10th and 90th percentile of mean annual rainfall across the TSF chronosequence, representing post-fire reproductive trajectories for 'low' (~720mm) and 'high' (~790mm) rainfall sites, respectively.

Herbivory was included as a two-level factor variable (absence or presence of kangaroo herbivores) in model sets for shrub species only (i.e., excluding *B. attenuata* and *B. prionotes*) as we lacked a strong a priori expectation of the effects of herbivory from kangaroos (generally <2m tall) on tree species that are typically >4m

tall at maturity. A two-way interaction between log-transformed TSF and herbivory was included in the model set for *G. tomentosum* only to explore if effects of herbivory varied by TSF. Replication of different herbivory levels across the range of log-transformed TSF was not considered to be adequate for the other shrub species and therefore was only included as an additive effect in other model sets. An identifier for the year of survey was included as a random smoother in all models for species where measurements were recorded in two successive years to account for repeat measures and any annual variation in environmental conditions (e.g., rainfall) other than an increase in TSF by 1year.

Modelling of flowering rate and flower counts was conducted separately for male and female plants of the dioecious species *A. humilis*. Top-ranking model comparisons are presented for models on female data only. Only female plants produce cones and seeds and so modelling of cone counts was necessarily restricted to female plant data. Juvenile period was calculated from the flowering rate of female plants. The sex ratio was, on average, 45% females and 55% males across all populations (excluding non-reproductive individuals), or 49% females and 51% males after the post-fire maturation period (i.e., after 4years) (Figure [S2\)].

#### **2.5.2**|**Time Since Fire as a Predictor of Reproduction**

To assess the strength of TSF as a predictor of reproduction, we compared GAMMs with single predictors of either TSF or plant size (height, canopy volume or effective DBH) for each of the three reproductive attributes measured. Models using plant size as the predictor represent the mechanistic relationship between TSF and reproduction, where the growth of plants following fire enables greater access to resources and an increase in reproductive output. For single-cohort populations (i.e., fire-killed species), we would expect that models using single predictors of TSF and plant size would explain similar amounts of variation (i.e., *R*2 ) and have a similar weight of evidence (i.e., AICc and ωAICc). However, for multi-cohort populations (usually resprouters, but also possible for some fire-killed species), we would expect that models using size would explain much more variation and have a much greater weight of evidence than models using TSF.

GAMMs were constructed as outlined above, where models of TSF or size alone were compared using *FSSgam*. Size measurements (height, canopy volume, effective DBH) were log-transformed to optimise the distribution of values across the predictor range and improve model fit. For the dioecious species (*A. humilis*), modelling was conducted separately for male and female plants, with top-ranking model comparisons presented for female data only.

#### **3   |   Results**

## **3.1   |   Flowering Rates and Juvenile Periods**

TSF consistently appeared in top-ranked models of flowering rates for all species (Table [2]). Flowering rate generally increased rapidly in the first few years after fire and stabilised thereafter (Figure [2]). *Acacia pulchella* was the only species with an apparent decline in flowering rate in longer unburnt sites; in sites older than 30years, predicted flowering rate fell below 50%, however,

### 2. Methods

# 2.1. Study site

The 154 ha Derrimut Grassland Reserve is 15 km south-west of Melbourne, Victoria (37480 3000S, 144470 4000E). Mean annual rainfall is 568 mm. The geology is Early Pleistocene olivine basalt (Douglas, 1982). The reserve is dominated by a Themeda triandra grassland in well-drained areas (Lunt, 1990a) and is a remnant of the Keilor Plains grassland described by Willis (1964). This grassland type is on the verge of extinction (McDougall and Kirkpatrick, 1994). Soils in grassland areas range from silty-clay to clay-loam with pH 7.0 (Lunt, 1990a).

The property was grazed by sheep until the 1960s and by cattle from then until 1985, when grazing was removed from the entire site after management changed to the state conservation agency for the purposes of grassland conservation.

Early recommendations for management of the reserve suggested that ®re at 2±5 yr intervals were necessary to maintain botanical values (Stuwe, 1986; Lunt, 1988). However, owing to perceived negative impacts of frequent burning on endangered fauna (Coulson, 1990), a management plan recommended that the reserve be divided into 10 zones, two of which were to be burnt every year, giving a 5 yr ®re interval in each zone (Craigie and Stuwe, 1992). In practice, the management plan has not been consistently implemented. Ten ®res occurred between 1986 and 1997 but all had dierent boundaries and burnt dierent areas. The number of ®res experienced in each zone ranged from 0 to 3 and the maximum inter-®re interval varied from 4 to over 12 yr (in areas which were never burnt).

# 2.2. Study species

Themeda triandra (syn. T. australis) is a perennial C4 tussock grass that dominates many grassy woodlands and tropical savannahs in both Australia and Africa. In southern Victoria, T. triandra is the dominant species of natural grassland communities on volcanic soils (Patton, 1935; Willis, 1964; McDougall et al., 1994). It grows primarily from October to January in southern Victoria and is most productive in the ®rst 3±4 yr after ®re (McDougall, 1989), after which time productivity declines (Groves, 1974; McDougall, 1989). It has no means of extensive vegetative spread. Tussocks are generally ®re-resistant, tillers resprouting after summer ®res from protected basal apices, even when burnt annually (Morgan, in prep). Aerial tillers form when swards remain undisturbed and these are easily damaged by trampling (McDougall, 1989). The ability of tussocks and tillers to recover from ®re after a long period of ®re exclusion is virtually unknown, although in a companion study, Lunt and Morgan (1998) found that post- ®re recovery of Themeda in areas unburnt for 17 yr lagged behind that of a grassland burnt more frequently. ### 2. Methods

# 2.1. Study site

The geology is Early Pleistocene olivine basalt (Douglas, 1982). The reserve is dominated by a Themeda triandra grassland in well-drained areas (Lunt, 1990a) and is a remnant of the Keilor Plains grassland described by Willis (1964). This grassland type is on the verge of extinction (McDougall and Kirkpatrick, 1994). Soils in grassland areas range from silty-clay to clay-loam with pH 7.0 (Lunt, 1990a).

The property was grazed by sheep until the 1960s and by cattle from then until 1985, when grazing was removed from the entire site after management changed to the state conservation agency for the purposes of grassland conservation.

Early recommendations for management of the reserve suggested that ®re at 2±5 yr intervals were necessary to maintain botanical values (Stuwe, 1986; Lunt, 1988). 1 ## n_pages=11 2 3 ######## PDF PAGE 1 ######## 4 {0} 5 6 ######## PDF PAGE 2 ######## 7 # **Reproductive trajectories over decadal time-spans after fire for eight obligate-seeder shrub species in south-eastern Australia** 8 9 *Annette M. Muir*A*,*D*, Peter A. Vesk* B *and Graham Hepworth*C 10 11 AArthur Rylah Institute for Environmental Research, Department of Environment and Primary Industries 12 13 (formerly Department of Sustainability and Environment), PO Box 137, Heidelberg, Vic. 3084, Australia. B 14 15 Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence in Environmental Decisions, School of Botany, 16 17 The University of Melbourne, Parkville, Vic. 3010, Australia. 18 19 CStatistical Consulting Centre, Department of Mathematics and Statistics, The University of Melbourne, Parkville, Vic. 3010, Australia. 20 21 DCorresponding author. Email: [annette.muir@depi.vic.gov.au](mailto:annette.muir@depi.vic.gov.au) 22 23 **Abstract.** Intervals between fires are critical for the persistence of obligate-seeding shrubs, and are often used in planning fires for fuel reduction and biodiversity conservation in fire-prone ecosystems worldwide. Yet information about the trajectories of reproductive performance for such species is limited and information is often qualitative. To test existing assumptions about reproductive maturity periods for eight obligate-seeding shrubs (with both canopy and soil seedbanks) in foothill forests of south-eastern Australia, we used a chronosequence approach, with sites from 2 years to >40 years post-fire. Quantitative measurements of flowering and fruiting were used to fit models of reproductive response in relation to timesince-fire for each species. Inferred reproductive maturity for each species, based on modelled times to reach 80% of maximum flower production, varied from 5 to 18 years post-fire. For a subset of three species, models predicted 80% maximum seed production occurring 1–7 years later than flowering. Our results confirmed or extended assumptions about post-fire reproductive maturity for these species, and provided a basis for improved incorporation of plant life-history in ecological fire planning. We infer that increased fire frequency makes one of our study taxa, *Banksia spinulosa* var. *cunninghamii* (Sieber ex Rchb.) A.S.George, vulnerable to decline because of its long reproductive maturity period and serotinous seed storage. 24 25 **Additional keywords:** *Banksia*, fire interval, fire planning, flower production, plant functional type, response curve, seed production. 26 27 Received 23 May 2014, accepted 30 July 2014, published online 24 September 2014 28 29 ## **Introduction** 30 31 Fire is important in shaping the species composition and vegetation structure of many ecosystems worldwide (Bond and Keeley [2005](#page-7-0)), especially open forests in south-eastern Australia (Gill [2012\)](#page-8-0). The response of plants and plant communities to fire depends on the local fire regime and the functional traits of individual plant species (Keith [2012\)](#page-8-0). A fire regime is the sequence of fire intervals, intensities and seasons (Gill [1975](#page-8-0)) at any point in the landscape (Gill and Catling [2002\)](#page-8-0), and this sequence affects plant survival and recruitment (Whelan *et al*. [2002](#page-9-0)). The spatial variability of fire regimes also creates mosaics of different vegetation types comprising species with different life history characteristics responsive to fire (Clark *et al*. [2002](#page-7-0)). Most studies examining the effects of fire regimes on plants have concentrated on fire intervals, because other aspects such as fire intensity are difficult to determine (Gill and Catling [2002\)](#page-8-0). 32 33 Species most affected by fire interval are obligate-seeder species, which are killed by fire and persist after fire only as seed (Pausas *et al*. [2004](#page-9-0)). Obligate seeders that have had their seed reserves exhausted by disturbance but require long periods to reach reproductive maturity are most vulnerable to repeated frequent fires (Gill and Catling [2002](#page-8-0); Bradstock and Kenny [2003](#page-7-0)). Conversely, intervals between infrequent fires can exceed the lifespan of existing plants or seedbanks of some species (Gill and Catling [2002](#page-8-0); Bradstock and Kenny [2003](#page-7-0)). Fire intensity also affects the survival of adult plants, and many seeds require the direct effects of heat and smoke to germinate (Bell [1999\)](#page-7-0). Additional factors, such as herbivory and weather conditions, can affect recruitment success following fire (Whelan *et al*. [2002\)](#page-9-0). By contrast, resprouting species persist in a vegetative form after fire and can survive more frequent fire disturbance (Pausas *et al*. [2004\)](#page-9-0). 34 35 Plant species can be grouped into functional types, on the basis of shared traits or responses to environment or disturbance (Reich *et al*. [2003;](#page-9-0) Pausas *et al*. [2004;](#page-9-0) Keith *et al*. [2007](#page-8-0)). Plant functional-type schemes have been used in fire-prone 36 37 {1} 38 39 ######## PDF PAGE 3 ######## 40 ecosystems to hypothesise likely responses of vegetation communities to fire regimes, based on the attributes of their component species (e.g. Menges [2007](#page-8-0); Pausas and Lloret [2007;](#page-9-0) van Wilgen *et al*. [2010](#page-9-0); Cheal [2010\)](#page-7-0). The 'plant vital attributes' scheme (Noble and Slatyer [1980](#page-8-0); Noble and Gitay [1996\)](#page-8-0) is one plant functional type scheme commonly used in studies of plant responses to fire in Australia, South Africa and USA (e.g. Bradstock and Kenny [2003](#page-7-0); Keeley *et al*. [2006](#page-8-0); Keith *et al*. [2007;](#page-8-0) Kraaij *et al*. [2013](#page-8-0)). Vital attributes refer to the persistence of propagules, mortality of plants and reproductive capacity of surviving plants, patterns of recruitment owing to competition or establishment prerequisites, and times to reach reproductive maturity and for all plants and propagules to die out in a site (Noble and Slatyer [1980](#page-8-0); Whelan *et al*. [2002](#page-9-0)). These attributes are frequently used by Australian land management agencies in planning fire frequencies to optimise the conservation of vascular plant diversity (Fire Ecology Working Group [2004](#page-8-0); Bradstock *et al*. [2012\)](#page-7-0). However, the application of the vitalattribute approach in fire planning often relies on subjective information on plant species (DSE [2010](#page-8-0)*e*) and there have been few empirical studies (Keith [2012](#page-8-0)). 41 42 To address this uncertainty surrounding several of the vital attributes of obligate-seeding shrubs in fire-prone areas of south-eastern Australia, we tested the existing hypothesised reproductive maturity periods for eight obligate-seeder shrubs with canopy and soil seedbanks. We developed empirical models of reproductive characteristics (flowers for each species, fruit for three species) in relation to decadal time-spans after fire, derived predictions from these models about the relationships between time-since-fire and thresholds of reproduction, and then compared these to the existing assumptions about the species' juvenile periods. Implications of these results for planning fire intervals to maintain plant populations are discussed. 43 44 # **Materials and methods** 45 46 # *Study area and sites selection* 47 48 We sampled open forests on the southern side of the Great Dividing Range in the state of Victoria. Target forest types on more exposed slopes were Lowland Forest and Shrubby Foothill Forest, which have eucalypt canopies with an understorey of narrow-leaved shrubs, grasses and herbs (DSE [2011](#page-8-0)). On more sheltered slopes, Damp Forest was targeted, which has a eucalypt canopy with a tall layer of broad-leaved shrubs, and a ground layer of grasses, herbs and ferns (DSE [2011](#page-8-0)). Sites were located in two clusters, one in Dandenong Ranges National Park and the other in Bunyip State Park/Kurth Kiln Regional Park. The climate for the two clusters of sites is similar, and is characterised by wet cold winters and dry warm summers. Long-term mean annual rainfall is 1200 mm, the highest rainfall month being August and lowest February (Bureau of Meteorology [2011](#page-7-0)). Long-term mean monthly temperatures are highest in February (23.3 C) and lowest in July (5.3 C) (Bureau of Meteorology [2011\)](#page-7-0). Study sites were on gentle to moderate slopes, on igneous geology (Parks Victoria [2011](#page-8-0)*a*, [2011](#page-8-0)*b*), at elevations of 220–410 m above sea level. 49 50 A space-for-time substitution approach was used to assess responses of species to fire over decadal periods. The study area was stratified using spatial databases maintained by the Victorian Department of Sustainability and Environment (DSE [2010](#page-8-0)*a*, [2010](#page-8-0)*b*, [2010](#page-8-0)*c*) to determine target vegetation types and fire histories and to exclude areas subjected to logging in the past 20 years. The study area was further confined to 'Asset Protection' and 'StrategicWildfireModeration'fire-management zones (DSE [2006\)](#page-8-0) because these areas have a high likelihood of complete burn coverage. Sites were selected within the following classes representing time since the last fire: 0–3 years, 4–10 years, 11–20 years, 21–40 years and 41 + years. These classes were informed by the timing of growth stages identified byCheal ([2010\)](#page-7-0) for thethree target forest types in relation to fire, and undefined after 40 years because of the limits of DSE fire records. Areas were identified with all fireage-class combinations for each target forest type located within close proximity and with similar environmental conditions (water availability, sun exposure, geographic spread, elevation and aspect) for each species, so as not to confound the responses of the plants to fire with their response to these factors. 51 52 ## *Species selection* 53 54 Shrubs were selected for study because they are prominent in forest communities and are easily identified, and obligate seeders were selected because they are most susceptible to local extinctions from inappropriate fire regimes. These species are killed by fire, recruitment is by seed only, and timing of fires can exhaust their seed supplies before plants reach reproductive maturity. Common species were chosen to enable a good representation of the typical vegetation communities (Cornelissen *et al*. [2003\)](#page-8-0), and because they were detectable in most fire-age classes. 55 56 Potential species for the study were identified from the Victorian database of vascular flora (DSE [2010](#page-8-0)*d*) and subsequent field searches, to identify those species with adequate representation at a range of fire-age sites. Species were selected and categorised according to their mode of persistence following fire (obligate seeder), seedbank type (soil or canopy), length of juvenile period (germination to reestablishment of seedbank adequate to replace parent plants) and individual plant lifespan (Table [1](#page-2-0)). These factors have been used in classification schemes that predict the response of plants to fire (Whelan *et al*. [2002](#page-9-0)). Plant functional-type categories used in the study have been adapted from Keith *et al*.([2007\)](#page-8-0), which is a simplified version of the vital-attribute scheme of Noble and Slatyer [\(1980](#page-8-0)). Estimates of the responses of individual species in these categories were derived from expert opinion about Victorian plant vital attributes (DSE [2010](#page-8-0)*e*). 57 58 #### *Sampling design* 59 60 The number of individuals sampled was a balance between obtaining enough replicates to capture the variability of the traits of interest and sampling enough species of interest (Cornelissen *et al*. [2003\)](#page-8-0). We followed Cornelissen *et al*. ([2003\)](#page-8-0), who recommended that at least 10 individuals at each site should be measured for plant height (which is more variable than many other plant traits). Individuals were selected using a transect method, modified from Cornelissen *et al*.([2003\)](#page-8-0). Within each fire-age site, a 100-m transect was located where the target species were observed, at least 20 m from a road or track, and 61 62 {2} 63 64 ######## PDF PAGE 4 ######## 65 searched for 10 m on either side. Ten individuals of each target species, haphazardly selected along the transect, were measured at each site. Where species were in low numbers, only five individuals were measured, and where there were fewer than 10 individuals along transects, we searched within the boundaries of the fire-age site. If different age cohorts were present, only the oldest cohorts (largest individuals) were measured. We sampled species at 17 sites representing 14 different time periods since fire (Table 2) and measured 325 plants. 66 67 ## *Measurement variables* 68 69 Data were collected on flowers and seeds because these represent two stages of reproduction. Flower counts were made for all eight target species, and seed counts for four species, between July 2010 and January 2011 and in December 2011. Seed counts for *Banksia spinulosa* and *Pomaderris aspera* were made on the same plants as for the flowers, but for *Hakea decurrens* and 70 71 *Acacia verticillata*, these counts were on different individuals. The number of flowers per plant was estimated by using sample units to scale up data (Kirmse and Norton [1985](#page-8-0); West [2009](#page-9-0)). At each fire-age site, a branching unit comprising stems, leaves and flowers was selected for each plant, and then the number of such units bearing flowers was estimated for that plant. The number of flowers on a unit was then counted. For species with more than one flower per inflorescence, the number of flowers per inflorescence was counted and then multiplied by the number of inflorescences on a unit. The number of flowers per unit was finally multiplied by the number of units per plant to obtain an estimate for the whole plant. For *Banksia spinulosa*, the number of inflorescences was counted and then multiplied by an estimate of 100flowers, because of the difficulty in counting individual flowers. 72 73 The number of seeds per plant was estimated in two ways. For the serotinous (canopy-seed) species, the total number of unopened infructescences was counted, because these are considered to represent viable seed (Enright and Goldblum [1999](#page-8-0)). As in other studies, we assumed that after release, seeds of the woody-fruited Proteaceae generally last only until the next wet season (Lamont and Groom [1998;](#page-8-0) Campbell *et al*. [2012](#page-7-0)). However, some fruits may stay unopened for several years after maturity. The number of fruits counted on a plant was multiplied by the estimated number of seeds per fruit. Average seed numbers per fruit for *Banksia spinulosa* were derived from collection of five fruits at each fire-age site, whereas an 74 75 assumption of two seeds per fruit was made for *Hakea decurrens* (Barker *et al*. [1996](#page-7-0)). For the species with soil seedbanks, sample units comprising stems, leaves and infructescences were used, followed by scaling up of data, as outlined for the flower measurements (Kirmse and Norton [1985;](#page-8-0) West [2009\)](#page-9-0). Estimating flower and seed numbers was more difficult for larger plants, and these results are likely to have greater errors. 76 77 The methodology to estimate flower and seed numbers was chosen because it enabled data to be collected fairly rapidly in one season, which may be useful for management-oriented research. Methods used in some other studies of reproductive maturity periods of Proteaceae species have used counts of flowers and seeds on permanently marked plants over several seasons (e.g. Kraaij *et al*. [2013;](#page-8-0) Enright and Goldblum [1999](#page-8-0)). 78 79 ## *Data analysis* 80 81 The purpose of the analysis was to build quantitative models of each species measured, in the form of response curves that could be used to understand reproductive maturity patterns following fire. Non-linear regression models were fitted to the relationships between reproduction (response variables) and time-since-fire (explanatory variable). These enabled comparisons to be made with current assumptions about times to reproductive maturity for the species. 82 83 Flower and seed numbers were at times very large and skewed to the right, and so numbers were log-transformed. An increment of either 1 or 10 was added before transforming because of the presence of zeros. Gompertz growth curves were used to model the relationship with time-since-fire, using the equation 84 85 *y* ¼ q1expðexpðq2 q3*x*ÞÞ: 86 87 **Table 1. 96 97 {3} 98 99 ######## PDF PAGE 5 ######## 100 We calculated 95% confidence intervals for the mean (fitted) responses. Various curves were tested for their fit to the relationship, where there is known to be a slow initial response, then a rapid increase followed by a plateau. The sigmoid curve of the Gompertz function (Tjørve [2003\)](#page-9-0) gave the best fit for most species. In the equation above, q1 is the upper asymptote, q2 sets the displacement in the vertical direction, and q3 represents the growth rate. The models were fitted using the statistical package Minitab 16 (Minitab Inc. [2010](#page-8-0)). 101 102 The variable 'time-since-fire' was determined by the year of fire, not by the classes used for the stratification of sites. Sites up to ~15 years post-fire could be recognised confidently as being completely burnt because of the uniform regeneration of plants. The precise number of years since fire was unknown at the oldest sites for all species measured, because detailed fire records date only back to 1970. An estimated time-since-fire was assigned to these sites on the basis of the last major wildfire recorded in the areas. 103 104 The final step in the analyses of each species was to predict thresholds for the reproductive variables. The fitted equations from the non-linear regressions were used to estimate the value of response variables for future observations. Predictions were made for the mean time-since-fire that an average plant takes to exceed 80% of its maximum annual flower production (eight species) or 80% of its seed production (three species only) on the log scale. Maximum production was taken as the upper asymptote of the fitted response curve. The threshold of 80% of the estimated asymptote was chosen for biological reasons. For example, at 50%, most species had few or no plants with flowers, whereas at 80%, all species had flowering individuals. Given that flowering is being used to infer reproductive maturity, this is more useful. Asymptotes for *Pomaderris aspera* had very large confidence intervals for both flowers and seeds, because of the model being based on only three non-zero time-since-fire points, and hence predictions were not made or fitted curves presented for this species. 105 106 ## **Results** 107 108 ## *Relationships of reproductive variables to time-since-fire* 109 110 The eight shrub species displayed similarly patterned trajectories of reproductive output, although their timing differed considerably. The fitted relationships for flowers and seeds showed a rapid increase in production, then a plateau, with the exception of *Pomaderris aspera*. Asymptotes for each species represented the annual flower or seed production for an average plant. Most of the variation in the response variables was explained by the explanatory variable. The flower models had *R*2 -values between 72% and 94% (Table 3), whereas the seed models had lower *R*2 values of between 45% and 85% (Table 3). 111 112 The highest maximum flower numbers were recorded for species with soil seedbanks and presumed long juvenile periods (*Prostanthera lasianthos* and *Pomaderris aspera*) (Fig. [1](#page-4-0), Table [4\)](#page-5-0). Species with soil seedbanks and presumed moderate juvenile periods (*Acacia oxycedrus*,*Acacia verticillata*, *Pultenaea scabra* and *Olearia lirata*) had fewer flowers at their maximum production (Fig. [1,](#page-4-0) Table [4](#page-5-0)). Species with canopy seedbanks (*Banksia spinulosa* and *Hakea decurrens*) had the lowest maximum flower numbers (Fig. [1](#page-4-0), Table [4](#page-5-0)). 113 114 The lowest estimated maximum seed production was also for species with canopy seedbanks, being 470 for *Banksia spinulosa* and five for *Hakea decurrens* (Fig. [2,](#page-5-0) Table [4\)](#page-5-0). In contrast, the maximum estimated seed production for the soil seedbank species *Acacia verticillata* was 2600 (Fig. [2,](#page-5-0) Table [4](#page-5-0)). 115 116 # *Predictions for flowering and seeding thresholds* 117 118 Predictions about the timing of flowering thresholds after fire were made from the data models (Table [4](#page-5-0)). Species with soil seedbanks and presumed moderate juvenile periods exceeded 80% of predicted mean flower asymptotes within the shortest time-since-fire. Species with soil seedbanks and presumed long juvenile periods exceeded 80% flower asymptotes in the longest periods since fire. Species with canopy seedbanks were intermediate in time to 80% of maximum flower production. 119 120 Predictions for seed-production thresholds were made for the two species with canopy-stored seed, and one species with soilstored seed (Table [4](#page-5-0)). For the two serotinous species, the gap between the predicted 80% asymptotes for flowers and seeds was 7 years for *Banksia spinulosa* and two years for *Hakea decurrens*. The species with soil-stored seed and a moderate juvenile period (*Acacia verticillata*) exceeded the 80% seed asymptote 1 year after flowers. 121 122 # **Discussion** 123 124 #### *Reproductive maturity times* 125 126 There are few published data on times to reproductive maturity after fire for Australian shrubs. Our results on the relationships between reproductive responses and decadal time-spans after fire add to the current knowledge of fire intervals needed for population maintenance of eight obligate-seeding shrub species in south-eastern Australia. The data models either confirmed or extended the hypothesised timing of reproductive maturity (Tables [1,](#page-2-0) [4](#page-5-0)) for the species used in this study to represent four plant functional types (shrubs with canopy-stored seed and moderate or long juvenile periods, shrubs with soil-stored seed and moderate or long juvenile periods). For two species (*Banksia spinulosa* and *Prostanthera lasianthos*), existing assumptions were shown to underestimate the time to reach reproductive maturity by up to 10 years. 127 128 Times to reproductive maturity for the species with serotinous seedbanks were longer than initially anticipated. Predictions from the data models for *Banksia spinulosa* indicated 80% maximum flower production (on the log scale) at 13 years post-fire and 80% maximum seed production (on the log scale) 129 130 **Table 3.** *R***2 -values for flowers and seeds models** 131 132

The response of plants and plant communities to fire depends on the local fire regime and the functional traits of individual plant species (Keith [2012\)](#page-8-0). A fire regime is the sequence of fire intervals, intensities and seasons (Gill [1975](#page-8-0)) at any point in the landscape (Gill and Catling [2002\)](#page-8-0), and this sequence affects plant survival and recruitment (Whelan *et al*. [2002](#page-9-0)). The spatial variability of fire regimes also creates mosaics of different vegetation types comprising species with different life history characteristics responsive to fire (Clark *et al*. [2002](#page-7-0)). Most studies examining the effects of fire regimes on plants have concentrated on fire intervals, because other aspects such as fire intensity are difficult to determine (Gill and Catling [2002\)](#page-8-0). Species most affected by fire interval are obligate-seeder species, which are killed by fire and persist after fire only as seed (Pausas *et al*. [2004](#page-9-0)). Obligate seeders that have had their seed reserves exhausted by disturbance but require long periods to reach reproductive maturity are most vulnerable to repeated frequent fires (Gill and Catling [2002](#page-8-0); Bradstock and Kenny [2003](#page-7-0)). Conversely, intervals between infrequent fires can exceed the lifespan of existing plants or seedbanks of some species (Gill and Catling [2002](#page-8-0); Bradstock and Kenny [2003](#page-7-0)). Fire intensity also affects the survival of adult plants, and many seeds require the direct effects of heat and smoke to germinate (Bell [1999\)](#page-7-0). Additional factors, such as herbivory and weather conditions, can affect recruitment success following fire (Whelan *et al*. [2002\)](#page-9-0). By contrast, resprouting species persist in a vegetative form after fire and can survive more frequent fire disturbance (Pausas *et al*. [2004\)](#page-9-0). Plant species can be grouped into functional types, on the basis of shared traits or responses to environment or disturbance (Reich *et al*. [2003;](#page-9-0) Pausas *et al*. [2004;](#page-9-0) Keith *et al*. [2007](#page-8-0)). Plant functional-type schemes have been used in fire-prone {1} ######## PDF PAGE 3 ######## ecosystems to hypothesise likely responses of vegetation communities to fire regimes, based on the attributes of their component species (e.g. Menges [2007](#page-8-0); Pausas and Lloret [2007;](#page-9-0) van Wilgen *et al*. [2010](#page-9-0); Cheal [2010\)](#page-7-0). The 'plant vital attributes' scheme (Noble and Slatyer [1980](#page-8-0); Noble and Gitay [1996\)](#page-8-0) is one plant functional type scheme commonly used in studies of plant responses to fire in Australia, South Africa and USA (e.g. Bradstock and Kenny [2003](#page-7-0); Keeley *et al*. [2006](#page-8-0); Keith *et al*. [2007;](#page-8-0) Kraaij *et al*. [2013](#page-8-0)). Vital attributes refer to the persistence of propagules, mortality of plants and reproductive capacity of surviving plants, patterns of recruitment owing to competition or establishment prerequisites, and times to reach reproductive maturity and for all plants and propagules to die out in a site (Noble and Slatyer [1980](#page-8-0); Whelan *et al*. [2002](#page-9-0)). These attributes are frequently used by Australian land management agencies in planning fire frequencies to optimise the conservation of vascular plant diversity (Fire Ecology Working Group [2004](#page-8-0); Bradstock *et al*. [2012\)](#page-7-0). However, the application of the vitalattribute approach in fire planning often relies on subjective information on plant species (DSE [2010](#page-8-0)*e*) and there have been few empirical studies (Keith [2012](#page-8-0)). To address this uncertainty surrounding several of the vital attributes of obligate-seeding shrubs in fire-prone areas of south-eastern Australia, we tested the existing hypothesised reproductive maturity periods for eight obligate-seeder shrubs with canopy and soil seedbanks. We developed empirical models of reproductive characteristics (flowers for each species, fruit for three species) in relation to decadal time-spans after fire, derived predictions from these models about the relationships between time-since-fire and thresholds of reproduction, and then compared these to the existing assumptions about the species' juvenile periods. Implications of these results for planning fire intervals to maintain plant populations are discussed. # **Materials and methods** # *Study area and sites selection* We sampled open forests on the southern side of the Great Dividing Range in the state of Victoria. Target forest types on more exposed slopes were Lowland Forest and Shrubby Foothill Forest, which have eucalypt canopies with an understorey of narrow-leaved shrubs, grasses and herbs (DSE [2011](#page-8-0)). On more sheltered slopes, Damp Forest was targeted, which has a eucalypt canopy with a tall layer of broad-leaved shrubs, and a ground layer of grasses, herbs and ferns (DSE [2011](#page-8-0)). Sites were located in two clusters, one in Dandenong Ranges National Park and the other in Bunyip State Park/Kurth Kiln Regional Park. The climate for the two clusters of sites is similar, and is characterised by wet cold winters and dry warm summers. Long-term mean annual rainfall is 1200 mm, the highest rainfall month being August and lowest February (Bureau of Meteorology [2011](#page-7-0)). Long-term mean monthly temperatures are highest in February (23.3 C) and lowest in July (5.3 C) (Bureau of Meteorology [2011\)](#page-7-0). Study sites were on gentle to moderate slopes, on igneous geology (Parks Victoria [2011](#page-8-0)*a*, [2011](#page-8-0)*b*), at elevations of 220–410 m above sea level. A space-for-time substitution approach was used to assess responses of species to fire over decadal periods. The study area was stratified using spatial databases maintained by the Victorian Department of Sustainability and Environment (DSE [2010](#page-8-0)*a*, [2010](#page-8-0)*b*, [2010](#page-8-0)*c*) to determine target vegetation types and fire histories and to exclude areas subjected to logging in the past 20 years. The study area was further confined to 'Asset Protection' and 'StrategicWildfireModeration'fire-management zones (DSE [2006\)](#page-8-0) because these areas have a high likelihood of complete burn coverage. Sites were selected within the following classes representing time since the last fire: 0–3 years, 4–10 years, 11–20 years, 21–40 years and 41 + years. These classes were informed by the timing of growth stages identified byCheal ([2010\)](#page-7-0) for thethree target forest types in relation to fire, and undefined after 40 years because of the limits of DSE fire records. Areas were identified with all fireage-class combinations for each target forest type located within close proximity and with similar environmental conditions (water availability, sun exposure, geographic spread, elevation and aspect) for each species, so as not to confound the responses of the plants to fire with their response to these factors. ## *Species selection* Shrubs were selected for study because they are prominent in forest communities and are easily identified, and obligate seeders were selected because they are most susceptible to local extinctions from inappropriate fire regimes. These species are killed by fire, recruitment is by seed only, and timing of fires can exhaust their seed supplies before plants reach reproductive maturity. Common species were chosen to enable a good representation of the typical vegetation communities (Cornelissen *et al*. [2003\)](#page-8-0), and because they were detectable in most fire-age classes. Potential species for the study were identified from the Victorian database of vascular flora (DSE [2010](#page-8-0)*d*) and subsequent field searches, to identify those species with adequate representation at a range of fire-age sites. Species were selected and categorised according to their mode of persistence following fire (obligate seeder), seedbank type (soil or canopy), length of juvenile period (germination to reestablishment of seedbank adequate to replace parent plants) and individual plant lifespan (Table [1](#page-2-0)). These factors have been used in classification schemes that predict the response of plants to fire (Whelan *et al*. [2002](#page-9-0)). Plant functional-type categories used in the study have been adapted from Keith *et al*.([2007\)](#page-8-0), which is a simplified version of the vital-attribute scheme of Noble and Slatyer [\(1980](#page-8-0)). Estimates of the responses of individual species in these categories were derived from expert opinion about Victorian plant vital attributes (DSE [2010](#page-8-0)*e*). #### *Sampling design* The number of individuals sampled was a balance between obtaining enough replicates to capture the variability of the traits of interest and sampling enough species of interest (Cornelissen *et al*. [2003\)](#page-8-0). We followed Cornelissen *et al*. ([2003\)](#page-8-0), who recommended that at least 10 individuals at each site should be measured for plant height (which is more variable than many other plant traits). Individuals were selected using a transect method, modified from Cornelissen *et al*.([2003\)](#page-8-0). Within each fire-age site, a 100-m transect was located where the target species were observed, at least 20 m from a road or track, and {2} ######## PDF PAGE 4 ######## searched for 10 m on either side. Ten individuals of each target species, haphazardly selected along the transect, were measured at each site. Where species were in low numbers, only five individuals were measured, and where there were fewer than 10 individuals along transects, we searched within the boundaries of the fire-age site. If different age cohorts were present, only the oldest cohorts (largest individuals) were measured. We sampled species at 17 sites representing 14 different time periods since fire (Table 2) and measured 325 plants. ## *Measurement variables* Data were collected on flowers and seeds because these represent two stages of reproduction. Flower counts were made for all eight target species, and seed counts for four species, between July 2010 and January 2011 and in December 2011. Seed counts for *Banksia spinulosa* and *Pomaderris aspera* were made on the same plants as for the flowers, but for *Hakea decurrens* and *Acacia verticillata*, these counts were on different individuals. The number of flowers per plant was estimated by using sample units to scale up data (Kirmse and Norton [1985](#page-8-0); West [2009](#page-9-0)). At each fire-age site, a branching unit comprising stems, leaves and flowers was selected for each plant, and then the number of such units bearing flowers was estimated for that plant. The number of flowers on a unit was then counted. For species with more than one flower per inflorescence, the number of flowers per inflorescence was counted and then multiplied by the number of inflorescences on a unit. The number of flowers per unit was finally multiplied by the number of units per plant to obtain an estimate for the whole plant. For *Banksia spinulosa*, the number of inflorescences was counted and then multiplied by an estimate of 100flowers, because of the difficulty in counting individual flowers. The number of seeds per plant was estimated in two ways. For the serotinous (canopy-seed) species, the total number of unopened infructescences was counted, because these are considered to represent viable seed (Enright and Goldblum [1999](#page-8-0)). As in other studies, we assumed that after release, seeds of the woody-fruited Proteaceae generally last only until the next wet season (Lamont and Groom [1998;](#page-8-0) Campbell *et al*. [2012](#page-7-0)). However, some fruits may stay unopened for several years after maturity. The number of fruits counted on a plant was multiplied by the estimated number of seeds per fruit. Average seed numbers per fruit for *Banksia spinulosa* were derived from collection of five fruits at each fire-age site, whereas an assumption of two seeds per fruit was made for *Hakea decurrens* (Barker *et al*. [1996](#page-7-0)). For the species with soil seedbanks, sample units comprising stems, leaves and infructescences were used, followed by scaling up of data, as outlined for the flower measurements (Kirmse and Norton [1985;](#page-8-0) West [2009\)](#page-9-0). Estimating flower and seed numbers was more difficult for larger plants, and these results are likely to have greater errors. The methodology to estimate flower and seed numbers was chosen because it enabled data to be collected fairly rapidly in one season, which may be useful for management-oriented research. Methods used in some other studies of reproductive maturity periods of Proteaceae species have used counts of flowers and seeds on permanently marked plants over several seasons (e.g. Kraaij *et al*. [2013;](#page-8-0) Enright and Goldblum [1999](#page-8-0)). ## *Data analysis* The purpose of the analysis was to build quantitative models of each species measured, in the form of response curves that could be used to understand reproductive maturity patterns following fire. Non-linear regression models were fitted to the relationships between reproduction (response variables) and time-since-fire (explanatory variable). These enabled comparisons to be made with current assumptions about times to reproductive maturity for the species. Flower and seed numbers were at times very large and skewed to the right, and so numbers were log-transformed. An increment of either 1 or 10 was added before transforming because of the presence of zeros. Gompertz growth curves were used to model the relationship with time-since-fire, using the equation *y* ¼ q1expðexpðq2 q3*x*ÞÞ: **Table 1. Various curves were tested for their fit to the relationship, where there is known to be a slow initial response, then a rapid increase followed by a plateau. The sigmoid curve of the Gompertz function (Tjørve [2003\)](#page-9-0) gave the best fit for most species. In the equation above, q1 is the upper asymptote, q2 sets the displacement in the vertical direction, and q3 represents the growth rate. The models were fitted using the statistical package Minitab 16 (Minitab Inc. [2010](#page-8-0)). The variable 'time-since-fire' was determined by the year of fire, not by the classes used for the stratification of sites. Sites up to ~15 years post-fire could be recognised confidently as being completely burnt because of the uniform regeneration of plants. The precise number of years since fire was unknown at the oldest sites for all species measured, because detailed fire records date only back to 1970. An estimated time-since-fire was assigned to these sites on the basis of the last major wildfire recorded in the areas. The final step in the analyses of each species was to predict thresholds for the reproductive variables. The fitted equations from the non-linear regressions were used to estimate the value of response variables for future observations. Predictions were made for the mean time-since-fire that an average plant takes to exceed 80% of its maximum annual flower production (eight species) or 80% of its seed production (three species only) on the log scale. Maximum production was taken as the upper asymptote of the fitted response curve. The threshold of 80% of the estimated asymptote was chosen for biological reasons. For example, at 50%, most species had few or no plants with flowers, whereas at 80%, all species had flowering individuals. Given that flowering is being used to infer reproductive maturity, this is more useful. Asymptotes for *Pomaderris aspera* had very large confidence intervals for both flowers and seeds, because of the model being based on only three non-zero time-since-fire points, and hence predictions were not made or fitted curves presented for this species. ## **Results** ## *Relationships of reproductive variables to time-since-fire* The eight shrub species displayed similarly patterned trajectories of reproductive output, although their timing differed considerably. The fitted relationships for flowers and seeds showed a rapid increase in production, then a plateau, with the exception of *Pomaderris aspera*. Asymptotes for each species represented the annual flower or seed production for an average plant. Most of the variation in the response variables was explained by the explanatory variable. The flower models had *R*2 -values between 72% and 94% (Table 3), whereas the seed models had lower *R*2 values of between 45% and 85% (Table 3). The highest maximum flower numbers were recorded for species with soil seedbanks and presumed long juvenile periods (*Prostanthera lasianthos* and *Pomaderris aspera*) (Fig. [1](#page-4-0), Table [4\)](#page-5-0). Species with soil seedbanks and presumed moderate juvenile periods (*Acacia oxycedrus*,*Acacia verticillata*, *Pultenaea scabra* and *Olearia lirata*) had fewer flowers at their maximum production (Fig. [1,](#page-4-0) Table [4](#page-5-0)). Species with canopy seedbanks (*Banksia spinulosa* and *Hakea decurrens*) had the lowest maximum flower numbers (Fig. [1](#page-4-0), Table [4](#page-5-0)). The lowest estimated maximum seed production was also for species with canopy seedbanks, being 470 for *Banksia spinulosa* and five for *Hakea decurrens* (Fig. [2,](#page-5-0) Table [4\)](#page-5-0). In contrast, the maximum estimated seed production for the soil seedbank species *Acacia verticillata* was 2600 (Fig. [2,](#page-5-0) Table [4](#page-5-0)). # *Predictions for flowering and seeding thresholds* Predictions about the timing of flowering thresholds after fire were made from the data models (Table [4](#page-5-0)). Species with soil seedbanks and presumed moderate juvenile periods exceeded 80% of predicted mean flower asymptotes within the shortest time-since-fire. Species with soil seedbanks and presumed long juvenile periods exceeded 80% flower asymptotes in the longest periods since fire. Species with canopy seedbanks were intermediate in time to 80% of maximum flower production. Predictions for seed-production thresholds were made for the two species with canopy-stored seed, and one species with soilstored seed (Table [4](#page-5-0)). For the two serotinous species, the gap between the predicted 80% asymptotes for flowers and seeds was 7 years for *Banksia spinulosa* and two years for *Hakea decurrens*. The species with soil-stored seed and a moderate juvenile period (*Acacia verticillata*) exceeded the 80% seed asymptote 1 year after flowers. # **Discussion** #### *Reproductive maturity times* There are few published data on times to reproductive maturity after fire for Australian shrubs. Our results on the relationships between reproductive responses and decadal time-spans after fire add to the current knowledge of fire intervals needed for population maintenance of eight obligate-seeding shrub species in south-eastern Australia. The data models either confirmed or extended the hypothesised timing of reproductive maturity (Tables [1,](#page-2-0) [4](#page-5-0)) for the species used in this study to represent four plant functional types (shrubs with canopy-stored seed and moderate or long juvenile periods, shrubs with soil-stored seed and moderate or long juvenile periods). For two species (*Banksia spinulosa* and *Prostanthera lasianthos*), existing assumptions were shown to underestimate the time to reach reproductive maturity by up to 10 years. Times to reproductive maturity for the species with serotinous seedbanks were longer than initially anticipated.
