Early reproductive maturity is a recognised floral trait in Australian acacias (Gibson *et al*. [2011\)](#page-8-0). 18 19 However, for one of the species with soil-stored seed and a long juvenile period our data indicated that time to reproductive maturity was longer than expected. *Prostanthera lasianthos* exceeded the 80% flowering asymptote (on the log scale) at 18 years. No published data were found on reproductive maturity times for this species. Although predictions were not made for time to 80% maximum flowering for *Pomaderris aspera*, flowering was first recorded at a site that had not had fire for 11 years, suggesting a long juvenile period. This is supported by a study of the soil seedbank in *Eucalyptus regnans* forest in Victoria, where seeds of *Pomaderris aspera* were not present at sites up to 18 years post-fire (Wang [1997](#page-9-0)). 20 21 The use of chronosequences to make inferences about fire-interval thresholds adequate for reproductive maturity has limitations. Flower and seed production can differ among years and sites owing to variations in weather and nutrients (Auld and Myerscough [1986;](#page-7-0) Copland and Whelan [1989](#page-8-0)), and fluctuating levels of pollination and herbivory (Vaughton [1990;](#page-9-0) Vaughton [1991](#page-9-0)). In particular, the decade of below-average rainfall preceding data collection may have influenced observed responses to fire intervals and also growth and reproduction. Our models could be verified by replicating measurements of the species at other sites, and including additional years of field data. 22 23 # *Seed production* 24 25 Maximum estimated seed numbers varied greatly among species. Our data on *Banksia spinulosa* var. *cunninghamii* predicted the asymptotic number of seeds per adult plant to be 470, although the actual seed numbers may be lower because of insect predation and other factors. We could find no comparative research on this taxon, but in a study of *B. spinulosa* var. *neoanglica* in New South Wales, a mean of 137.6 seeds per adult plant was recorded (Vaughton [1990](#page-9-0)). Our results for *Hakea decurrens* predicted the asymptotic number of seeds per adult plant to be five. In contrast, the study of *H. decurrens* recruitment after fire in western Victoria estimated the mean number of viable seeds released per adult to be 42.7 (Enright and Goldblum [1999](#page-8-0)). The low numbers of seeds in our study may be due to granivory by birds, as the remains of infructescence stems were often observed on *H. decurrens*, and high levels of granivory are common on the woody-fruited Proteaceae because of the highly nutritious seeds (Lamont and Groom [1998](#page-8-0)). An additional factor in our study of *H. decurrens* compared with that in western Victoria was the collection of data at the end of a 13-year period of below-average rainfall, which was likely to have reduced seed production. 26 27 In comparison to species with canopy-stored seed, the species with soil seedbanks had much larger numbers of seed produced per plant. For example, the maximum estimated seed number was ~2600 for *Acacia verticillata*, and high seed numbers are typical of acacias (Gibson *et al*. [2011\)](#page-8-0). 28 29 Higher seed output is often related to lower seed mass because of trade-offs in resource allocation (Henery and Westoby [2001;](#page-8-0) Campbell *et al*. [2012](#page-7-0)). In our study, *Pomaderris aspera* had the largest seed output and the smallest mean seed mass (0.56 g: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens [2012\)](#page-8-0). Conversely, *Hakea decurrens* had the smallest seed output and the largest mean seed mass (25.2 g: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens [2012](#page-8-0)). However mean seed masses for *Banksia spinulosa* (13.45 g: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens [2012](#page-8-0)) and *Acacia verticillata* (11.49 g: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens [2012](#page-8-0)) were fairly close although there was a large difference between the seed outputs of these species. This may be explained by the higher accessory costs of fruit structures affecting seed production in *Banksia spinulosa* (Henery and Westoby [2001](#page-8-0)). 30 31 ## *Recruitment* 32 33 Seed production is not a direct indicator of successful recruitment (Kraaij *et al*. [2013](#page-8-0)), and measurement of recruitment success would strengthen results from our study. Seedling establishment and population trajectories are limited by granivory, herbivory and unsuitable weather and habitat conditions (Bell [1999;](#page-7-0) Lamont *et al*. [2007](#page-8-0)). 34 35 Obligate-seeder species with canopy seed storage are reliant on successful germination of seeds after adult plants are killed by fire for population persistence (Noble and Slatyer [1980](#page-8-0)). A review of woody-fruited Proteaceae in Western Australia reported that following fire, typically less than 5% of seeds become seedlings that survive the first summer (Lamont and Groom [1998](#page-8-0)). Observations of *Banksia spinulosa* at our study sites indicated that seedling regeneration is low after fires. Seed numbers per adult plant for *Hakea decurrens* are low; however, in the western Victorian study of this species by Enright and Goldblum ([1999\)](#page-8-0) an estimated 22.8% of seeds became seedlings. The large seed mass of *H. decurrens* is likely to contribute to high germination and establishment success (Lamont and Groom [1998\)](#page-8-0). Recruitment in the absence of fire has also been reported for *H. decurrens*, associated with adult mortality (Enright and Goldblum [1999](#page-8-0)). Multi-age stands of *B. spinulosa* have been observed at our study sites, suggesting inter-fire recruitment, and the gradual seed-release mechanism that enables this in other *Banksia* species has been recorded in a study of serotinous shrubs in high-rainfall areas of New South Wales (Clarke *et al*. [2010\)](#page-7-0). In the South African study of Proteaceae (Kraaij *et al*. Early reproductive maturity is a recognised floral trait in Australian acacias (Gibson *et al*. [2011\)](#page-8-0). However, for one of the species with soil-stored seed and a long juvenile period our data indicated that time to reproductive maturity was longer than expected. *Prostanthera lasianthos* exceeded the 80% flowering asymptote (on the log scale) at 18 years. No published data were found on reproductive maturity times for this species. Although predictions were not made for time to 80% maximum flowering for *Pomaderris aspera*, flowering was first recorded at a site that had not had fire for 11 years, suggesting a long juvenile period. This is supported by a study of the soil seedbank in *Eucalyptus regnans* forest in Victoria, where seeds of *Pomaderris aspera* were not present at sites up to 18 years post-fire (Wang [1997](#page-9-0)). The use of chronosequences to make inferences about fire-interval thresholds adequate for reproductive maturity has limitations. Flower and seed production can differ among years and sites owing to variations in weather and nutrients (Auld and Myerscough [1986;](#page-7-0) Copland and Whelan [1989](#page-8-0)), and fluctuating levels of pollination and herbivory (Vaughton [1990;](#page-9-0) Vaughton [1991](#page-9-0)). In particular, the decade of below-average rainfall preceding data collection may have influenced observed responses to fire intervals and also growth and reproduction. Our models could be verified by replicating measurements of the species at other sites, and including additional years of field data. # *Seed production* Maximum estimated seed numbers varied greatly among species. Our data on *Banksia spinulosa* var. *cunninghamii* predicted the asymptotic number of seeds per adult plant to be 470, although the actual seed numbers may be lower because of insect predation and other factors. We could find no comparative research on this taxon, but in a study of *B. spinulosa* var. *neoanglica* in New South Wales, a mean of 137.6 seeds per adult plant was recorded (Vaughton [1990](#page-9-0)). Our results for *Hakea decurrens* predicted the asymptotic number of seeds per adult plant to be five. In contrast, the study of *H. decurrens* recruitment after fire in western Victoria estimated the mean number of viable seeds released per adult to be 42.7 (Enright and Goldblum [1999](#page-8-0)). The low numbers of seeds in our study may be due to granivory by birds, as the remains of infructescence stems were often observed on *H. decurrens*, and high levels of granivory are common on the woody-fruited Proteaceae because of the highly nutritious seeds (Lamont and Groom [1998](#page-8-0)). An additional factor in our study of *H. decurrens* compared with that in western Victoria was the collection of data at the end of a 13-year period of below-average rainfall, which was likely to have reduced seed production. In comparison to species with canopy-stored seed, the species with soil seedbanks had much larger numbers of seed produced per plant. For example, the maximum estimated seed number was ~2600 for *Acacia verticillata*, and high seed numbers are typical of acacias (Gibson *et al*. [2011\)](#page-8-0). Higher seed output is often related to lower seed mass because of trade-offs in resource allocation (Henery and Westoby [2001;](#page-8-0) Campbell *et al*. [2012](#page-7-0)). In our study, *Pomaderris aspera* had the largest seed output and the smallest mean seed mass (0.56 g: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens [2012\)](#page-8-0). Conversely, *Hakea decurrens* had the smallest seed output and the largest mean seed mass (25.2 g: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens [2012](#page-8-0)). However mean seed masses for *Banksia spinulosa* (13.45 g: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens [2012](#page-8-0)) and *Acacia verticillata* (11.49 g: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens [2012](#page-8-0)) were fairly close although there was a large difference between the seed outputs of these species. This may be explained by the higher accessory costs of fruit structures affecting seed production in *Banksia spinulosa* (Henery and Westoby [2001](#page-8-0)). ## *Recruitment* Seed production is not a direct indicator of successful recruitment (Kraaij *et al*. [2013](#page-8-0)), and measurement of recruitment success would strengthen results from our study. Seedling establishment and population trajectories are limited by granivory, herbivory and unsuitable weather and habitat conditions (Bell [1999;](#page-7-0) Lamont *et al*. [2007](#page-8-0)). Obligate-seeder species with canopy seed storage are reliant on successful germination of seeds after adult plants are killed by fire for population persistence (Noble and Slatyer [1980](#page-8-0)). A review of woody-fruited Proteaceae in Western Australia reported that following fire, typically less than 5% of seeds become seedlings that survive the first summer (Lamont and Groom [1998](#page-8-0)). Observations of *Banksia spinulosa* at our study sites indicated that seedling regeneration is low after fires. Seed numbers per adult plant for *Hakea decurrens* are low; however, in the western Victorian study of this species by Enright and Goldblum ([1999\)](#page-8-0) an estimated 22.8% of seeds became seedlings. The large seed mass of *H. decurrens* is likely to contribute to high germination and establishment success (Lamont and Groom [1998\)](#page-8-0). Recruitment in the absence of fire has also been reported for *H. decurrens*, associated with adult mortality (Enright and Goldblum [1999](#page-8-0)). [2010\)](#page-7-0). In the South African study of Proteaceae (Kraaij *et al*. 1	## n_pages=9
2	
3	######## PDF PAGE 1 ########
4	{0}
5	
6	######## PDF PAGE 2 ########
7	Research article
8	
9	# The importance of fire season when managing threatened plant species: A long-term case-study of a rare Leucopogon species (Ericaceae)
10	
11	Mark K.J. Ooi
12	
13	Centre for Ecosystem Science, School of Biological, Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of New South Wales, UNSW, Sydney, NSW, 2052, Australia
14	
15	#### ARTICLE INFO
16	
17	#### Keywords:
18	
19	Fire ecology
20	
21	Plant functional traits
22	
23	Fire interval squeeze Mediterranean versus non-Mediterranean
24	
25	climates
26	
27	Physiological dormancy
28	
29	Seed ecology
30	
31	#### ABSTRACT
32	
33	Implemented burns are a primary source of fire in natural systems and occur outside of the wildfire season. However, the impacts of fire season shift on native plant species are rarely studied. Understanding fire season effects are particularly important for managing threatened species, which are often the focus of managed burns. To assess the impacts of fire seasonality and identify potential limiting traits, I studied the threatened Leucopogon exolasius and two common congeners, all of which persist via fire-driven population dynamics. All species were monitored over a 16 year period to assess seedling survival, growth and primary juvenile period after fire. For L. exolasius and the common L. esquamatus, comparisons of survival, growth and maturation were made after winter and summer fires, to assess the effects of season of burn. A key difference was found in primary juvenile period, which was exceptionally long for L. exolasius (> 11 years for 80% of the population to flower) compared to the common congeners (3.2–7.57 years). Seasonal seed dormancy mechanisms meant that winter fires delayed emergence, leading to increases in primary juvenile period for both species. A long primary juvenile period may limit L. exolasius population persistence because plants are more likely to be killed by subsequent fire before maturation, while seasonal dormancy cues is a trait that would exacerbate the effects of this interval squeeze. In fire-prone systems, fire frequency is the key factor assumed to drive persistence, however, interactions with fire season can influence recruitment success. There are scant data on recruitment variation in response to fire seasonality, a factor that may have broad implications for rare and common species with seasonal germination requirements.
34	
35	# 1. Introduction
36	
37	Fire regime components include frequency, intensity (or severity) and season [\(Whelan, 1995; Hammill et al., 2016](#page-7-0)). The impact of fire frequency has been the focus of numerous studies, with a decrease in the intervals between fires limiting to obligate-seeding shrub species with long primary juvenile periods (e.g. [Santana et al., 2014](#page-6-0)). Projected changes to climate could exacerbate this interval squeeze [\(Enright](#page-6-1) [et al., 2015; Fairman et al., 2016\)](#page-6-1). Nevertheless, other fire regime factors, such as season and severity, can also undoubtedly affect plant population persistence and recovery (e.g. [Ooi et al., 2004, 2014; Liu](#page-6-2) [et al., 2005; Ooi, 2010; Céspedes et al., 2014; Hammill et al., 2016\)](#page-6-2) but there are few empirical studies measuring these effects over long time periods. Furthermore, managed burns are a primary source of fire in natural systems and are shifting fire season away from the peak time of natural wildfire. Understanding fire seasonality effects are particularly important for managing threatened species, however, the impacts of fire season shift on native plat populations are rarely studied.
38	
39	In many fire-prone regions, fire causes plant mortality and
40	
41	successful recruitment is restricted to the post-fire environment. For perennial species from such habitats, this means that long-term studies are required to understand population dynamics, because inter-fire periods can last for decades [\(Whelan, 1995](#page-7-0); [Menges and Quintana](#page-6-3) [Ascencio, 2004](#page-6-3)), and shifts between life-history stages may run over similar time scales. For example, gaining an estimate of primary juvenile period is important for determining the fire frequency that a species may be able to persist under ([Keith, 1996\)](#page-6-4). This can take from between two and 10 (or more) years for species in areas such as temperate Australia ([Benson, 1985; Burrows et al., 2008; Kubiak, 2009](#page-6-5)), where fire return intervals range from approximately seven to 30 years ([Bradstock and Gill, 2001; Lucas et al., 2007](#page-6-6)). Shorter term correlates of these measurements, such as size-class distributions for population age structure (e.g. [Ooi et al., 2007\)](#page-6-7), may be more easily achievable but do not provide the necessary resolution for parameterising predictive population models. However, long-term demographic studies, beyond a few years, are extremely rare.
42	
43	Demographic studies are valuable for both the management of rare and threatened plant species, and predicting persistence [\(Schemske](#page-6-8)
44	
45	E-mail address: [mark.ooi@unsw.edu.au.](mailto:mark.ooi@unsw.edu.au)
46	
47	{1}
48	
49	######## PDF PAGE 3 ########
50	[et al., 1994; Menges et al., 2006; Keith et al., 2008](#page-6-8)). Comparative studies that investigate the biology of ecologically similar rare species and common congeners can help to detect possible limiting factors within the rare species [\(Kunin and Gaston, 1993; Bevill and Louda,](#page-6-9) [1999; Mattana et al., 2010](#page-6-9)). Although it is unlikely that generalisations exist regarding the causes of rarity [\(Gaston, 1994\)](#page-6-10), insights gained from data collected in comparative studies are particularly useful for the conservation of threatened species and the detection of broader ecological patterns [\(Bevill and, Louda, 1999; Lavergne et al., 2004\)](#page-6-11). These broader patterns may help to identify traits that could be limiting under changing environmental conditions, for both rare and common species, and provide insights to the evolutionary development of specific traits.
51	
52	Regeneration from seeds is necessary for short-term regeneration and long-term persistence in fire-prone regions ([Whelan, 1995; Bond](#page-7-0) [and van Wilgen, 1996; Ooi et al., 2014](#page-7-0)). Plants that do not resprout, known as obligate-seeding species, are particularly dependent on recruitment from stored seed. As such, critical factors for the persistence of these species, and potential causes of rarity, are often related to seed ecology and recruitment stages [\(Burne et al., 2003; Risberg and](#page-6-12) [Granström, 2014\)](#page-6-12). Additionally, fire is the predominant driver of plant population dynamics in these regions and aspects of the fire regime itself needs to be considered as a potential contributor to rarity ([Burne](#page-6-12) [et al., 2003](#page-6-12)).
53	
54	An increased use of managed fires, in addition to climate change, is causing a shift from current peak fire seasons, in addition to increasing the frequency of fire [\(McLoughlin, 1998; Williams et al., 2001; Cary](#page-6-13) [et al., 2006; Enright et al., 2015\)](#page-6-13). The threats caused by altered fire regimes may not only affect the persistence of those plant species that are already threatened with extinction, but also of many common species. Such common species may be at risk because they possess traits that have little plasticity in relation to projected changes. The most inflexible traits are likely to be those that are not adapted to current environmental conditions, but have ecologically fit well enough to have persisted. Evidence suggests that species composition within ecological communities may be strongly influenced by the relative abilities of species to cope with climate-driven changes ([Suttle et al., 2006\)](#page-6-14).
55	
56	There is growing evidence that rates of extinction of plant species are increasing, across local and regional scales ([Thomas et al., 2004a;](#page-6-15) [Thuiller et al., 2005](#page-6-15)). This rate is influenced by human population growth, and the associated escalating demands on resources and climate-driven changes ([Gaston, 2005; Hahs et al., 2009](#page-6-16)). Species most at risk by the threat of extinction are those that are already rare, and therefore already limited in abundance and/or distribution [\(Gaston,](#page-6-10) [1994; Wilson et al., 2004](#page-6-10)). Understanding the possible anthropogenic and ecological causes of rarity are therefore crucial to designing and implementing conservation actions. In this study, I investigated postfire recruitment and development over a 16 year period for the species Leucopogon exolasius (F. Muell.) F. Muell. ex Benth. and the closely related common congeners L. setiger R. Br. and L. esquamatus R. Br. The demographic parameters following regeneration were compared between species in order to determine any potential causes of rarity for one of them, the threatened L. exolasius. All three species inhabit the fire-prone temperate sandstone vegetation around the Sydney region in south-eastern Australia, occurring on similar soil types and in similar micro-climates. The vegetation here is adapted to fire and there is a mean natural wildfire return interval ranging from approximately 14 to 20 years, a similar interval to shrublands in Mediterranean-climate regions in southwestern Australia [\(Miller and Murphy, 2018](#page-6-17)). Fires occur primarily in the hot late spring and summer periods (approximately November to February). The Sydney sandstone basin is one of several centres of high species richness and endemism on the Australian continent ([Crisp et al., 2001](#page-6-18)), but also highly urbanised. Prescribed fires are therefore implemented regularly to reduce fuel loads and protect assets, as well as for ecological purposes such as the conservation of biodiversity [\(Penman et al., 2011\)](#page-6-19).
57	
58	Because limited abundance or distribution of plant species are
59	
60	unlikely to be attributed to a single factor, investigations into several critical biological traits and life-history stages are the most likely to highlight limiting processes [\(Rabinowitz et al., 1984; Bevill and Louda,](#page-6-20) [1999\)](#page-6-20). Part of the benefit of using a small number of species in a comparative study, is that a larger number of factors may be examined with relative ease, and species can also be more easily selected to control for phylogenetic relatedness [\(Kunin and Gaston, 1993; Walck](#page-6-9) [et al., 2001\)](#page-6-9). Additionally, understanding demographic responses to environmental disturbance is crucial in habitats situated on the urban interface where the numbers of implemented fires are increasing ([McLoughlin, 1998\)](#page-6-13) and climate change is projected to drive changes to fire season and frequency [\(Williams et al., 2001; Cary et al., 2006;](#page-7-1) [Enright et al., 2015](#page-7-1)). I therefore assessed the demographic responses measured in the context of the fire regime to identify potential limiting traits. Specifically, I wanted to address the following questions:
61	
62	- (1) How do key life-history stages of the three Leucopogon study species differ, and what are their responses to the fire regime, particularly season?
63	- (2) Can predicted changes to the fire regime potentially affect the persistence of the rare or common species studied?
64	- (3) Are there any identifiable factors that limit Leucopogon exolasius?
65	
66	# 2. Materials and methods
67	
68	# 2.1. Study species and sites
69	
70	The Ericaceae family occurs in a number of habitats throughout the world floras including in South Africa and the Mediterranean Basin ([Ojeda et al., 1997\)](#page-6-21). In Australia, members compromise a significant part of the understorey in fire-prone plant communities. Leucopogon (Ericaceae) is a large genus consisting of about 230 species. This fireprone region of south-eastern Australia contains approximately 2000 plant species [\(Auld et al., 2000](#page-6-22)), and unlike its Mediterranean-type climate counterparts, has an aseasonal rainfall climate with no pronounced dry season, which may have consequences for the post-fire recovery of species with innate seasonal germination requirements ([Ooi, 2010](#page-6-23)). The three study species are all obligate-seeding woody shrubs with soil-stored seed banks ([Ooi et al., 2006a,b; 2007\)](#page-6-24). Although they do not co-occur at the same sites, they inhabit adjoining heath and woodland vegetation types, and have overlapping ranges. Leucopogon fruit are drupes and fresh exocarps of both L. exolasius and L. setiger are fleshy, while the endocarp is hard and lignified. Leucopogon esquamatus exocarp is papery and the endocarp comparatively more fibrous than hard [\(Ooi et al., 2006a\)](#page-6-24).
71	
72	Leucopogon exolasius is an erect shrub that grows to approximately 2 m tall, and is a threatened species listed as 'vulnerable' both under the national Australian Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act (1999), and under the state of New South Wales (NSW) Threatened Species Conservation Act (1995). The species is endemic to the southern Sydney region of NSW and is restricted to approximately 14 known populations. It occurs in woodlands, and is restricted particularly to riverbank areas punctuated with outcropping sandstone. Leucopogon setiger, morphologically very similar to L. exolasius, is an erect shrub also approximately 2 m tall, and is distributed more widely ([Table 1](#page-2-0)), extending from the central western slopes of NSW to the coast. It is found in woodlands and open forest. Leucopogon esquamatus is a slender shrub, which grows to approximately 1 m tall. It is also widespread, occurring from the coast to the mountains (as for L. setiger), but extending south into the states of Victoria and Tasmania ([Table 1](#page-2-0)). It occurs in heath, woodlands and open forests. Taxonomy follows [Harden](#page-6-25) [\(1992\).](#page-6-25) Geographic distribution of each species were calculated using [IUCN \(2012\)](#page-6-26) criteria for extent of occurrence, which is defined as the area contained within the shortest continuous imaginary boundary which can be drawn to encompass all known sites of occurrence of a species.
73	
74	{2}
75	
76	######## PDF PAGE 4 ########
77	# 2.2. Background data
78	
79	Reproductive attributes, including fecundity, seed viability, seed bank longevity, seed dormancy, germination, seedling survival and growth were collated from the literature and compared between all three species to identify limiting factors. Information on the habitat and substrate preferences of the study species, population structure, seed dormancy, seedling emergence phenology, seed bank longevity and seed viability were also included.
80	
81	# 2.3. Study sites, habitat attributes and plant fecundity
82

# The importance of fire season when managing threatened plant species: A long-term case-study of a rare Leucopogon species (Ericaceae)

Mark K.J. Ooi

Centre for Ecosystem Science, School of Biological, Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of New South Wales, UNSW, Sydney, NSW, 2052, Australia

#### ARTICLE INFO

#### Keywords:

Fire ecology

Plant functional traits

Fire interval squeeze Mediterranean versus non-Mediterranean

climates

Physiological dormancy

Seed ecology

#### ABSTRACT

Implemented burns are a primary source of fire in natural systems and occur outside of the wildfire season. However, the impacts of fire season shift on native plant species are rarely studied. Understanding fire season effects are particularly important for managing threatened species, which are often the focus of managed burns. To assess the impacts of fire seasonality and identify potential limiting traits, I studied the threatened Leucopogon exolasius and two common congeners, all of which persist via fire-driven population dynamics. All species were monitored over a 16 year period to assess seedling survival, growth and primary juvenile period after fire. For L. exolasius and the common L. esquamatus, comparisons of survival, growth and maturation were made after winter and summer fires, to assess the effects of season of burn. A key difference was found in primary juvenile period, which was exceptionally long for L. exolasius (> 11 years for 80% of the population to flower) compared to the common congeners (3.2–7.57 years). Seasonal seed dormancy mechanisms meant that winter fires delayed emergence, leading to increases in primary juvenile period for both species. A long primary juvenile period may limit L. exolasius population persistence because plants are more likely to be killed by subsequent fire before maturation, while seasonal dormancy cues is a trait that would exacerbate the effects of this interval squeeze. In fire-prone systems, fire frequency is the key factor assumed to drive persistence, however, interactions with fire season can influence recruitment success. There are scant data on recruitment variation in response to fire seasonality, a factor that may have broad implications for rare and common species with seasonal germination requirements.

# 1. Introduction

Fire regime components include frequency, intensity (or severity) and season [\(Whelan, 1995; Hammill et al., 2016](#page-7-0)). The impact of fire frequency has been the focus of numerous studies, with a decrease in the intervals between fires limiting to obligate-seeding shrub species with long primary juvenile periods (e.g. [Santana et al., 2014](#page-6-0)). Projected changes to climate could exacerbate this interval squeeze [\(Enright](#page-6-1) [et al., 2015; Fairman et al., 2016\)](#page-6-1). Nevertheless, other fire regime factors, such as season and severity, can also undoubtedly affect plant population persistence and recovery (e.g. [Ooi et al., 2004, 2014; Liu](#page-6-2) [et al., 2005; Ooi, 2010; Céspedes et al., 2014; Hammill et al., 2016\)](#page-6-2) but there are few empirical studies measuring these effects over long time periods. Furthermore, managed burns are a primary source of fire in natural systems and are shifting fire season away from the peak time of natural wildfire. Understanding fire seasonality effects are particularly important for managing threatened species, however, the impacts of fire season shift on native plat populations are rarely studied.

In many fire-prone regions, fire causes plant mortality and

successful recruitment is restricted to the post-fire environment. For perennial species from such habitats, this means that long-term studies are required to understand population dynamics, because inter-fire periods can last for decades [\(Whelan, 1995](#page-7-0); [Menges and Quintana](#page-6-3) [Ascencio, 2004](#page-6-3)), and shifts between life-history stages may run over similar time scales. For example, gaining an estimate of primary juvenile period is important for determining the fire frequency that a species may be able to persist under ([Keith, 1996\)](#page-6-4). This can take from between two and 10 (or more) years for species in areas such as temperate Australia ([Benson, 1985; Burrows et al., 2008; Kubiak, 2009](#page-6-5)), where fire return intervals range from approximately seven to 30 years ([Bradstock and Gill, 2001; Lucas et al., 2007](#page-6-6)). Shorter term correlates of these measurements, such as size-class distributions for population age structure (e.g. [Ooi et al., 2007\)](#page-6-7), may be more easily achievable but do not provide the necessary resolution for parameterising predictive population models. However, long-term demographic studies, beyond a few years, are extremely rare.

Demographic studies are valuable for both the management of rare and threatened plant species, and predicting persistence [\(Schemske](#page-6-8)

{1}

######## PDF PAGE 3 ########
[et al., 1994; Menges et al., 2006; Keith et al., 2008](#page-6-8)). Comparative studies that investigate the biology of ecologically similar rare species and common congeners can help to detect possible limiting factors within the rare species [\(Kunin and Gaston, 1993; Bevill and Louda,](#page-6-9) [1999; Mattana et al., 2010](#page-6-9)). Although it is unlikely that generalisations exist regarding the causes of rarity [\(Gaston, 1994\)](#page-6-10), insights gained from data collected in comparative studies are particularly useful for the conservation of threatened species and the detection of broader ecological patterns [\(Bevill and, Louda, 1999; Lavergne et al., 2004\)](#page-6-11). These broader patterns may help to identify traits that could be limiting under changing environmental conditions, for both rare and common species, and provide insights to the evolutionary development of specific traits.

Regeneration from seeds is necessary for short-term regeneration and long-term persistence in fire-prone regions ([Whelan, 1995; Bond](#page-7-0) [and van Wilgen, 1996; Ooi et al., 2014](#page-7-0)). Plants that do not resprout, known as obligate-seeding species, are particularly dependent on recruitment from stored seed. As such, critical factors for the persistence of these species, and potential causes of rarity, are often related to seed ecology and recruitment stages [\(Burne et al., 2003; Risberg and](#page-6-12) [Granström, 2014\)](#page-6-12). Additionally, fire is the predominant driver of plant population dynamics in these regions and aspects of the fire regime itself needs to be considered as a potential contributor to rarity ([Burne](#page-6-12) [et al., 2003](#page-6-12)).

An increased use of managed fires, in addition to climate change, is causing a shift from current peak fire seasons, in addition to increasing the frequency of fire [\(McLoughlin, 1998; Williams et al., 2001; Cary](#page-6-13) [et al., 2006; Enright et al., 2015\)](#page-6-13). The threats caused by altered fire regimes may not only affect the persistence of those plant species that are already threatened with extinction, but also of many common species. Such common species may be at risk because they possess traits that have little plasticity in relation to projected changes. The most inflexible traits are likely to be those that are not adapted to current environmental conditions, but have ecologically fit well enough to have persisted. Evidence suggests that species composition within ecological communities may be strongly influenced by the relative abilities of species to cope with climate-driven changes ([Suttle et al., 2006\)](#page-6-14).

There is growing evidence that rates of extinction of plant species are increasing, across local and regional scales ([Thomas et al., 2004a;](#page-6-15) [Thuiller et al., 2005](#page-6-15)). This rate is influenced by human population growth, and the associated escalating demands on resources and climate-driven changes ([Gaston, 2005; Hahs et al., 2009](#page-6-16)). Species most at risk by the threat of extinction are those that are already rare, and therefore already limited in abundance and/or distribution [\(Gaston,](#page-6-10) [1994; Wilson et al., 2004](#page-6-10)). Understanding the possible anthropogenic and ecological causes of rarity are therefore crucial to designing and implementing conservation actions. In this study, I investigated postfire recruitment and development over a 16 year period for the species Leucopogon exolasius (F. Muell.) F. Muell. ex Benth. and the closely related common congeners L. setiger R. Br. and L. esquamatus R. Br. The demographic parameters following regeneration were compared between species in order to determine any potential causes of rarity for one of them, the threatened L. exolasius. All three species inhabit the fire-prone temperate sandstone vegetation around the Sydney region in south-eastern Australia, occurring on similar soil types and in similar micro-climates. The vegetation here is adapted to fire and there is a mean natural wildfire return interval ranging from approximately 14 to 20 years, a similar interval to shrublands in Mediterranean-climate regions in southwestern Australia [\(Miller and Murphy, 2018](#page-6-17)). Fires occur primarily in the hot late spring and summer periods (approximately November to February). The Sydney sandstone basin is one of several centres of high species richness and endemism on the Australian continent ([Crisp et al., 2001](#page-6-18)), but also highly urbanised. Prescribed fires are therefore implemented regularly to reduce fuel loads and protect assets, as well as for ecological purposes such as the conservation of biodiversity [\(Penman et al., 2011\)](#page-6-19).

Because limited abundance or distribution of plant species are

unlikely to be attributed to a single factor, investigations into several critical biological traits and life-history stages are the most likely to highlight limiting processes [\(Rabinowitz et al., 1984; Bevill and Louda,](#page-6-20) [1999\)](#page-6-20). Part of the benefit of using a small number of species in a comparative study, is that a larger number of factors may be examined with relative ease, and species can also be more easily selected to control for phylogenetic relatedness [\(Kunin and Gaston, 1993; Walck](#page-6-9) [et al., 2001\)](#page-6-9). Additionally, understanding demographic responses to environmental disturbance is crucial in habitats situated on the urban interface where the numbers of implemented fires are increasing ([McLoughlin, 1998\)](#page-6-13) and climate change is projected to drive changes to fire season and frequency [\(Williams et al., 2001; Cary et al., 2006;](#page-7-1) [Enright et al., 2015](#page-7-1)). I therefore assessed the demographic responses measured in the context of the fire regime to identify potential limiting traits. Specifically, I wanted to address the following questions:

- (1) How do key life-history stages of the three Leucopogon study species differ, and what are their responses to the fire regime, particularly season?
- (2) Can predicted changes to the fire regime potentially affect the persistence of the rare or common species studied?
- (3) Are there any identifiable factors that limit Leucopogon exolasius?

# 2. Materials and methods

# 2.1. Study species and sites

The Ericaceae family occurs in a number of habitats throughout the world floras including in South Africa and the Mediterranean Basin ([Ojeda et al., 1997\)](#page-6-21). In Australia, members compromise a significant part of the understorey in fire-prone plant communities. Leucopogon (Ericaceae) is a large genus consisting of about 230 species. This fireprone region of south-eastern Australia contains approximately 2000 plant species [\(Auld et al., 2000](#page-6-22)), and unlike its Mediterranean-type climate counterparts, has an aseasonal rainfall climate with no pronounced dry season, which may have consequences for the post-fire recovery of species with innate seasonal germination requirements ([Ooi, 2010](#page-6-23)). The three study species are all obligate-seeding woody shrubs with soil-stored seed banks ([Ooi et al., 2006a,b; 2007\)](#page-6-24). Although they do not co-occur at the same sites, they inhabit adjoining heath and woodland vegetation types, and have overlapping ranges. Leucopogon fruit are drupes and fresh exocarps of both L. exolasius and L. setiger are fleshy, while the endocarp is hard and lignified. Leucopogon esquamatus exocarp is papery and the endocarp comparatively more fibrous than hard [\(Ooi et al., 2006a\)](#page-6-24).

Leucopogon exolasius is an erect shrub that grows to approximately 2 m tall, and is a threatened species listed as 'vulnerable' both under the national Australian Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act (1999), and under the state of New South Wales (NSW) Threatened Species Conservation Act (1995). The species is endemic to the southern Sydney region of NSW and is restricted to approximately 14 known populations. It occurs in woodlands, and is restricted particularly to riverbank areas punctuated with outcropping sandstone. Leucopogon setiger, morphologically very similar to L. exolasius, is an erect shrub also approximately 2 m tall, and is distributed more widely ([Table 1](#page-2-0)), extending from the central western slopes of NSW to the coast. It is found in woodlands and open forest. Leucopogon esquamatus is a slender shrub, which grows to approximately 1 m tall. It is also widespread, occurring from the coast to the mountains (as for L. setiger), but extending south into the states of Victoria and Tasmania ([Table 1](#page-2-0)). It occurs in heath, woodlands and open forests. Taxonomy follows [Harden](#page-6-25) [\(1992\).](#page-6-25) Geographic distribution of each species were calculated using [IUCN \(2012\)](#page-6-26) criteria for extent of occurrence, which is defined as the area contained within the shortest continuous imaginary boundary which can be drawn to encompass all known sites of occurrence of a species.

######## PDF PAGE 1 ########
Aust. J. Bot., 1983, 31, 293-6

# Relationship between Time Since the Last Fire and Flowering in *Telopea speciosissima* R. Br. and *Lambertia formosa* Sm.

*Graham H. Pyke*

The Australian Museum, 6-8 College St, Sydney, N.S.W., 2000.

## Abstract

For *Telopea speciosissima* the percentage (or density) of plants in flower, the average number of flowers per inflorescence and the average number of fruits per inflorescence all appear to peak 2 years after a summer fire and decline thereafter. On the other hand, the average height of the inflorescences above the ground increases with time since the last fire. For *Lambertia formosa* the density of inflorescences appears to reach a peak 2 or 3 years after a summer fire.

## Introduction

The effects of fire on the Australian flora are many and are increasingly well studied (see Gill *et al.* 1981). There appears, however, to be little quantitative information on the relationships between time since the last fire and flowering of Australian plants (Gill 1981; Specht 1981). Only for *Xanthorrhoea australis* is there a well established relationship (Specht *et al.* 1958; Garnet 1971; Gill and Ingwersen 1976; Gill 1981): in some places this species flowers only rarely in the absence of fire (Specht *et al.* 1958; Garnet 1971).

The aim of this paper is to analyse spatial and temporal variation in flowering of *Telopea speciosissima* (waratah) and *Lambertia formosa* with respect to time since the last fire. This analysis is possible as a result of studies on the pollination biology of these plants and the foraging ecology of honeyeaters that visit them for nectar (Pyke 1980, 1981*a*, 1981*b*).

## Methods

The data presented were collected between December 1979 and December 1981 in the Brisbane Water National Park (lat. 33°32′22″S., long. 151°16′56″E.; elevation 170 m above sea level) and Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park (lat. 33°36′18″S., long. 151°16′16″E.; elevation 145 m above sea level). In each region, study sites are located in plateau-type, low open-forest (Benson and Fallding 1981) dominated by *Eucalyptus gummifera* (Gaertn.) Hochr., *E. haemastoma* Sm. and *E. oblonga* DC., with a shrub understory composed mainly of *Lambertia formosa* Sm. Both regions are located on plateau tops and hence all study sites have the same aspect. In both regions soils are deep, yellow and earthy (Benson and Fallding 1981) with no apparent differences between the study sites.

The Brisbane Water study site contains two areas in terms of fire history: one area last burnt in December 1976, the other in December 1979. The two areas are separated by a vehicle trail which stopped the more recent fire from spreading further. There are no apparent differences between the two areas in terms of soil or vegetation. The entire Ku-ring-gai Chase study site last burnt in 1965.

Flowering in *Telopea speciosissima* has been recorded in two ways. In the 1976 burn study area in Brisbane Water National Park, the total number of flowering plants was recorded for the spring flowering periods of 1979, 1980 and 1981. For each inflorescence

0067-1924/83/030293$02.00

######## PDF PAGE 2 ########
294 G. H. Pyke

the total number of flowers, height above the ground and number of fruits were also recorded. In each year peak flowering occurred about mid September with high synchrony among plants. In this area and in the other two study areas, permanent circular plots of 20 m radius were established and the numbers of flowering plants within these circles counted every 3 weeks during spring 1981. The numbers of non-flowering plants in each circle were also recorded for spring 1981. Flowering in *Lambertia formosa* was recorded by counting the number of inflorescences in each circle during spring 1981 and in two of the present Brisbane Water circles during spring 1980. During spring 1981, there were four circles in the Brisbane Water area of the 1976 fire, two in the area of the 1979 fire and two in the Ku-ring-gai Chase area.

## Results

### *Flowering of* Telopea *in Successive Years*

In the Brisbane Water area which last burnt in December 1976, the total number of flowering *Telopea* plants has declined dramatically since spring 1979 (Table 1). Since spring

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1976 fire | Spring 1979 | 306 | 79·5±0·9 | 162·4±2·5 | 2·45±0·11 |
| 1976 fire | Spring 1980 | 100 | 64·9±1·4 | 186·0±3·4 | 0·86±0·11 |

# Relationship between Time Since the Last Fire and Flowering in *Telopea speciosissima* R. Br. and *Lambertia formosa* Sm.

*Graham H. Pyke*

The Australian Museum, 6-8 College St, Sydney, N.S.W., 2000.

## Abstract

For *Telopea speciosissima* the percentage (or density) of plants in flower, the average number of flowers per inflorescence and the average number of fruits per inflorescence all appear to peak 2 years after a summer fire and decline thereafter. On the other hand, the average height of the inflorescences above the ground increases with time since the last fire. For *Lambertia formosa* the density of inflorescences appears to reach a peak 2 or 3 years after a summer fire.

## Introduction

The effects of fire on the Australian flora are many and are increasingly well studied (see Gill *et al.* 1981). There appears, however, to be little quantitative information on the relationships between time since the last fire and flowering of Australian plants (Gill 1981; Specht 1981). Only for *Xanthorrhoea australis* is there a well established relationship (Specht *et al.* 1958; Garnet 1971; Gill and Ingwersen 1976; Gill 1981): in some places this species flowers only rarely in the absence of fire (Specht *et al.* 1958; Garnet 1971).

The aim of this paper is to analyse spatial and temporal variation in flowering of *Telopea speciosissima* (waratah) and *Lambertia formosa* with respect to time since the last fire. This analysis is possible as a result of studies on the pollination biology of these plants and the foraging ecology of honeyeaters that visit them for nectar (Pyke 1980, 1981*a*, 1981*b*).

## Methods

The data presented were collected between December 1979 and December 1981 in the Brisbane Water National Park (lat. 33°32′22″S., long. 151°16′56″E.; elevation 170 m above sea level) and Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park (lat. 33°36′18″S., long. 151°16′16″E.; elevation 145 m above sea level). In each region, study sites are located in plateau-type, low open-forest (Benson and Fallding 1981) dominated by *Eucalyptus gummifera* (Gaertn.) Hochr., *E. haemastoma* Sm. and *E. oblonga* DC., with a shrub understory composed mainly of *Lambertia formosa* Sm. Both regions are located on plateau tops and hence all study sites have the same aspect. In both regions soils are deep, yellow and earthy (Benson and Fallding 1981) with no apparent differences between the study sites.

The Brisbane Water study site contains two areas in terms of fire history: one area last burnt in December 1976, the other in December 1979. The two areas are separated by a vehicle trail which stopped the more recent fire from spreading further. There are no apparent differences between the two areas in terms of soil or vegetation. The entire Ku-ring-gai Chase study site last burnt in 1965.

Flowering in *Telopea speciosissima* has been recorded in two ways. In the 1976 burn study area in Brisbane Water National Park, the total number of flowering plants was recorded for the spring flowering periods of 1979, 1980 and 1981. For each inflorescence

# **INTRODUCTION**

The natural fire regimes of the treeless high mountain vegetation of Australia are difficult to quantify, and the role of fire in the dynamics of alpine and subalpine vegetation in Australia is largely unknown. At the landscape scale (that of square kilometres or more), fire appears to be relatively rare in these environments (Kirkpatrick & Dickinson 1984; Leigh *et al*. 1987; Wimbush & Forrester 1988; Williams & Costin 1994). Given that few fires have occurred in alpine and subalpine vegetation, knowledge of post-fire ecology, especially initial impacts and early responses, in alpine and treeless subalpine vegetation is also scant.

Aboriginal people utilized the high country, but little is known about their use of fire there. Good evidence exists for fire-stick farming in lowlands surrounding high mountains, but there is little evidence for the extensive use of fire, or even the need to use fire extensively, in the treeless vegetation (Flood 1980). Prior to European settlement, landscape-scale fires are likely to have occurred in high mountain treeless vegetation in mainland Australia only once or twice per century (Leigh *et al*. 1987). European settlement in and around the high country commenced in the mid-19th century. Prescribed burning was used by pastoralists in the late 19th and early 20th centuries to improve the quality of green pick, and miners used fire to clear undergrowth to expose geological features (Costin

# Early post-fire regeneration in subalpine heathland and grassland in the Victorian Alpine National Park, south-eastern Australia

C-H. A. WAHREN,1† W. A. PAPST2‡ AND R. J. WILLIAMS<sup>3</sup> \*

1 *Department of Agricultural Sciences, La Trobe University, Victoria,* <sup>2</sup> *Centre for Land Protection Research, Bendigo, Victoria and* <sup>3</sup> *CSIRO Sustainable Ecosystems, PMB 44, Winnellie Northern Territory 0822, Australia (Email: dick.williams@terc.csiro.au)*

**Abstract** Landscape fire (at the scale of square kilometres or more) is relatively rare in the alpine and subalpine environments of Australia. In early 1998, a major fire (the 'Caledonia Fire'), burnt approximately 35 000 ha, of which approximately 3000 hectares was subalpine heathland, grassland and wetland within the Victorian Alpine National Park. This fire was one of only three landscape-scale fires that have occurred anywhere in the treeless vegetation of the Victorian Alps in the past 100 years, the others being in 1939 and 1985. Monitoring of regeneration in subalpine vegetation commenced 3 weeks postfire. Sites were established in burnt grassland at Holmes Plain (1400 m a.s.l.) and burnt grassland and heathland at Wellington Plain (1480 m a.s.l.), and in unburnt grassland at both sites. In burnt grassland and heathland, the fire consumed much of the vegetation, leaving extensive areas of bare ground. The cover of dense vegetation declined from > 70% prefire, to approximately 15% immediately postfire. Bare ground at the Holmes and Wellington Plains sites ranged from 70% to 85% immediately postfire. By May 2000, approximately 2.5 years postfire, dense vegetation cover in grassland had increased to approximately 20%, and bare ground had decreased to an average of approximately 30%. In unburnt grassland, dense vegetation cover was generally > 95%, and the amount of bare ground less than 5%. The tussock-forming snow grasses resprouted vigorously following fire, and had 

**Key words**: alpine, bare ground, biomass, Caledonia Fire, catchment protection, disturbance, fire regime, litter, vegetation cover.

Accepted for publication May 2001.

<sup>\*</sup>Corresponding author.

Present address: Boreal Ecology Cooperative Research Unit, University of Alaska Fairbanks, Alaska USA.

Present address: Department of Agricultural Sciences, La Trobe University, Victoria, Australia.

{1}

######## PDF PAGE 3 ########
1954; Carr & Turner 1959a; Lawrence 1999). These practices all increased the frequency of fire in alpine and subalpine vegetation (Pryor 1939; Stretton 1946; Raeder-Roitzsch & Phillips 1958; Leigh *et al*. 1987; Banks 1989; Kershaw & Strickland 1989; Lawrence 1999). On mainland Australia, prescribed fire in treeless subalpine and alpine vegetation was banned in the 1940s and 1950s, as its use was linked clearly to land degradation in the high mountain catchments (Australian Academy of Science 1957; Costin *et al*. 1959; Williams & Costin 1994).

In Victoria, there are few detailed data on the occurrence of fires and their effects on alpine and subalpine plant communities. Extensive fires in treeless vegetation are known to have occurred on two occasions in the 20th century. According to Carr & Turner (1959a) '. . . small fires spread onto the high plains from the neighbouring slopes prior to 1939, such as in 1926, but these fires were of minor importance'. In contrast, the State-wide fires of 1939 burnt approximately 80% of the snow gum country on the Bogong High Plains above approximately 1500 m a.s.l. (Carr & Turner 1959a). Although these fires burnt much treeless subalpine and alpine vegetation, that is, heathland, grassland, and wetland (Carr & Turner 1959a), we do not know the precise extent or severity of these fires. In 1985, a fire at Mount Buffalo burnt approximately 11 000 ha of lowland and forested foothill vegetation, and approximately 150 ha of treeless subalpine heathland, grassland and wetland (Wahren *et al*. 1999). The subject of the present paper is an extensive fire that occurred in the south-eastern parts of the Victorian Alpine National Park in January 1998: the 'Caledonia Fire'.

Subsequent to the last glaciation, Australian alpine environments have evolved in response to relatively small-scale disturbances (1 m<sup>2</sup> –1 ha) such as localized frost heave, wind blasting and insect herbivory. Larger scale disturbances such as fire and extensive grazing by large vertebrate herbivores over square kilometres of country are rare or non-existent (Williams 1990; Williams & Costin 1994). Under such a native regime of small-scale disturbances, Australian alpine environments are characterized by a high cover of vegetation (normally close to 100%) and relatively little exposed bare soil (< 1–2%; Australian Academy of Science 1957; Costin 1958; Williams & Costin 1994). The removal of vegetation and litter by fire, and the consequent exposure of bare soil, has major implications in Australian alpine landscapes, because exposure of alpine soils is undesirable for soil conservation purposes, and subsequent regeneration to adequate soil cover is slow (Wahren *et al*. 1994; Williams & Costin 1994).

In the present paper, we summarize the early postfire changes in vegetation and ground cover conditions that have occurred in grassland and heathland on Holmes and Wellington Plains, two of the larger high plains burnt in the Caledonia Fire (Fig. 1). We focus on the first 2 years post-fire because there have been no detailed, quantitative studies of early post-fire responses in Australian alpine landscapes following fires of such magnitude. The specific aim is to document the changes in vegetation cover, the amount of bare ground, and changes to gaps that have occurred in grassland and heathland over the first 2 years post-fire. Both communities are extensive in treeless high mountain environments in Australia. Within each, the amount of bare ground and both the quality and quantity of vegetation cover, and the nature of gaps created by the death of grass tussocks or shrubs, are critical determinants of both vegetation change and landscape condition in Australian high mountain landscapes (Wahren *et al*. 1994; Williams & Costin 1994).

#### **Fire and study sites**

The Caledonia Fire started on 31 December 1997, from an abandoned campfire on the Caledonia River, in mixed lowland eucalypt forest. 1 January 1998 was a day of extreme fire weather: the predicted forest fire danger index (Luke & McArthur 1978) for the nearby town of Heyfield was 50 (Tolhurst 1998). Fire weather and drought conditions at this time were broadly similar to those of other years in the past century when widespread fires occurred in Victoria: 1983, 1967, 1964, 1939 and 1926 (McCarthy & Tolhurst 2000). The fire burnt approximately 35 000 ha of the Carey Forest, of which approximately 22 000 ha was within the Alpine National Park, and approximately 3000 ha was treeless subalpine vegetation.

The landscape above approximately 1400 m is a mosaic of high ridges, wooded slopes, rolling grassy plains and wetlands. The treeless plains and surrounding snow gum (*Eucalyptus pauciflora*) woodlands have been grazed during summer and autumn by free ranging cattle since the late 19th century and cattle were present at the time of the fire. Sporadic grazing continued for 3 months post-fire, but grazing was excluded from the fire-affected area for the 1998–1999 and 1999–2000 seasons.

The fires were intense crown fires in both the eucalypt forests of the foothills and the subalpine snow gum woodlands. In the treeless vegetation, fire intensity was unknown, but field observations indicated that the fire at Wellington Plain was more intense and burnt more of the vegetation than at Holmes Plain. At Holmes and Wellington Plains, > 90% of the grassland, heathland and snow gum woodlands were burnt, and the subalpine bogs were also extensively burnt. This represents the most extensive fire in alpine and subalpine vegetation since 1939 (McCarthy & Tolhurst 2000).

{2}

######## PDF PAGE 4 ########
# **METHODS**

#### **Monitoring sites**

At the end of January 1998, 3 weeks after the fire, monitoring sites were established at Holmes Plain (146°45-14--E, 37°24-32--S; 1400 m a.s.l.) and Wellington Plain (146°49-54--E, 37°29-46--S; 1480 m a.s.l.). These plains were selected because they were representative of the extensive subalpine high plains in this region of the Victorian Alps (Walsh *et al*. 1984, 1986) and, in the case of Holmes Plain, because two sites had been established in grassland in 1991 as part of a general monitoring program in the high country. At both sites, the soil was alpine humus soil, a wellstructured organic loam that is acid, nutrient poor, and is typical of most alpine and subalpine grasslands and heathlands in mainland Australia (Williams & Costin 1994). One of these sites was burnt, the other was outside the fire perimeter; both sites were used for the present study. Extra sites were established in burnt heathland and grassland at both Holmes and Wellington Plains, and in an unburnt area of grassland at Wellington Plain, close to the burnt grassland. This unburnt grassland was within the fire perimeter. Using this network of sites, the changes in the burnt grassland over time could be compared with those in longunburnt grassland. Unfortunately, there were no suitable unburnt heathland sites.

# **Estimation of ground cover and biomass**

# **Post-fire regeneration**

#### *Changes in vegetation cover and biomass*

In burnt grassland, both at Holmes and Wellington Plains, and in burnt heathland at Wellington Plain, CC1 increased significantly, and CC3 decreased significantly over the 2.5-year study period, with most of the changes occurring in the first 18 months post-fire. There was a significant change in both CC1 and CC3 between February 1998 and May 1999, but between May 1999 and May 2000, there was little or no significant change in the average value of either cover class across sites (Fig. 2a). Similarly, there were significant changes in the cover classes in both grassland and heathland at Wellington Plain between January 1998 and May 1999, but relatively little change between May 1999 and May 2000 (Fig. 2b). By May 2000, the average CC3 in burnt grassland was 35% at Holmes Plain (Fig. 2a) and 25% at Wellington Plain (Fig. 2b). The respective figures for CC1 were 23 and 36%. In burnt heathland at Wellington Plain, average CC3 in May 2000 was 53%, and average CC1 was 16% (Fig. 2b).

The post-fire increase in vegetation cover at both Holmes and Wellington Plains was primarily due to the rapid resprouting of snow grass tussocks and forbs (Figs 3a,4). The cover of *Poa* increased rapidly postfire in both grassland and heathland. At Holmes Plain it was 84% by January 1999 (Fig. 3a); at Wellington

Plain it was approximately 65% in grassland by May 1999, and 55% in heathland (Fig. 4a,b). *Poa* cover remained at or near these levels at both sites until May 2000. This cover was almost completely due to surviving tussocks resprouting post-fire, rather than seedling establishment and growth. The rapid resprouting of the snow grasses was accompanied by pyrogenic flowering, which commenced in the year following the fire and occurred in virtually all tussocks. Forbs also re-established rapidly from perennating subterranean organs or seedlings. Forb cover was approximately 40% by January 1999 at both grassland sites, and by December 1999 at the heathland site (Figs 3a,4). Most forb cover was provided by *Asperula gunnii, Craspedia* spp. and *Leptorhynchos squamatus*. Some, such as *Bracteantha subundulata* and *Podolepis robusta*, occurred in distinct patches of 0.5–3 m<sup>2</sup> .

In contrast to the rapid regeneration of snow grasses and forbs, shrubs in the heathland of Wellington Plain were slow to regenerate (Fig. 4b). # **INTRODUCTION**

The natural fire regimes of the treeless high mountain vegetation of Australia are difficult to quantify, and the role of fire in the dynamics of alpine and subalpine vegetation in Australia is largely unknown. At the landscape scale (that of square kilometres or more), fire appears to be relatively rare in these environments (Kirkpatrick & Dickinson 1984; Leigh *et al*. 1987; Wimbush & Forrester 1988; Williams & Costin 1994). Given that few fires have occurred in alpine and subalpine vegetation, knowledge of post-fire ecology, especially initial impacts and early responses, in alpine and treeless subalpine vegetation is also scant.

EOF

1	## n_pages=30
2	
3	######## PDF PAGE 1 ########
4	# REGENERATION OF SOME FOREST AND GULLY COMMUNITIES IN THE ANGAHOOK-LORNE STATE PARK (NORTH-EASTERN OTWAY RANGES) 1-10 YEARS AFTER THE WILDFIRE OF FEBRUARY 1983
5	
6	MARGARET C. WARK
7	
8	Angair Incorporated (Anglesea and Aireys Inlet Society for the Protection of Flora & Fauna), PO Box 12, Anglesea, Victoria 3230, Australia
9	
10	WARK, M. C., 1997:11:30. Regeneration of some forest and gully communities in the Angahook-Lorne State Park (north-eastern Otway Ranges) 1-10 years after the wildfire of February 1983. *Proceedings of the Royal Society of Victoria* 109 (1): 7-36. ISSN 0035-9211.
11	
12	Forest communities in the Angahook-Lorne State Park near Aireys Inlet include dry sclerophyll open-forest dominated by 18 m tall *Eucalyptus tricarpa* and various gully complexes. The number of plant species per community ranges from 43-130 and reflects differences in moisture, soils and topography.
13	
14	Following the wildfire of February 1983, 77% of all species of vascular plants present before the fire reappeared within the first year and 98% (all but two species) returned within three years. The two species which did not reappear by year 3 (*Amyema pendulum* and *Hymenophyllum cupressiforme*) had still not returned by year 10.
15	
16	Maximum post-fire species richness of vascular plants occurred in the early years after fire, then decreased by year 10 as vascular plant cover increased. In contrast, maximum post-fire species richness of non-vascular plants occurred 10 years after fire as canopy and understorey cover increased. Extensive carpets of two minerotrophic bryophytes (*Marchantia berteroana* and *Funaria hygrometrica*) and the fungus *Gerronema postii* appeared in damper areas of all communities during the first year after fire, and were not seen after year 3.
17	
18	Approximately 62% of all vascular species which appeared in the first 3 years after fire, and still remained at year 10, had the capacity to regenerate vegetatively (or both vegetatively and from seed). The other 38% of vascular species regenerated from seed only.
19	
20	The canopy in all communities recovered between 3 and 10 years reaching approximate pre-fire height and cover levels. Rate of recovery was faster in gully complexes than in drier *E. tricarpa* open-forest.
21	
22	Seventy per cent of all species flowered or produced spores by the end of the third year. Twenty-five per cent of all species of trees and shrubs had not flowered or set seed by year 3, but did so by year 10.
23	
24	Floristic and structural changes were seen in *E. tricarpa* open-forest where the previously open grassy understorey of *Poa sieberiana* (0.2 m tall) was replaced by a dense (4.0 m tall) understorey of fire induced or 'hard-seeded' shrubs including *Acacia verticillata*, *Goodenia ovata* and *Pultenaea daphnoides*.
25	
26	Major floristic and structural changes also occurred in a gully complex where a peat fire was ignited by the wildfire and burnt to a depth of over 2 m for 3.5 months after the wildfire. Here the *Eucalyptus obliqua*/*Cyathea australis*/*Prostanthera lasianthos* complex was completely killed and replaced by seedling eucalypts which, by 10 years post-fire, formed a dense canopy (18 m tall) with no discernible understorey.
27	
28	ON 17 February 1983 (Ash Wednesday) a wildfire burnt approximately 40 000 hectares of vegetation near Anglesea and Aireys Inlet, in the north-eastern Otway Ranges, Victoria (Rawson et al. 1983). Prior to 1983 there had been no published study on the fire ecology of the flora of this area. Following the wildfires, a ten year study of the post-fire recovery of vegetation and fauna was initiated (Reilly 1985, 1991a, 1991b; Wilson & Moloney 1985a, 1985b; Andersen 1987; Wark et al. 1987; Wark 1996).
29	
30	The aims of the botanical study were to describe vegetation regeneration following wildfire in six of the major plant communities in the district (coastal heath, heath woodland, open-forest, sand-dune scrub, swamp thicket and gully complexes), and to provide information for use in the planning of conservation management. Regeneration of the heath and heath woodland communities in the first 10 years after fire has already been described (Wark et al. 1987; Wark 1996).
31	
32	This paper presents data on regeneration of
33

Soils derived from Tertiary Eastern View Formation | No fire for approx. 100 years | Crown fired | F1 | N 0° (bottom of gully beside Distillery Creek) | >90 cm peaty loam | Gully Complex | *Eucalyptus obliqua*, *Cyathea australis*, *Prostanthera lasianthos* | 14.0 | 14.0 | 5, 5 | 0.1 |
43	| F | | No fire for approx. 100 years | Crown fired, then peat fire | F2 | N 0° (bottom of gully) | >90 cm burnt peat | Modified Gully Complex | *Eucalyptus obliqua*, *Eucalyptus willisii* | 14.0 | 5.0 | 2, 5 | 0.1 |
44	
45	*Table 1.* Site descriptions of forest and gully communities. \*Modified by human interference. \*\*Tallest stratum. #ND=not done.
46	
47	######## PDF PAGE 3 ########
48	REGENERATION IN THE ANGAHOOK-LORNE STATE PARK 9
49	
50	*E. tricarpa* open-forest and various gully complexes ten years after the 1983 fire and describes their floristics and structure. Regeneration strategies and post-fire flowering response of species are also described. Mammal, bird and insect data have been studied and reported separately (Reilly 1985, 1991a, 1991b; Wilson & Moloney 1985a, 1985b; Andersen 1987).
51	
52	## SITE DESCRIPTIONS
53	
54	Two sites (E and F) which supported native vegetation, and which were relatively undisturbed by European man (Fig. 1, Table 1), were selected in undulating terrain on soils derived from Tertiary sediments known as the Eastern View Formation (Pitt 1977, 1981). The sites were located 2.5-4.0 km inland from the coast, in the Angahook-Lorne State Park, near Aireys Inlet. Each contained one or more plant communities (subsites), including *Eucalyptus tricarpa* (red Ironbark) open-forest (subsite E1), *E. tricarpa* mixed open-forest (subsite E2), and various gully complexes (subsites E3, F1 and F2). The term open-forest follows Specht (1970), the term 'gully complex' is used because these small riparian communities were very narrow, disjunct and uncommon, and contained varied proportions of broad leaf and sclerophyll vegetation.
55	
56	Subsite E1 was on a north-facing slope. Here the overstorey was an almost pure stand of *E. tricarpa*, generally of a similar age and density. On the adjacent southerly slope (subsite E2) the overstorey eucalypts were of mixed age, density and species and included *E. tricarpa*, *Eucalyptus cypellocarpa*, *Eucalyptus aromaphloia* and others. Both subsites E1 and E2 had light grassy understoreys before the fire (Parsons et al. 1977).
57	
58	Both sites had been affected by timber cutting between 1860 and 1920, and were controlled by the Forests Commission of Victoria between 1921 and 1987. During this second period, understorey reduction and thinning was carried out from time to time, as part of local fire-prevention strategies (P. Denham, pers. comm.). It is not known whether subsites E1 and E2 were affected by these practices.
59	
60	The gully complexes studied were discontinuous, often occurring in narrow bands (max. width 20-50 m) beside semi-permanent streams. All were surrounded by dry sclerophyll open-forest with a eucalypt overstorey. The complex adjacent to the creek running through Ironbark Gorge (subsite E3) occurred on silty soil, and those adjacent to Distillery Creek (subsites F1 and F2) on peaty soil and (after Feb. 1983) burnt peat soil respectively. Overstorey species in these included *Eucalyptus cypellocarpa* and *Eucalyptus obliqua*, varying proportions of the broad-leafed understorey shrubs *Pomaderris aspera* and *Prostanthera lasianthos* and the ferns *Cyathea australis* and *Todea barbara*.
61	
62	[Map: eastern Otway Ranges near Anglesea and Aireys Inlet, sites E and F, burnt area stippled]
63	
64	**Fig. 1.** Locality map showing location of the eastern Otway Ranges, Victoria and sites E and F near Anglesea. Stippling indicates the area burnt on 17 February 1983. The fire advanced from the south west.
65	
66	The previous fire history of each site differed (Table 1). The high-intensity wildfire of February 1983 destroyed all ground strata vegetation and crown-fired the eucalypt overstorey at all subsites (Table 1). The fire occurred following a drought in 1982, which intensified in January, February and March 1983 (in 1982 the total annual rainfall of Anglesea was 452 mm compared with the annual mean of 657 mm). Over 80 mm of rain fell one month after the fire and then at 3, 7 and 8 months post-fire causing soil erosion and hill wash at subsites E1, E2 and E3, and often removing the top 2-4 cm of humus and ash-rich soil of the upper A horizon. Total rainfalls for 1983-1993 were about or above average except for years 1986, 1988, 1990 and 1991, when they were 622, 643, 596 and 614 mm respectively (Wark et al. 1987; Wark 1996).
67	
68	A peat fire, started by the wildfire, established at subsite F2 and gradually burnt the soil in half the gully to a depth of about 2.0 m. It was finally extinguished by early winter rains in June 1983. In the area where this peat fire burnt for 3 months, the ground sank, the creek bank collapsed, and large areas of burnt peat were washed away.
69	
70	######## PDF PAGE 4 ########
71	10 MARGARET C. WARK
72	
73	Because of the extent of the Ash Wednesday fires, no unburnt sites comparable with sites E and F were available for study.
74	
75	## METHODS
76	
77	### Soils
78	
79	*Soil profile data.* Methods of soil description and analysis follow Wark et al. (1987). Surface (0-10 cm) soil samples collected at 2 months and 1 and 2 years after fire were analysed for pH, available P, total Kjeldahl N, organic C, and exchangeable Na, K, Ca and Mg by the State Chemistry Laboratory, Victoria. The A horizon profile was examined at 3 years (by Dr D J Robertson, Wark et al. 1987) by digging pits down to the upper B2 horizon, and recording colour, texture and depth.
80	
81	*Pot experiments.* A bioassay was carried out to assess fertility of black unburnt peat soil from F1 and red burnt soil from F2 using samples collected two years after the wildfire. Seed of *Eucalyptus obliqua* was collected adjacent to subsites F1 and F2. *E. obliqua* seedlings were grown at Aireys Inlet for 8 months on the two soils (1 seedling/75 mm diameter pot, 15 pots/treatment) in a shade house from autumn to spring. Shoot height of each group was measured monthly for 8 months, and mean growth rates determined. After 8 months, dry weight of roots and shoots and root/shoot ratios were determined.
82	
83	### Vegetation
84

Singer (May & Fuhrer 1989); and the herb *Viola hederacea* ssp. *sieberiana* now known to be *Viola cleistogamoides*. 4	# REGENERATION OF SOME FOREST AND GULLY COMMUNITIES IN THE ANGAHOOK-LORNE STATE PARK (NORTH-EASTERN OTWAY RANGES) 1-10 YEARS AFTER THE WILDFIRE OF FEBRUARY 1983
5	
6	MARGARET C. WARK
7	
8	Angair Incorporated (Anglesea and Aireys Inlet Society for the Protection of Flora & Fauna), PO Box 12, Anglesea, Victoria 3230, Australia
9	
10	WARK, M. C., 1997:11:30. Regeneration of some forest and gully communities in the Angahook-Lorne State Park (north-eastern Otway Ranges) 1-10 years after the wildfire of February 1983. *Proceedings of the Royal Society of Victoria* 109 (1): 7-36. ISSN 0035-9211.
11	
12	Forest communities in the Angahook-Lorne State Park near Aireys Inlet include dry sclerophyll open-forest dominated by 18 m tall *Eucalyptus tricarpa* and various gully complexes. The number of plant species per community ranges from 43-130 and reflects differences in moisture, soils and topography.
13	
14	Following the wildfire of February 1983, 77% of all species of vascular plants present before the fire reappeared within the first year and 98% (all but two species) returned within three years. The two species which did not reappear by year 3 (*Amyema pendulum* and *Hymenophyllum cupressiforme*) had still not returned by year 10.
15	
16	Maximum post-fire species richness of vascular plants occurred in the early years after fire, then decreased by year 10 as vascular plant cover increased. In contrast, maximum post-fire species richness of non-vascular plants occurred 10 years after fire as canopy and understorey cover increased. Extensive carpets of two minerotrophic bryophytes (*Marchantia berteroana* and *Funaria hygrometrica*) and the fungus *Gerronema postii* appeared in damper areas of all communities during the first year after fire, and were not seen after year 3.
17	
18	Approximately 62% of all vascular species which appeared in the first 3 years after fire, and still remained at year 10, had the capacity to regenerate vegetatively (or both vegetatively and from seed). The other 38% of vascular species regenerated from seed only.
19	
20	The canopy in all communities recovered between 3 and 10 years reaching approximate pre-fire height and cover levels. Rate of recovery was faster in gully complexes than in drier *E. tricarpa* open-forest.
21	
22	Seventy per cent of all species flowered or produced spores by the end of the third year. Twenty-five per cent of all species of trees and shrubs had not flowered or set seed by year 3, but did so by year 10.
23	
24	Floristic and structural changes were seen in *E. tricarpa* open-forest where the previously open grassy understorey of *Poa sieberiana* (0.2 m tall) was replaced by a dense (4.0 m tall) understorey of fire induced or 'hard-seeded' shrubs including *Acacia verticillata*, *Goodenia ovata* and *Pultenaea daphnoides*.
25	
26	Major floristic and structural changes also occurred in a gully complex where a peat fire was ignited by the wildfire and burnt to a depth of over 2 m for 3.5 months after the wildfire. Here the *Eucalyptus obliqua*/*Cyathea australis*/*Prostanthera lasianthos* complex was completely killed and replaced by seedling eucalypts which, by 10 years post-fire, formed a dense canopy (18 m tall) with no discernible understorey.
27	
28	ON 17 February 1983 (Ash Wednesday) a wildfire burnt approximately 40 000 hectares of vegetation near Anglesea and Aireys Inlet, in the north-eastern Otway Ranges, Victoria (Rawson et al. 1983). Prior to 1983 there had been no published study on the fire ecology of the flora of this area. Following the wildfires, a ten year study of the post-fire recovery of vegetation and fauna was initiated (Reilly 1985, 1991a, 1991b; Wilson & Moloney 1985a, 1985b; Andersen 1987; Wark et al. 1987; Wark 1996).
29	
30	The aims of the botanical study were to describe vegetation regeneration following wildfire in six of the major plant communities in the district (coastal heath, heath woodland, open-forest, sand-dune scrub, swamp thicket and gully complexes), and to provide information for use in the planning of conservation management. Regeneration of the heath and heath woodland communities in the first 10 years after fire has already been described (Wark et al. 1987; Wark 1996).

It is not known whether subsites E1 and E2 were affected by these practices.
